About Siemens Digital Industries Software

Siemens Digital Industries Software is a global leader in the growing field of product lifecycle management (PLM),
manufacturing operations management (MOM), and electronic design automation (EDA) software, hardware,
and services. Siemens works with more than 100,000 customers, leading the digitalization of their planning and
manufacturing processes. At Siemens Digital Industries Software, we blur the boundaries between industry
domains by integrating the virtual and physical, hardware and software, design and manufacturing worlds.
With the rapid pace of innovation, digitalization is no longer tomorrow's idea. We take what the future promises
tomorrow and make it real for our customers today. Where today meets tomorrow. Our culture encourages
creativity, welcomes fresh thinking and focuses on growth, so our people, our business, and our customers can
achieve their full potential.

                             Chapter 1
                          Introduction

Welcome to the Questa® Functional Verification suite, a collection of formal-based functional verification
applications from Siemens Digital Industries Software. Questa Functional Verification provides a
complete, integrated environment for the verification of your complex HDL designs using powerful formal
engines, session orchestrators, clock domain modeling, and reset domain modeling.

Questa Functional Verification includes the following domain analysis applications:

  · Questa CDC for clock domain crossing analysis, CDC transfer protocol checking, and CDC-FX
     metastability effects injection.

       · Questa Gate-CDC for clock domain crossing analysis of gate-level netlists.

       · Questa RDC for reset domain crossing, and static and functional reset analysis.

These analysis environments, plus the Questa SIM simulator use a common set of front-end utilities to
compile and maintain design and resource libraries. The Questa Functional Verification products analyze
synthesizable logic, so some variance with simulation is common as with logic synthesis and design
emulation.

Each analyzer comes with a GUI debugger environment for organizing, waiving, and debugging
verification results. These GUI environments are tightly integrated with their verification applications. All
have a common look-and-feel including the Questa SIM GUI environment.

In addition to tabs and windows for organizing source data and running the analyzers, the GUIs provide
useful analysis windows including as source code editors, tree browsers, schematic browsers, waveform
viewers, finite-state-machine viewers and assertion thread viewers. Since their use models are so similar,
once you are familiar with the operation of one GUI environment, you can easily learn how to run the
others.

Compiling Design Libraries                                                                                  

Compiling Design Libraries

The analysis tools and the Questa SIM simulation tools all work off design libraries created with the
Questa SIM compilers. The compilers and supporting utilities provide a "common front end" for design
compilation.

The same setup used for compiling libraries for simulation can be used for the analysis tools with little
modification (see Figure 1).

                                            Figure 1. Compiling Design Libraries

Each analysis tool runs on a compiled image of the design logic plus a static analysis model.

A set of design compilation utilities (vlib, vmap, vlog and vcom) is used to compile the design logic from
source files. Each analysis tool creates its own analysis model--a clock domain or formal model--Figure
2 shows the design compilation utilities. These front-end utilities are used to create and maintain the
compiled design library data. The same utilities and procedures work for all Questa tools.

                                                 Figure 2. Design Compilation

        Preparing a Design Library
        Compiling Design Files

Preparing a Design Library

Before you can compile source code into the work library, you must generate an initial library and prepare
the environment for design compilation.

16                          Questa® CDC User Guide
                                                              Introduction

                                                              Compiling Design Files

                        Figure 3. Preparing the work Library

Procedure

     1. Generate the initial library. For example:

            prompt> vlib work

     2. Map the work directory to the work library.

            prompt> vmap work work

         The name work is the default working library. A library statement (for work) is not needed in the
         source. The work library is the default destination of compiled design units. So, the above mapping
         is not necessary. The vmap command generates a modelsim.ini file in the current run directory.
         The modelsim.ini file sets the library mappings used for simulation by vsim and for compilation/
         analysis by the Questa Verify analysis tools. It also sets the default values for compiler and
         simulator arguments. These default values can be adjusted.

     3. Edit the modelsim.ini default file to adjust the defaults to fit your environment.

            prompt> vim modelsim.ini

         The vcom and vlog compilers have an array of compilation parameters that control exactly how
         source and resource data are compiled. Some of these compilation parameters can be overridden
         at compile time by compiler switches. For example, the 2008 argument to vcom directs the
         compiler to assume VHDL-2008 semantics when compiling source files. Compilation parameters
         that are not overridden with compiler switches assume the "defaults" specified in a modelsim.ini
         file.

Compiling Design Files

After initializing the work design library and setting up the modelsim.ini file, you can compile design files
into the work library.

                                               Figure 4. Compiling Design Files

Questa® CDC User Guide                                        17
Introduction

Compiling Design Files                                                                                       

Procedure

Use vcom to compile VHDL style source files and vlog to compile Verilog style (including SystemVerilog)
source code. For example:

   qverify> vcom -f pci.f
   or
   qverify> vlog dut.v

To compile the Verilog design source files:

   $ vlog verilog_file1 verilog_file2 ...

To compile the VHDL design source files:

   $ vcom VHDL_file1 VHDL_file2 ...

You can use either of the following methods to compile your design source files using qrun within qverify.

· Use qverify with qrun to compile the design source files into a design or resource library.

    Note:
    When the qrun command is specified directly within qverify, the -compile argument is implicitly
    added to the qrun command.

    To compile the Verilog design source file using qrun:
     $ qverify -c -do "qrun verilog_file1 verilog_file2 ..."
    To compile the VHDL design source file using qrun:
     $ qverify -c -do "qrun VHDL_file1 VHDL_file2 ..."
    To compile the list using qrun:
     $ qverify -c -do "qrun -f <file_name>"

· Use qrun within qverify using "custom compile" to compile the design source files.

           Note:
           When using qrun within qverify using "custom compile" to compile the design source files, add
           the -compile argument to the qrun command within external scripts (that is, Makefile) to compile
           only the source files while skipping optimizations and simulation.

  i. Create the Makefile. The following Makefile uses qrun to compile the sub.vhd and top.sv RTL files:

              qrun -sv top.sv -compile

The following replaceable variables in Tcl command syntax statements represent the shown object types:

    · signal: Single-bit register or wire.

    · variable: Expression that can change value at any time.

    · constant: Expression that evaluates to a statically constant value.

       · "string": String enclosed in double-quotes.

When specifying a command from a command syntax statement, substitute for each meta-variable an
HDL identifier, or an expression enclosed in braces, that evaluates to an object of the corresponding type.

Wildcard Pattern Matching

Wildcard pattern matching matches a pattern determined by using the question mark (?) for single
character matches and the asterisk (*) for a collection of characters consisting of zero or more characters.
Wildcard matching is the default.

Regular Expression Pattern Matching

The -regexp option changes the style of pattern matching from wildcard to regular expression matching.
Matches occur when the regular expression exactly matches items in the collection. A backslash (\)
precedes specific characters to be matched in the pattern; square brackets ( [] ) enclose a range or
collection of characters.

Regular expressions have implied string start (^) and string end ($) tokens. For example, to match strings
with the substrings "arb1" use: {.*arb1.*}. Note that {arb1} only matches the string "arb1".

    Note:
    Signals and instance names in VHDL logic and mixed VHDL/SystemVerilog designs use case-
    insensitive matching due to inferred case insensitivity support.

Examples

                             Chapter 2
                          CDC Basics

Most complex designs have more than one clock. Many of these clocks are asynchronous. For these
designs, the logic clocked by each asynchronous clock forms the clock domain for the clock. Logic
entirely inside a clock domain can be verified with the same approach as that for a single-clock design.
However, problems arise from signals that connect logic in different clock domains. Signals that cross
clock domain "boundaries" must be properly synchronized, and they must obey all relevant transfer
protocols. The process of verifying these requirements is called clock domain crossing (CDC) analysis.

But, even properly synchronized CDC signals that obey protocol rules do not guarantee valid functionality.
If any CDC signal does not hold steady during the setup and hold time of its receiving register, then the
register can become metastable--its output can settle at random to a value that is different from the RTL
simulated value.

In effect, data values that cross clock domains can be advanced or delayed randomly relative to RTL
simulation. If the receiving logic is not specifically designed to tolerate these metastability effects, then
functional errors can occur. Unfortunately, standard simulation cannot accurately model metastability in a
design. An extension to standard functional verification is needed to model the effects of metastability in a
design. The CDC-FX product does just that; CDC-FX runs standard simulation with metastability injected
into the circuit.

The method of verifying CDC signals using the CDC compiler and CDC-FX metastability injection
combines static CDC analysis, inference of design intent, assertions from an assertion checker library,
simulation, and CDCFX metastability injection. Refer to "CDC-FX Metastability Injection" on page 313
for additional information.

Questa CDC Methodologies

Questa CDC contains integrated methodologies for verification of complex HDL designs. The goal of
these pre-defined methodologies is to have strategic configurations that target IP, SoC, and FPGA

Questa® CDC User Guide                                                                             27
CDC Basics

Questa CDC Methodologies                                                                                 

designs. Each methodology contains a set of goals that map to common design phases. Each goal
contains a set of commands and directives appropriate for each design phase.

Types of Methodologies

Methodologies are the collection of goals for different types of design, predefined to get ahead on the
project timeline. Questa CDC introduces four types of well-structured, and reusable methodologies, based
on the design type:

    · SoC

       The ever-increasing complexities of SoCs make it difficult for the designers to design all the
       components individually. The Questa CDC predefined SoC methodology contains a superset
       of available goals that progress through Start, Planning, Implementation, and Release phases.
       Pre-designed blocks reduce the project timetomarket and enable reusability for complex
       designs. To view default enabled CDC directives for SoC methodology and goals, see the cdc
       methodology soc reference topic.

    · IP

       Intellectual Property (IP) is the RTL description along with the elements that describe the
       functionality of the design through a process of testing or validation. Testing and verification
       constitute for 70 percent of the total design work. Hence, a set of functional tests that validate the
       design is as important as the design itself. Questa CDC provides a set of pre-defined goals under
       IP methodology that progresses through Start, Planning, Implementation, and Release phases
       of the design. To view default enabled CDC directives for IP methodology and goals, see the cdc
       methodology ip reference topic.

    · FPGA

       FPGAs are fabricated in nanometer technologies with multi-million gate densities, including
       RAMs, embedded processors, multipliers, DSP blocks, analog cells, and high speed input and
       output (I/O) ports. Using HDLs or schematics, Questa CDCs' FPGA methodology captures
       the algorithm to be implemented on FPGA. Depending on the complexity of the design, it
       provides set of pre-defined goals which progress through Start, Planning, Implementation, and
       Release phases. This helps to achieve high performance with short development cycle, and
       consistent results with faster turn-around time. To view default enabled CDC directives for FPGA
       methodology and goals, under various goals, see the cdc methodology fpga reference topic.

28                        Questa® CDC User Guide
                                                          CDC Basics

                                                          Questa CDC Methodologies

                        Figure 5. Types of Methodologies

Goals

Goals are a set of directives configured based on following steps in the design flow:

       · Start -- Contains the initial set of directives and schemes.

       · Planning -- Includes a set of directives to validate that a design is ready to hand off to the
          implementation team for initial place and route planning.

       · Implementation -- Includes a set of directives to validate that a design is ready for synthesis.

       · Release -- Includes the strictest set of directives to validate that a design is ready for final
          release and broader use, such as an IP release, an FPGA commit, or an SoC tape out/tape
          release.

Questa CDC increases the rigor of the commands and directives as the design matures. This increasing
rigor of the goal progression allows designers to incrementally improve their design quality. On further
stages of the design, the designers can select a set of directives that are stricter in both scope and
severity.

Default Methodology

You can choose to specify the methodology while configuring the CDC analysis. However, if you do not
specify a methodology, the tool chooses the SoC methodology along with the Start goal, by default. In
case you choose a methodology but do not specify the goal, the tool uses the Start goal, by default.

Questa® CDC User Guide                                    29
CDC Basics

Questa CDC Methodologies

     1. To run the methodology in batch:
            cdc methodology fpga
          To set the methodology in batch for an FPGA design in the implementation phase:
            cdc methodology fpga -goal implementation

    2. To add the methodology from GUI:
         a. Double-click the Methodology button in the Flow Navigator tab of the GUI. The Flow
              Navigator window will appear.
         b. Select the appropriate option (soc, ip, or fpga) from the Methodology list box.

  This will trigger the [cdc-75] message.

Pathname Softening

Questa CDC supports the portability of compiled source code files through the softening of pathnames.

When multiple users work on a design in a shared environment, each of their relative filepaths may have
a similar directory hierarchy but use a different prefix path. In this situation, environment variables are
commonly used to set the prefix path to a variable representing their respective directory structure. By
default, environment variables are replaced with the fully qualified pathname when compiling the source
code file using vcom or vlog in the qverify shell. With pathname softening, you can set a variable to a path
and configure your setup for a CDC run to maintain this variable through CDC analysis. This allows the
compiled source code and results generated by CDC analysis to be easily ported to another directory
structure.

Pathname softening is useful when multiple users working on a common set of design files that are
maintained in one location (such as a version control system), and an environment variable is used for
the compiled source code files and CDC database results. Users can check out or copy the files to their
individual working directories and configure their setup to use the environment variable, ensuring the
variable is maintained in the compiled source code and through CDC analysis (see example 2).

The pathname softening functionality softens the references to source code files for the following items:

       · Design compilation files (for example, filelist references to source code files)

       · Waiver input files

       · Analysis reports

       · Results in GUI display

Questa® CDC User Guide                                                                            31
CDC Basics

Pathname Softening                                                                                          

    · New waiver declarations

    · Tool-generated log messages

     Note:
     The RTL source file paths are not softened after porting a database that was compiled using
     soften paths, which causes either of the following situations when re-running CDC in the GUI:
       · For RTL with relative paths, the RTL source files are shown in the GUI with the relative paths

         and re-running CDC in the GUI generates an error that the RTL does not exist.
       · For RTL with full paths, the RTL source files are shown in the GUI with the full (original) paths

         and re-running CDC in the GUI uses the RTL data from the original location.

    Note:
    For other user input files (such as TCL, SDC, or other user input files), the paths are softened
    only if absolute path is added and are not softened for relative paths.

         Note:
         Currently, the UCDB database file (cdc.ucdb) cannot be softened.

The requirements for using pathname softening are:

       · Set the SOFTEN_ENV_VAR_PATH variable to enable pathname softening. For example:

            $ setenv SOFTEN_ENV_VAR_PATH 1

       · Define the environment variable(s) in the shell or a setup Tcl file. The variable_name must consist
          solely of alphanumeric characters and may contain underscores (_). For example:

            $ setenv <variable_name> <path>

       · In the CDC setup Tcl file, use configure environment to specify the environment variable name
          and path to set it within the qverify shell. The syntax for configure environment is:

            configure environment variable_name path

          The variable_name must match the name specified in the shell or setup Tcl file.
          If configure environment is specified multiple times with the same variable name, then the
          variable name specified by the last setting overrides any previously specified settings.
          For example, if the CDC setup specifies the following, then only the path /home/mike/
          design_examples/top_module/dut.v is softened to $MY_PATH/top_module/dut.sv.

            configure environment MY_PATH /home/jane/design_examples/
            configure environment MY_PATH /home/mike/design_examples/

            configure environment soften_paths MY_PATH

32                  Questa® CDC User Guide
                        CDC Basics

                        Pathname Softening

  · In the CDC setup Tcl file, use configure environment soften_paths to specify the environment
     variable(s) that should be used for the softening of paths within the qverify shell. Multiple
     environment variables, separated by a space, can be specified. The syntax for "configure
     environment soften_paths" is:

       configure environment soften_paths variable_name1 variable_name2 ...

  Note:
  If multiple "configure environment soften_paths" directives are specified, the last one wins
  and the others will be ignored.

       · If multiple users are using pathname softening to work on the same design, then the same
          variable name must be used to define the relative path for each user.

       · When relocating a results database to another location, both the CDC database file (cdc.db) and
          qcache directory must be placed in the same parent directory. Attempting to open the database
          file without the qcache directory reports the following error:

            Failed to restore db/project file <path>/cdc.db. Please make sure that
              the corresponding qcache directory is available in the parent path of
              db file.

CDC Design Issues

CDC verification initially ensures that all appropriate CDC signals have correct synchronization logic. But,
CDC verification really addresses the larger question of whether or not the CDC synchronization logic
prevents data corruption across clock domains.
For example, even for a design that has correct synchronizers on all signals, you must consider questions
such as:

       · What happens if the CDC signals are changing when the handshake signal indicates they are
          stable?

       · Does the gray-code logic on a multiple bit bus using 2FF synchronization have a bug?

       · Does the input to a data synchronizer change in two successive clock cycles of the receiving
          domain?

       · What happens when multiple CDC signals are recombined and used together in the receiving
          domain?

Problems such as these often do not cause simulations to fail; instead, they commonly manifest as
intermittent post-silicon failures.
To protect against these types of failures (and ensure CDC problems are addressed early in the design
process), you can use the CDC verification methodology that consists of a three-pronged approach as
follows:

       · Static CDC analysis with the CDC compiler.

       · Assertion-based verification with CDC protocol checkers.

       · Metastability effects analysis with CDC-FX metastability injected simulation.

36                 Questa® CDC User Guide
                        CDC Basics

                        Clock Domains

Clock Domains

A clock domain is a section of a design that has a clock asynchronous to (or which has a variable phase
relationship to) another clock in the design.

For example, suppose one clock is derived from another clock through a clock divider. These two clocks
have a constant phase relationship; therefore, the two sections of the design that use these clocks are
really part of the same clock domain (Figure 6A). However, suppose two clocks have frequencies of 50
MHz and 33 MHz. These clocks' phase relationships change over time; therefore, they clock two different
clock domains (Figure 6B).

                                       Figure 6. Clock Domains and Clock Dividers

If the primary inputs to a circuit include multiple clocks, then these asynchronous clocks determine
separate clock domains (Figure 7A). If the inputs to a circuit are asynchronous to the circuit itself, then
these asynchronous inputs are in separate clock domains (Figure 7B). Clocks are the clock signals of
registers and the enable signals of latches (when properly identified).

                                          Figure 7. Asynchronous Clock Domains

        Clock Groups

Clock Groups

All the clocks that are part of the same clock domain constitute a clock group. Hence, clock groups
partition all of the clocks in the design. The clock groups identify the various clock domains in the design.

Questa® CDC User Guide                                                                                       37
CDC Basics

Metastability                                                                                    

Metastability

A clock domain crossing (CDC) signal is a signal originating in a clock domain that crosses the boundary
into another domain (whose clock is asynchronous to the original clock) and is then sampled by a register
in that asynchronous clock domain.

When the active edge of a CDC signal's transmit clock is too close to the active edge of the receive
register's clock, metastability occurs if data changes within the setup/hold time. With the TX/RX clock very
close, input to the RX register changes within the setup/hold window, which causes metastability. The
register's output settles to an unpredictable value. Metastability can occur if the clocks are asynchronous,
or if they are synchronous but have unpredictable or drifting skews. Every type of bi-stable storage
element is susceptible to metastability. Logic subject to metastability must be designed to "tolerate" its
effects.

The effects of metastability are unpredictable in hardware as the output signal can settle randomly
to 1 or 0. However, RTL simulation provides predictable results. As a result, RTL simulation does not
accurately model the hardware implementation when metastability is present. To ensure a circuit design is
immune to metastability effects, functional verification methods must incorporate technology beyond RTL
simulation.

To design circuits that tolerate the effects of metastability, you must understand: How registers
in hardware exhibit metastability and how registers function in simulation when the conditions for
metastability are present.

        Metastability in Hardware
        Metastability in Standard RTL Simulation
        CDC-FX Injected RTL Simulation

Metastability in Hardware

In hardware, a register value is metastable when its input signal changes value in the transmit domain too
close to the time the signal is sampled in the receive domain.

Consider the 1-bit CDC signal s that is sampled by the flip-flop DFF in Figure 8. Since s comes from a
different clock domain, its value can change at any time with respect to the DFF clock (clk). If the value of
s is not held constant at 0 or 1 during the DFF setup and hold time, then the output (q) might assume an
intermediate voltage for an indeterminate amount of time. Then, q settles randomly to either 0 or 1. The
flip-flop is said to be metastable for that interval.

                                                 Figure 8. Metastable Flip-Flop

The following mean-time-between-failure (MTBF) formula predicts how often metastability occurs:

38             Questa® CDC User Guide
                        CDC Basics

                        Metastability in Standard RTL Simulation

Metastability in Standard RTL Simulation

Standard RTL simulation models metastability in single-bit registers predictably.
For example:

       · If the simulated input switches value before the simulated clock edge, then the simulated output
          switches value at the clock edge.

       · If the simulated input switches value after the simulated clock edge, then the simulated output
          does not switch value.

Therefore, for both setup time and hold time violations, two results are possible as follows:

       · The hardware output value matches the value predicted by simulation.

       · The hardware value differs from the value predicted by simulation.
Figure 9 shows the resulting four metastability scenarios. Comparing hardware with RTL simulation
behavior: When a setup time violation occurs, the hardware transition is delayed randomly by one cycle.
When a hold time violation occurs, the hardware transition is advanced randomly by one cycle.
Note that metastability models can be generalized for multibit registers by treating them as aggregate
single-bit registers.

Questa® CDC User Guide  39
CDC Basics

Metastability in Standard RTL Simulation                                                                    

            Figure 9. Four Metastability Scenarios

Pseudorandom Delay Insertion

A common method of modeling metastability in standard RTL simulation is to introduce pseudorandom
delays in CDC signals at the synchronizers. For example, Figure 10 shows a two-register synchronizer
with a MUX that selects a 3-cycle delayed value (instead of the normal 2-cycle delayed value) in a
pseudorandom manner. End-to-end functional simulation with these types of pseudorandom delays helps
to verify that the design works properly in the presence of CDC metastability.

                    Figure 10. Synchronizer with Pseudorandom 1-Cycle Delay on Output

However, this method has the following limitations:

    · It is incomplete, because it only models two of the four possible metastability scenarios.

    · It models metastability only across synchronized CDC signals.

    · Results are difficult to predict, because metastability is introduced into the simulation at random.

       · Synchronization violations are difficult to debug, because the offending metastability can occur
          any number of cycles before the cycle in which the simulation check first fails (and irrelevant
          metastability can occur along the way).

Clock Jitter

Another method of modeling CDC metastability effects in standard RTL simulation is to jitter the clocks
in simulation and see if end-to-end functional simulation still works when the clock phase relationships

40                                                                   Questa® CDC User Guide
                        CDC Basics

                        CDC-FX Injected RTL Simulation

change. This method is good for verifying that the design works properly in the presence of clock jitter and
clock skews. But, this method does not completely model CDC metastability effects.

CDC-FX Injected RTL Simulation

For metastability injected simulation, circuitry for injecting metastability on a CDC signal or data bus is
inserted between the transmitting register and the first register along the path to the receiver.

For a path without a synchronizer, this is the receiving register itself. For a path with a synchronizer, this is
the first register in the synchronizer (Figure 11).

                                 Figure 11. Metastability Injector for a CDC Data Bus

The compile assertions cdc run option generates the checker logic for running metastability injected
simulation (CDC-FX) . To do this, it adds metastability injection logic for each affected CDC signal or bus
in the following two parts:

       · CDC clocks monitor logic

          Glue logic used to extract load and timing conditions from the circuit.

       · cdc_fx checker

          Checkers that monitor conditions that might cause metastability on a CDC bus and injects
          metastability at the receiver outputs.

The cdc_fx checkers maintain statistics and corner-case counts for the metastability and CDC effects
modeled by the transformed circuit. The cdc_fx checkers have default-off checks (cdc_fx) that fire in
cycles in which metastability might occur (for use on data buses that are presumed to be synchronized
properly).

See "CDC-FX Metastability Injection" on page 313 for additional information.

Synchronizers

Designers generally assume signals are in-band, which means they have a value of either logic 0 or logic
1. Metastable signals can have values that are neither 0 nor 1; therefore, they are considered out-of-
band signals. Out-of-band signals have unexpected effects and propagate unpredictably. To handle CDC
signals, designers fence in potentially metastable logic to ensure logic beyond the fence only needs to
handle in-band signals. The logic inside the fence is called a synchronizer.

Questa® CDC User Guide  41
CDC Basics

Synchronizers                           

               Figure 12. Synchronizer

Metastability manifests as variable delays in transitions of the outputs of registers driven by CDC signals.
Relative to normal simulation, transitions are randomly delayed or advanced. This affects every CDC
signal. Even if a CDC signal or data bus has a synchronizer, the output of the synchronizer is subject to
variable delays. Logic outside the fence in the receiving domain might not interpret receive data correctly
in the presence of variable delays. Such intolerance of metastability effects can lead to functional errors in
hardware, even when normal simulation cannot detect the problem.

Designers implement various types of synchronizers as appropriate for particular situations and design
styles. Logic for each synchronizer type assumes a set of preconditions about the logic connecting
the synchronizer and about the function of the circuit during simulation. Rules for the synchronizer's
connections can be checked during compilation before simulation. Transfer protocols can only be
checked as the circuit operates in simulation. A synchronizer, along with its connection rules and transfer
protocol, is called a synchronization scheme as shown in Figure 13.

                                             Figure 13. Synchronization Scheme

Most CDC implementations use one or more synchronizers from a set of popular, well-characterized
synchronization schemes. These structured synchronizers must follow well-defined connection rules
and should obey specific transfer protocols. CDC identifies clock domains, CDC signals, and structured
synchronizers; and it verifies that the structured synchronizers follow their connection rules. Then, CDC
promotes their transfer protocols to CDC protocol checkers for use with assertion-based simulation and
formal verification.

Any clock domain crossing that does not have a structured synchronizer must be synchronized by custom
logic or software. These ad hoc synchronizers prevent receive registers from sampling CDC signal values
when they are changing. Therefore, the receive register outputs can never go metastable. For example,
an ad hoc synchronizer might use custom logic to control its receive register's load enable signal, or
software might control the loading of a circuit's configuration registers.

Questa CDC reports control signal synchronizers, data bus synchronizers, multibit data synchronizers,
custom synchronizers, and ad hoc synchronizers.

Control Signal Synchronizers

In most technologies related to a 2DFF 1-bit synchronizer, if the first register (R1) becomes metastable,
it almost always settles to 0/1 before the second register (R2) samples its output (q1). The 2DFF
synchronizer is the most commonly used synchronizer for single-bit CDC connections such as individual

                        Synchronizers

control signals. Other structured synchronizers are available, such as the 4-latch synchronizer (similar to
2DFF) and the pulse synchronizer (2DFF with a pulse).

Data Bus Synchronizers

2DFF synchronizers are used for CDC control signals, but not data buses. Control signal synchronization
does not ensure that correlated bits of a bus are transmitted together, since variable delays on any bit of
the bus corrupt the data. Data bus synchronizers ensure that all bits of the bus are transmitted together
and prevents the corruption of data. DMUX, handshake, and FIFO synchronizers are used to synchronize
multibit CDC data in various logic configurations. Questa CDC reports all structured synchronizers.
For many synchronizer types, it promotes protocol checkers that verify the CDC transfer protocols in
simulation and formal verification. DMUX, FIFO, and handshake schemes are examples of data bus
synchronizers.

       · DMUX synchronizer:

Multibit Data Synchronizer

Multibit data synchronizers are used to synchronize multibit signals, but these synchronizers do not
ensure that the bits of a bus are transmitted together. 2DFF synchronizer synchronizes each bit, but only
a single transmit bit at a time should change during any receive clock cycle. If multibit data synchronizers
are used to transmit data bus signals, this synchronizer requires a hamming-distance protocol to prevent
data corruption due to metastability delays.

Custom Synchronizer

Custom synchronizers are special-purpose signal or data synchronizers that you design, specify, and
implement. As custom synchronizers are pre-verified, CDC analysis skips the verification of its internal
structure and verifies only the correct instantiation and use aspects. CDC analysis verifies a custom
synchronizer once during the first instantiation, thus avoiding the need to reverify it on each subsequent
instantiation.

Reconvergence                                                                                               

Reconvergence

Reconvergence is the utilization of separately-propagated correlated information. An example of
reconvergence is information crossing clock domain boundaries that is recombined in the receive logic.

The singular problem with reconvergence is:

     Can you assure that all of the correlated information used at the destination is consistent with the
     information that was transmitted from the source?

CDC signal values might be metastable. Even when proper synchronizers are used, they are subject to
variable delays, which might cause reconverging information to be inconsistent.

Reconvergence occurs in two ways: Local reconvergence -- a single item of information propagates and
is reconstituted in the receive logic, and global reconvergence -- multiple items of information propagate
and are integrated in the receive logic.

An example of local reconvergence is multibit reconvergence of a CDC data bus. Here, a data unit splits
into pieces, crosses a clock domain boundary and then recombines in the receive logic. In the following
example, a reconverged word value is used as the next state of a finite state machine. The individual
bits of the word are synchronized to the receive clock domain, but each bit is subject to variable delays.
As a result, the next_state input to the finite-state machine (FSM) can represent a command that is not
consistent with the current state.

Another example of local reconvergence is multicycle reconvergence of a CDC signal that contains
sequential information transmitted to receive logic. Here, variable delays in the propagated signal can
disturb correlations between consecutive transitions. In the following example, the cdc_s pulse is not
propagated to the receive logic. To avoid problems with multicycle reconvergence, either the transmit

46             Questa® CDC User Guide
                        CDC Basics

                        Reconvergence

logic must not transition data too quickly or the receive logic must tolerate the loss of information in
consecutive cycles.

An example of global reconvergence is a set of data items transmitted across a clock domain boundary
through different synchronizers that are combined in the receive clock domain. Another example of global
reconvergence is the transmission of multiple items of information across a clock domain boundary at
different times using the same synchronizer.

CDC classifies local reconvergence, defined as reconvergence among two or more signals belonging to
the same bus (and no other signal), as reconvergence_bus. If the reconvergence involves two or more
bits of the same bus (local) as well as other scalar signals or bits of other bus signals, then it is classified
as reconvergence_mixed. Reconvergence among scalar signals or bits of different bus signals (explained
as global reconvergence) is classified as reconvergence.

Global and local reconvergence problems in CDC circuits are avoided by using proper synchronizers and
good reconvergence schemes. A good implementation ensures information is always consistent. Either
variable delay data cannot be sampled in the receive domain or the receive domain logic can recover
from variable delayed values. In the following example of a good scheme, an arbiter selects a receive
data value when the corresponding asynchronous FIFO read data value is guaranteed to be ready.

A bad implementation results in unrecoverable errors in simulation or in the hardware implementation. In
the following example of a bad scheme, variable delays can cause the wrong command to be applied to
the data.

Knowing which paths are reconvergent CDC paths is important for assessing reconvergence issues. But
for many multiple-clock architectures, the number of reconvergent CDC paths can be staggering. To help
rank paths for assessment, reconvergent paths can be filtered by several characteristics.

Questa® CDC User Guide                                                                                    47
CDC Basics

Reconvergence Verification                                                                                     

The reconvergence depth of a group of reconvergent CDC paths is the sequential depth from the
synchronizers to the reconvergence point. Sometimes, heuristic information about the functional
characteristics of the circuit can specify a reconvergence depth limit for problems to occur. General
reconvergent CDC paths can start anywhere in the transmit domain. Reconvergent paths that start at
different points can have reconvergence problems. However, single-source reconvergence paths--those
reconvergent paths that start from the same transmit domain source--are characteristically vulnerable
to reconvergence issues. Analogous to general reconvergent CDC paths, each group of single-source
reconvergence paths has a sequential distance (called the divergence depth) from the single source to
the synchronizers.

Reconvergence of two signals might result in synchronization problems. When multiple bits reconverge,
their relative timing is unpredictable. Logic that receives these signals should account for potential cycle
skew--for example, by using a hamming encoding scheme for signals in the receiving domain. For
signals that have large guard times between changes, this encoding happens naturally.

Reconvergence paths are inverted trees starting from Tx "leaf" nodes that are the outputs of
synchronizers for the reconverging crossings and end at the Rx "root," which is the reconvergence point.
CDC reconvergence analysis recognizes all synchronizers (including custom synchronizers) for detecting
these start points. However, some highly complex custom synchronizers with multiple synchronization
through different ports cannot be included in reconvergence analysis.

        Reconvergence Verification

        Reconvergence Methodology

Reconvergence Verification

Simulation alone is not sufficient to verify that a circuit's hardware implementation tolerates metastability
effects and will operate correctly without reconvergence issues. Normal simulation does not model
metastability robustly and completely misses behavior that can manifest in the circuit's hardware
implementation. A multi-faceted approach to CDC verification is necessary for a high degree of
confidence that a particular reconvergence scheme is a good one.

    · Static reconvergence analysis.

       Questa CDC creates static reconvergence reports showing general and single-source
       reconvergence points organized by signature. These reports can uncover reconvergence
       scenarios that might be overlooked.

    · CDC transfer protocol checking.

       Questa CDC identifies structured synchronizers and promotes their CDC transfer protocols to
       CDC assertion checkers for use in simulation and formal verification.

48                          Questa® CDC User Guide
                        CDC Basics

                        Reconvergence Methodology

  · Metastability injected verification.

     CDC-FX identifies registers that can become metastable. For each such register, Questa CDC
     generates a cdc_fx checker directive for metastability injected simulation. This checker includes
     metastability injection and analysis logic.

     During simulation, the cdc_fx checker assumes control of the register's output. It injects variable
     delays on bits that transition when transmit and receive clocks are almost aligned. This causes
     some outputs to mimic metastable behavior in simulation. Problems are detected by end-to-end
     test failures. If the verification environment is instrumented with assertions, problems also can be
     detected by assertion failures.

Reconvergence Methodology

Data coherency is a significant issue in CDC analysis, with reconvergence violations ranging from
thousands to hundreds of thousands. A specific methodology is needed for faster resolution of
reconvergence violations. This section outlines setup and performance of Reconvergence checking for
Questa CDC analysis, ensuring efficient use of time.

Reconvergence Checks Categories

Reconvergence checks are categorized and reported under the following schemes.

       · reconvergence - Two or more sources on the same domain, synchronised in the same domain
          and then converge. Severity- Caution.

          The coherency does not happen if it is assured that the sources are gray-coded or mutually
          exclusive. User can apply relevant directive to change this caution to reconvergence_gray
          evaluation.

       · reconvergence_bus - Two or more bus bit sources on the same domain, synchronised in the
          same domain and then converge. Severity- Violation.

          The coherency does not happen if it is assured that the sources are gray-coded or mutually
          exclusive. User can apply relevant directive to change this violation to reconvergence_gray
          evaluation.

       · reconvergence_mixed ­ Two or more bus bit sources and non-bus bit sources on the same
          domain, synchronised in the same domain and then converge. Severity- Caution.

          The coherency does not happen if it is assured that the sources are gray-coded or mutually
          exclusive. User can apply relevant directive to change this caution to reconvergence_gray
          evaluation.

       · reconvergence_multi_tx_clock - Two or more sources on different domains, synchronized in
          same domain and then converge. Severity- Violation.

          This needs to be fixed in the design to prevent the coherency problem. This cannot be handled
          by gray-coding or mutually exclusive directives as the sources are from different clock domains/
          groups.

       · single_source_reconvergence ­ In the same domain, a single source diverges, synchronises, and
          then reconverges. Severity- Violation.

Questa® CDC User Guide  49
CDC Basics

Reconvergence Methodology                                                                                

    This needs to be fixed in the design to prevent the coherency problem. This cannot be handled
    by gray-coding or mutually exclusive directives as the same source diverges and then converges
    back.

    · reconvergence_gray - In the same domain, two or more gray-coded sources, synchronises, and
       then reconverges. Severity- Evaluation.

       This evaluation serves just to let the user know that the reported reconvergence is secure since
       the converging source has user specified directives that have been gray-coded or are mutually
       exclusive.

Enabling Reconvergence Checks

Reconvergence checking is disabled in CDC analysis by default. To enable it, the user must specify
cdc reconvergence on. It enables the combo reconvergence (convergence of synchronizers before
any sequential element). For instance, after synchronizers there are no sequential elements before it
converges at combo logic.

The user must specify cdc preference reconvergence depth <value> to enable the sequential
reconvergence checking (the convergence of any synchronizers after one or more sequential elements),
where the value specified for depth is the maximum sequential element allowed after synchronizers until
convergence. For example, reconvergence in the below case would only be reported if the sequential
depth was set to 3.

Any sequential items between the diverging source and the synchronizers are not allowed for single-
source reconvergence checking. To allow sequential components, the user might specify cdc preference
reconvergence -divergence_depth <value>. For instance, if the divergence depth is set to 2, the Questa
CDC Reconvergence Flow case shown below would be flagged under single_source_reconvergence.

50                         Questa® CDC User Guide
                        CDC Basics

                        Reconvergence Methodology

For reconvergence_multi_tx_clock type convergence, where two or more different domain sources are
synchronised and converged, there is a separate control for sequential depth, which is controlled by
the  argument in cdc preference reconvergence. By default, its value is 0, that is, it does not allow any
sequential elements after the synchronizer before it reaches the converging gate. For example, the below
case would be flagged under reconvergence_multi_tx_clock only if multi_tx_clock_depth is set to 2 or
more.

  Note:
  The depth specified for multi-clock reconvergence analysis, using the multi_tx_clock_depth
  option, must be less than or equal to the depth specified for reconvergence analysis, using the
  depth option, or its default value.

The standard CDC methodologies and goals recommendation is not to enable reconvergence
checking for Start and Planning goals. It should be enabled for the less mature stage of RTL design
(Implementation and Release goals).

Reconvergence Flows

There are a few different reconvergence checking flows, and depending on whether protocol-based CDC
analysis is enabled or only static checks are performed, one of them can be adopted.

Structural Reconvergence Flow

Users that are still relying only on the structural checks made during CDC analysis and have not yet
implemented protocol-based CDC analysis should choose this flow.

Questa® CDC User Guide                                                                             51
CDC Basics

Reconvergence Methodology                                                                                     

    1. When the design is little mature, enable reconvergence checking and use the following settings.

          cdc reconvergence on
          cdc preference reconvergence ­depth 2 divergence_depth 1 ­effort

            medium multi_tx_clock_convergence -multi_tx_clock_depth 2

            Note:
            Consider the following points:

              If the design is a little larger and the reconvergence checking is taking too long, you
               can consider deleting -effort medium and letting it run with low effort. Reduce the value
               entered for the -depth and multi_tx_clock_depth depth arguments as well.

              Reconvergence is not by default reported for reset synchronizers.You can enable it by
               giving cdc preference reconvergence the option reset_sync_as_recon_start.

     2. Analyse reconvergence_multi_tx_clock violations first since they are more serious and can
          only be fixed by removing reconvergence from the design. In comparison to other warnings or
          violations, there is a higher chance of seeing data coherency issues that have not been rectified.

     3. Analyze single_source_reconvergence violation as typically these also need the design fix. If
          there is some source that is first diverging and then synchronized and further converging, these
          cannot be handled through gray-coded or mutually exclusive directives, as the same source
          diverges and then converges back.

     4. Next, fix the reconvergence, reconvergence_bus, and reconvergence_mixed warnings and
          violations in the design. Specify cdc signal <source-name> -gray_coded/-mutually_exclusive
          if the participating sources are mutually exclusive or gray-coded. By doing this, they become
          reconvergence_gray evaluations.

     5. Try a final signoff run with the report_concise_off option also specified in the cdc preference
          reconvergence setting after you have corrected all of the reconvergence violations and cautions.
          This is just to make sure that this run does not encounter any new reconvergence violations or
          cautions.

Clock Domain Crossing Schemes  

Clock Domain Crossing Schemes

The CDC compiler analyzes the design netlist and identifies logic involving CDC signals that matches
various pattern templates. Each occurrence of logic that matches a template is called a clock domain
crossing. In general, a crossing is a logic structure that spans two or more clock domains.

A simple clock domain crossing is a path. For example, you might have a 1-bit CDC signal sig from
clock domain A being synchronized by two in-phase D flip-flops in clock domain B. A complex clock
domain crossing is one that contains other crossings. For example, a MUX crossing is complex. The MUX
crossing itself is a logic structure that spans two clock domains. Inside the MUX crossing is a MUX select
signal structure that is a simple 2DFF crossing.

The CDC compiler identifies clock domain crossings and their synchronization logic. Classes of crossings
with the same functionality are called CDC schemes. For example, a MUX select signal path with its
synchronization logic is a "two_dff" scheme; the parent data MUX crossing is an instance of a "dmux"
scheme.

"CDC Schemes" on page 403 contain the detailed data sheets for the CDC schemes.

        Attributes of CDC Schemes
        CDC Synchronization Schemes
        Schemes with Potential CDC Problems

Attributes of CDC Schemes

Each CDC crossing detected by the CDC compiler has two attributes: severity and promotion.

Use cdc report scheme and cdc promote scheme to change these settings from the factory defaults (see
Figure 14).

You cannot change the severity at the individual crossing level. But you can set the promotion attribute for
single crossings or groups of crossings with the cdc promote crossing directive.

54                             Questa® CDC User Guide
                                                             CDC Basics

                                                    Attributes of CDC Schemes

  Figure 14. Severity and Promotion Attributes of Crossings

CDC Analysis Results

Severity is an indicator of the seriousness of the particular logic pattern for the crossing. The severity
levels are:

  · Violation
     A violation is considered a must-fix problem.

  · Caution

     A caution is considered a valid crossing, but it has an associated CDC transfer protocol that
     should be verified in simulation or by formal verification. Most cautions have designated CDC
     protocol checkers that the CDC compiler configures automatically and "promotes" for assertion-
     based verification.

  · Evaluation

     An evaluation is a valid CDC scheme that uses an appropriate synchronizer. The scheme's CDC
     protocol must still be checked.

       · Proven

          A proven scheme is a valid CDC scheme with an associated CDC transfer protocol that formal
          CDC analysis has proven cannot be violated. No CDC protocol checkers for the scheme are
          "promoted" for assertion-based verification.

Promotion

Whenever possible, CDC creates and configures one or more CDC transfer protocol assertions for a
scheme. Most synchronizers have corresponding protocol assertions. The process of identifying a CDC
scheme and creating its protocol assertion is called checker CDC assertion promotion. Here, a CDC

Questa® CDC User Guide                                                                                      55
CDC Basics

CDC Synchronization Schemes                                                                              

scheme is deemed OK from a static perspective. The compiler does not have enough information to
determine whether or not a synchronization problem will occur. The answer depends on the operating
environment of the design.

Promoted checkers can be used during simulation to monitor CDC activity and verify proper
synchronization of CDC signals. They are also used in static and dynamic formal verification. Use the cdc
promote directives to turn off CDC checker promotion for specific CDC schemes.

Signals in Unnamed Blocks

By default, CDC protocol checker (and FX checker) promotion is disabled for signals inside IF-generate
blocks (the current Questa implementation does not allow access to these block names). But if the
specified simulator is VCS (that is, configure simulator vcs), these checkers are promoted. However,
checkers with signals in regular RTL unnamed blocks are not promoted. If the specified simulator is NC
(that is, configure simulator nc), checkers with signals in implicit generate blocks are not promoted.

Most CDC scheme types refer to synchronization logic. Some schemes apply to single-bit CDC signal
synchronization, some apply to multiple-bit data bus synchronization, and some apply to both.

a two_dff scheme uses two in-phase D flip-flops clocked in the receive domain as a synchronizer.
