                        Complex Crossings

Complex Crossings

A simple crossing has logic in two domains, but the logic that crosses the clock domain boundary is a
single net (signal or bus). A complexcrossing also has logic in two (or more) domains, but the logic that
crosses the clock domain boundary is an amalgamation of multiple nets.
The two_dff, bus_two_dff and custom_sync schemes are classes of simple crossings. FIFO
synchronization and DMUX synchronization are examples of complex crossings. All complex crossings
contain separately reported simple crossings.

        FIFO Memory and FIFO Crossings
        DMUX Crossings

FIFO Memory and FIFO Crossings

A FIFO memory crossing (fifo_memory) is a crossing that looks like a FIFO crossing.
It has a dual clock memory with write clock and write address pointer on the Tx side of the crossing and
read clock and read address pointer on the Rx side of the crossing (Figure 15).

                                               Figure 15. FIFO Memory Scheme

Memories can be:

       · Memory (2-D Arrays). Automatically identified by CDC or specified using the netlist memory
          command.

       · Register/latch file. As specified by cdc fifo.

       · Black box memory. As specified by cdc blackbox memory.

FIFO Scheme Detection

A crossing must satisfy the following sequence of qualifications to be classified as a fifo_memory crossing
(Figure 16):

     1. The crossing involves a memory or a register file.

     2. Memory is in the same clock domain as the write data signal to the memory. If not, a synchronizer
          is missing between the Tx driver and the memory (no_sync).

Questa® CDC User Guide                                                                                     61
CDC Basics

FIFO Memory and FIFO Crossings                                                                         

    3. The write address pointer must be in the same clock domain as the memory write data input.
         Similarly, the read address pointer must be in the same clock domain as the memory read
         data output. If not, the clock domains of the pointers and data mismatch cannot be detected
         (fifo_memory_ptr_mismatch).

                                          Figure 16. FIFO Memory and FIFO Detection

For a FIFO memory crossing to be classified as a FIFO crossing (fifo), the write address pointer must
also synchronize in the Rx domain and the read address pointer must also synchronize in the Tx domain
(Figure 17). You can relax these requirements using the -no_write_sync and no_read_sync options with
the cdc fifo directive.

Categorizing FIFO memory crossings between FIFO crossings and FIFO memory crossings with missing
pointer synchronization (fifo_ptr_no_sync) is an unnecessary performance-degrading step in most
analysis runs, and is off by default. To turn FIFO detection on:

   cdc scheme on fifo

62                              Questa® CDC User Guide
                                                CDC Basics

                                                FIFO Memory and FIFO Crossings

                        Figure 17. FIFO Scheme

Register-based FIFO Synchronizers
For a register-based FIFO synchronizer, the FIFO's registers must be declared with the cdc fifo directive.
FIFO detection checks the following characteristics of the FIFO synchronization logic:

       · Register is specified with cdc fifo and is in the write (Tx) clock domain.

       · Register is MUXed by the read address pointer.

       · MUXed register output is registered in the read (Rx) clock domain.

       · Write address is in the clock domain inferred from the register enable or clk pin.

       · Full signal synchronizer for the write (Tx) clock domain logic.

       · Empty signal synchronizer for the read (Rx) clock domain logic.
Missing FIFO Synchronizers
If a FIFO synchronizer is expected, but missing from the results, do the following:

     1. Is FIFO detection turned on? In cdc_setting.rpt, ensure that fifo scheme is TRUE.
          If not, specify cdc scheme on fifo to turn on FIFO detection.

     2. Is the FIFO memory compiled? Examine any compilation warnings in the compiler logs.

     3. Are the memory synchronizers detected? For a register-based FIFO, see "FIFO Memory and
          FIFO Crossings" on page 61Register-based FIFO Synchronizers on page 4. For an MDA:

             Is the memory model compiled? If the memory is unsynthesizable, black-box the memory with
                cdc blackbox memory.

             If the read data port domain is not correct, specify the correct port domain with netlist port
                domain.

Questa® CDC User Guide                          63
CDC Basics

FIFO Memory and FIFO Crossings  

     4. Is the crossing a fifo_memory_ptr_mismatch crossing?) In this case, it is most likely that the
          address and data ports in the transmit and/or receive domains have different clock domains,
          therefore FIFO detection cannot identify the read and write addresses. Note that the write
          address and write data domains must be the same. Similarly, read address and read data
          domains should also be the same. If required, set the port domains (netlist port domain) of the
          read and write data registers or black boxes. Also, try increasing the fifo effort level with cdc
          preference fifo -effort.

     5. Is the crossing a fifo_memory crossing? Then the FIFO is acting like a real synchronizer.
          However, additional checks are needed to verify if it is a true FIFO synchronizer. Double check
          these checks are enabled with cdc scheme on fifo.

     6. Is the crossing a fifo_ptr_no_sync crossing? A write or read address synchronizer was not found.
          By default, FIFO detection looks up to two sequential levels from an address source to find its
          synchronizer and reports a fifo_ptr_no_sync crossing if not found. If the synchronizers are further
          away from their address sources, you can increase the address distance checked by specifying
          cdc preference fifo -sync_effort with level medium or high.

          If the address synchronizer is not found, generate a detailed CDC report (cdc generate
          report). Check that the address pointers are reported as bus_two_dff crossings. If not, how are
          these paths categorized? You can override the check for address synchronizers with: cdc fifo
          -no_write_sync and cdc fifo -no_read_sync.

FIFO Synchronizer Verification

The functionality of proper FIFO crossing synchronization logic must still be verified as follows;

       · Overflow/underflow

          To prevent FIFO overflow and underflow, the FIFO crossing control logic must be sensitive
          to full and empty FIFO conditions. Tx/Rx logic maintain counters to detect these conditions.
          These counters are typically gray-coded address pointers that must be synchronized to the clock
          domains of the opposite logic to determine the full/empty status of the FIFO. For example, the
          read address pointer is synchronized to the transmit clock domain and the write address pointer
          is synchronized to the receive clock domain.

       · Separate binary address counter and gray-code status counters

          If a FIFO has a separate binary counter (for the memory address) and a separate gray counter
          (for the empty/full calculation), you must verify that the counters are equivalent. Write assertions
          for the counter equivalence properties and use simulation or formal verification to verify proper
          functionality.

       · Simultaneous read/write

          A FIFO synchronizer should not implement simultaneous reading from and writing to FIFO
          memory locations. The simultaneous read/write of a memory location might allow a read of a
          register value that is changing on the write clock edge, which can result in a setup/hold violation
          during the cross domain data transfer.

FIFO Custom Synchronizers

A FIFO crossing is a complex crossing that has several domain-crossing paths (data address pointers
and gray-code counters). Since all of these crossings are reported as separate crossings in addition to
the complex logic structure, a design with many instances of FIFO crossings can result in many reported
results, which might be considered extraneous.

64                              Questa® CDC User Guide
                        CDC Basics

                        DMUX Crossings

One solution is to split off the FIFO synchronization logic into a separate design unit, verify the design unit
has functional FIFO synchronization logic and specify the design unit as a custom synchronizer.

FIFO custom synchronizers are useful for another purpose. Often memory models are simulation models
and are not synthesizable. A memory model with unsynthesizable constructs is not compiled into the
clock domain model and all instances of the memory are inferred as black boxes. By packaging the
FIFO synchronizer as a custom synchronizer CDC analysis reports all instances of the FIFO custom
synchronizer crossings.

DMUX Crossings

A DMUX-style crossing is a crossing through a MUX (or MUX equivalent expression) with selection logic
originating from the Tx domain.
Figure 18 shows one basic form of a DMUX scheme.

                                                    Figure 18. DMUX Scheme

DMUX Scheme Detection

Figure 19 shows the DMUX-style scheme detection process. DMUX-style crossings are analyzed as
follows:

     1. Start with a crossing that has an expression in the RX fanin.

     2. If the expression terms are not synchronized to the RX domain, the crossing has a missing select
          logic synchronizer and it is reported as a no_sync or multi_bits violation. To properly synchronize
          the crossing, you must add the missing synchronizer to the select logic.

     3. Otherwise, if the expression has multiple synchronizers in the fanin of the Rx register, it is
          reported as an instance of a multi_sync_mux_select scheme. Possibly, the crossing has a valid
          data synchronizer. However, functional checking of the synchronizer is incomplete, so you must
          verify that the synchronized signals disable the Tx data path. It is recommended to change the
          default severity of the multi_sync_mux_select scheme to violation (using a cdc report scheme
          directive), to avoid a reconvergence issue and skipped functional checks on the select signals.

     4. Otherwise if the crossing matches one of the strict DMUX-style logic templates, the crossing
          has a valid data synchronizer and it is reported as an instance of one of the following schemes:
          simple_dmux, forward_simple_dmux, and_gate_dmux or mux_lock_dmux.

     5. Otherwise, CDC analysis performs a functional check on the DMUX-style logic. The functional
          check verifies that the synchronized select will disable the Tx data path.

Questa® CDC User Guide  65
CDC Basics

DMUX Crossings  

    6. If the functional check fails, the crossing is reported as an instance of a partial_dmux scheme.
         If the check failure is mitigated by custom DMUX-style logic, such as timing or structural
         considerations that may prevent the crossing from transmitting unstable Tx data, the partial_dmux
         scheme can be waived. However, if the failure indicates that the Rx register may sample unstable
         Tx data, correct the DMUX logic. The default severity of the partial_dmux scheme is caution. It is
         recommended to change the default severity to violation (with the cdc report scheme directive),
         because the functional check failure may indicate a scenario where the synchronized select
         signal will not block the Tx data and the unstable Tx data may be sampled by the Rx register.

    7. Otherwise, the crossing is reported as an instance of a dmux scheme. The crossing has a valid
         DMUX-style data synchronizer that passes all functional checks.

                                             Figure 19. DMUX Synchronization

66              Questa® CDC User Guide
                        CDC Basics

                        Custom Synchronizers

Custom Synchronizers

Custom synchronizers are user-defined abstraction models that identify pre-verified synchronization
blocks.
Custom synchronizers are used for the following reasons:

       · Synchronizer's implementation is not yet developed.

       · Synchronizer's abstraction model is provided as part of a block's IP.

       · Synchronizer's abstraction model is used in a pre-verified block instantiated many times (which
          improves performance and reduces CDC reporting noise).

       · Synchronizer is a user-specified RTL block that does not fit "standard" synchronizer templates.
CDC analysis considers custom synchronizers as gray-box models that are guaranteed to synchronizer
their data paths when instantiated properly.

        Standard vs. Custom Synchronizers
        Custom Synchronizer Specification
        Split Synchronizer Specification

Standard vs. Custom Synchronizers

CDC analysis recognizes two types of synchronizers: standard and custom.

Standard synchronizers are logic components that fit various standard "template patterns" defined for
CDC analysis. Standard schemes include 2DFF, bus 2DFF, 4-latch, bus 4-latch, pulse, FIFO, DMUX
and handshake synchronizers. CDC analysis also reports logic schemes that are possible for partial
synchronizers--such as phase and various FIFO/DMUX-style circuits.

Custom synchronizers are user-defined objects that identify validated synchronization logic. CDC
analysis considers custom synchronizers as gray-box models that are guaranteed to perform correct
synchronization when they are properly connected.

Note the distinctions between the two synchronizer types:

       · Internal logic

          For a standard synchronizer, its internal logic is needed so CDC analysis can match the
          various logic templates. For a standard synchronizer, the primary focus of CDC analysis is the
          synchronization logic: CDC analysis tries to detect not only correct synchronizer usage, but it also
          tries to detect correct structure and implementation.

          Custom synchronizers can be detected even when identified as black boxes. For a custom
          synchronizer, CDC results show all instances of the various custom synchronizers. However,
          the same mechanism used to pass relevant properties of a block to higher hierarchical levels
          --hierport domain directives--is also applicable to custom synchronizers. You add hier
          portdomain directives to pass a "gray-box" specification of a custom synchronizer to the analyzer.
          CDC analysis can then guarantee clock domain properties internal to the synchronizer for use in
          identifying synchronization and clock domain relationships.

Questa® CDC User Guide                                                                                    67
CDC Basics

Custom Synchronizer Specification                                                                          

       · External Connections

          For a standard synchronizer, the analyzer examines synchronization logic to see if it really does
          synchronize its crossing. A synchronizer's connections are built into this analysis. The analyzer
          does not examine the custom synchronizer logic to ensure it is indeed a synchronizer; but it does
          check that the custom synchronizer is properly instantiated.

You either manually specify custom synchronizers' connection assumptions or generate them by
running hierarchical CDC analysis of the synchronizer modules. The analyzer checks these connection
assumptions for each custom synchronizer. If all connection assumptions are satisfied, the crossing is
reported as one of the various custom synchronizers (evaluation); if any assumption is not satisfied, the
crossing is one of the various custom synchronizer mismatches (violation). Connection checking is a
primary benefit of using custom synchronizers.

Custom Synchronizer Specification

The minimal definition of a custom synchronizer is a design unit (module) and a pair of ports with a data
path direction. The port-pair must consist of one input port and one output port. The data path direction
identifies the input port as the "from" port and the output port as the "to" port.

If a custom synchronizer is properly connected, CDC analysis assumes it is a valid synchronizer for any
data signal that goes from the from-port to the to-port (Figure 20).

                                              Figure 20. Custom Synchronizers

The cdc custom sync directive specifies a module of a custom synchronizer:

     cdc custom sync module -type sync_type

The -type <sync_type> argument is a user-specified name for instances of the synchronizer type being
defined. For example, you might define two FIFO-style custom synchronizers and call them FIFO_large
and FIFO_small. CDC analysis identifies crossings that are synchronized by them as bus_custom_sync
(FIFO_large) and bus_custom_sync (FIFO_small) crossings.

A cdc custom sync data directive specifies the two ports of the custom synchronizer data path:

     cdc custom sync data -module module -from port -to port [-internal _crossing]

         Note:
         If -no_combo directive is not specified, the tool will not report combo_logic crossings to the
         custom synchronizer. To ensure all potential issues are detected during CDC verification, it is
         recommended to always include -no_combo assumption on the data pin when defining custom
         synchronizers. For example:

            hier assume port D -no_combo -module dff_sync

68                                 Questa® CDC User Guide
                        CDC Basics

                        Custom Synchronizer Specification

Custom synchronizers can be specified for the control signal, data bus, multibit data, and ad hoc
synchronizer types. Each path of a custom synchronizer may be single-bit or multiple-bit wide. Single-bit
custom synchronizer data paths act as control or ad hoc synchronizers. CDC assumes that a multiple-
bit custom synchronizer data path is synchronized by a data bus synchronizer, implying all the bits of
the data path are transmitted together in the receiving clock domain. Reconvergence analysis among
these bits is not required. To override this default behavior, specify that a multibit data synchronizer
independently synchronizes the different bits.

Assumptions Specification

CDC analyses of standard and custom synchronizers are quite different. CDC analysis of standard
synchronizers assures synchronization is correct; checking synchronization logic connections is built
into the analysis. Alternately, CDC analysis of custom synchronization logic assumes each custom
synchronizer performs proper synchronization--if the synchronizer is connected correctly. The logic
designer must ensure custom synchronizer logic does proper synchronization. See "Hierarchical CDC
Assumptions" on page 244 for details about HDM related assumptions. The following assumption
directives can be specified for custom synchronizers.

  · hier assume clock -module module
     [-tx_clock clock_pattern...] [-rx_clock clock_pattern...
     [-exclude_tx_clock clock_pattern...] [-exclude_rx_clock clock_pattern...]
     Verify assumed clock domains of signals connected to data ports of a custom synchronizer.

  · hier assume port port_pattern... -module module
     [[-sync] [-no_combo] [-same_clock | -clock clock_port]

     | -stable | -constant value]

     [-instance instance] [-instance_scope module] [-dataport port_pattern...]

     Verify assumed properties of signals connected to instances of hierarchical blocks or custom
     synchronizers.

       · hier assume connection

          [-from port] -from_module module [-from_instance instance]

          [-to port] -to_module module [-to_instance instance] [-add]

          Verify the connections between the ports of custom synchronizer and ports of an instance of
          another module. Typically, the directive is used to specify connectivity between halves of a split
          synchronizer.

The hier assume clock directive verifies across which clock domain boundaries instances of the
synchronizer may and may not be used. The hier assume port directive specifies properties of the logic
driving or driven by the synchronizer's ports:

  · Port must connect directly to a synchronized signal (-sync) or only non-combinational logic.

       · Port must connect directly to logic in the same domain (same_clock).

For information on HDM related assumptions, refer "Hierarchical CDC Assumptions" on page 244.

If a synchronizer instance satisfies all of its assumptions, the synchronizer is guaranteed (by the designer)
to perform proper synchronization. But, the value of using assumptions is more than just ensuring proper

Questa® CDC User Guide                                                                                        69
CDC Basics

Custom Synchronizer Specification                                

synchronization. By knowing what style of logic drives--or is driven by--particular ports, the designer can
tailor synchronizer placement.

For example, a designer might create three synchronizer types for a particular crossing style. One type
might assume the "synchronized" output drives combo logic; another type might assume the output drives
only registers; and another type might assume the output drives another synchronizer. The purpose of
placing the correct synchronizer in the right location is to reduce logic complexity and gate count. By
specifying synchronizer assumptions, the designer is notified not only of non-functional synchronization,
but the designer is also notified of incorrect synchronizer selection.

Example: 2DFF Synchronizer

                                   Figure 21. 2DFF Synchronizer

This 2DFF custom synchronizer has the specification:

   cdc custom sync dff_sync -type dff
   cdc custom sync data -module dff_sync \

                 -from in -to out;
   hier clock clk -module dff_sync
   hier port domain in -module dff_sync \

                 -clock clk
   hier port domain out -module dff_sync \

                 -clock clk
   hier assume port in -no_combo -module dff_sync

The custom synchronizer module dff_sync is defined as the type dff custom synchronizer. The
synchronization path is from the in input port to the out output port. The two hier port domain directives
guarantee the in and out ports are connected internally to signals in the same clock domain as the signal
driving the clk port. The first hier port domain directive also guarantees the in input internally drives only a
synchronizer to the clk domain. The second hier port domain directive guarantees the out output is driven
by a synchronizer to the clk domain. The hier assume port directive verifies that in port is not connected to
combinational logic in the fanin.

Example: DMUX Synchronizer with two synchronized paths

Figure 26 shows a DMUX-style custom synchronizer with its specification. The synchronizer model
is defined as a single module (dmux2) with its synchronizing data path going from the tx_data port to
the rx_data port. Consider an instance of dmux2 for which the driver of tx_data and the consumer of
rx_data are in different clock domains. The clock domain crossing from tx_data to rx_data is reported
as a bus_custom_sync crossing. The clock domain crossing from tx_sel to rx_sel is reported as a
custom_sync crossing. The dmux2 string is the qualifier of the type argument. For single-module
synchronizers, the type must be unique: only one synchronizer module per type.

Questa® CDC User Guide                                                                                     73
CDC Basics

Custom Synchronizer Specification                                     

            Figure 26. DMUX Synchronizer with two synchronized paths

This DMUX-style custom synchronizer has the specification:

   cdc custom sync dmux2 -type dmux2
   cdc custom sync data -module dmux2 -from tx_data -to rx_data
   cdc custom sync data -module dmux2 -from tx_sel -to rx_sel

   hier clock rx_clk -module dmux2
   hier port domain rx_data -module dmux2 -clock rx_clk
   hier port domain tx_data rstn -module dmux2 -clock rx_clk
   hier assume port tx_sel -module dmux2 -clock rx_clk

   hier assume port -module dmux2 -same_clock tx_data tx_sel
   hier reset rstn -module dmux2 -async -active_low

The hier port domain directives notify CDC analysis at the higher hierarchical level about the nature of the
custom synchronizer internal logic:

       · TXRST, TXSEL are consumed in the RXCLK domain.

       · TXDATA is consumed in the RXCLK domain and drives combinational logic.

       · RXSEL, RXDATA are driven by the RXCLK domain.
The hier assume port directive specifies a combinational logic check on the TXSEL port and generates a
violation if the TXSEL port is driven by combinational logic. The hier assume port directive also specifies
that TXSEL and TXDATA are driven by the same clock domain.

Internal Crossing Synchronizers

For the previous dmux1_sync example: all logic in dmux1_sync is in the same clock domain as the
logic driven by the synchronized output port (RXDATA) and all the transmit domain logic is external

74                                 Questa® CDC User Guide
                                                                                              CDC Basics

                                               Custom Synchronizer Specification

to dmux1_sync. The actual crossing from the Tx domain to the Rx domain is external to the custom
synchronizer.

For some custom synchronizers, the Tx domain to Rx domain crossing for the synchronized data
path is internal to the custom synchronizer. Such a custom synchronizer is called an internal
crossing synchronizer. Crossings synchronized by internal crossing synchronizers are reported as
internal_custom_sync and internal_bus_custom_sync crossings. To indicate a custom synchronizer is an
internal crossing synchronizer, add an -internal_crossing argument to the synchronizer's cdc custom sync
data directive.

Example: Internal; Crossing DMUX Synchronizer

This DMUX-style internal crossing synchronizer has the following specification:

   cdc custom sync dmux2_sync -type dmux2
   cdc custom sync data -module dmux2_sync \

     -from TXDATA -to RXDATA -internal_crossing
   hier port domain TXSEL TXDATA -module dmux2_sync -clock TXCLK
   hier port domain RXDATA -module dmux2_sync -clock RXCLK

This synchronizer is similar to the dmux1_sync synchronizer. But for dmux2_sync, some transmit domain
logic--that is, tlogic containing registers driven by the TXDATA and TXSEL ports--is brought inside
the synchronizer. So, the Tx-to-Rx crossing of the dmux2_sync synchronization path is internal to
dmux2_sync. The cdc custom sync data directive includes the -internal_crossing argument to specify this
is the case.

Example: Handshake Synchronizer with Assumptions

This handshake-style internal crossing synchronizer with assumptions has this specification:

Questa® CDC User Guide                                                                            75
CDC Basics

Split Synchronizer Specification  

   cdc custom sync hs1_sync -type handshake1
   cdc custom sync data -module hs1_sync \

      -from TXDATA -to RXDATA -internal_crossing
   cdc custom sync data -module hs1_sync -from RXACK -to TXACK
   cdc custom sync data -module hs1_sync -from TXVALID -to RXVALID
   hier port domain TXDATA -module hs1_sync -clock TXCLK
   hier port domain RXACK TXACK -module hs1_sync -clock TXCLK
   hier port domain RXDATA -module hs1_sync -clock RXCLK
   hier port domain TXVALID RXVALID -module hs1_sync -clock RXCLK
   hier assume port TXDATA TXVALID TXACK -module hs1_sync -same_clock
   hier assume port RXVALID RXDATA RXACK -module hs1_sync -same_clock
   hier assume port TXVALID RXACK -module hs1_sync -no_combo

As with the other custom synchronizers, a cdc custom sync directive identifies hs1_sync as a custom
synchronizer model; the cdc custom sync data directive identifies the synchronization path as going from
TXDATA to RXDATA with an internal crossing.

The hier port domain directives specify that TXVALID/RXVALID are synchronized to the domain of
RXCLK and that TXACK/RXACK are synchronized to the domain of TXCLK. This information alerts the
analyzer that these paths are properly synchronized. These directives are used to identify synchronized
paths--rather than having multiple cdc custom sync data directives--because only one custom
synchronizer should be reported for the instance (which corresponds to the data path specified by the cdc
custom sync data directive).

The hier assume port directives specify the assumptions for instances of hs1_sync. TXDATA/TXVALID/
TXACK must be connected to signals in the same clock domain; RXVALID/RADATA/RXACK also must
be connected to signals in the same clock domain. In addition, since ports TXVALID and RXACK drive
internal synchronizers directly, to work properly they must not be driven by combinational logic. The
-no_combo argument in the last hier assume port directive ensures this.

An instance of hs1_sync that connects TXDATA to one clock domain and RXDATA to another clock
domain reports the crossing between the driver of TXDATA and the consumer of RXDATA as:

       · internal_bus_custom_sync(handshake1)

          If all assumptions are satisfied.

       · internal_bus_custom_sync_mismatch(handshake1)

          If any assumption is not satisfied.

Split Synchronizer Specification

A split synchronizer consists of two modules connected by signal paths.

As shown in Figure 27, the connecting paths can include combinational logic and can drive other external
logic.

76                                Questa® CDC User Guide
                                                                CDC Basics

                                                                Split Synchronizer Specification

                        Figure 27. Split Synchronizer Examples

Specification of a dual-module synchronizer model consists of four directives: two cdc custom sync
directives that identify the two modules and two cdc custom sync data directives that identify the two
ports of the data path through the synchronizer instance that produces the synchronized signal. Both cdc
custom sync directives specify -split_sync to indicate the synchronizer is a split synchronizer. If two halves
of a split synchronizer have the same value for the -type attribute, the split synchronizer crossings are
detected.

For example, in Figure 27, for split synchronizer crossings to be reported, fifo_wr_sync and fifo_rd_sync
should have the same value for the -type attribute. The port domain specifications and assumptions are
handled in a manner similar to that of single-module custom synchronizers. The hier assume connection
directive assures proper connection between the two halves of split synchronizer.

     hier assume connection

     [-from port] -from_module module [-from_instance instance]

     [-to port] -to_module module [-to_instance instance] [-add]

Example: Handshake Split Synchronizer

This 2-module example of a handshake-style split synchronizer with connection related assumptions has
this specification:

   cdc custom sync hs2_write_sync -type handshake2 -split_sync
   cdc custom sync hs2_read_sync -type handshake2 -split_sync
   cdc custom sync data -module hs2_write_sync -from WDATA
   cdc custom sync data -module hs2_read_sync -to RDATA
   hier port domain ASYNC_IN -module hs2_write_sync -clock WCLK -sync
   hier port domain ASYNC_IN -module hs2_read_sync -clock RCLK -sync
   # must drive synchronizers
   hier assume port WFLAG -module hs2_write_sync -sync

Questa® CDC User Guide                                          77
CDC Basics

Split Synchronizer Specification                                                                       

hier assume port RFLAG -module hs2_read_sync -sync
# same clock domain
hier assume port WVALID WRDY -module hs2_write_sync -same_clock
hier assume port RVALID RRDY -module hs2_read_sync -same_clock

The two halves of the synchronizer are specified with two cdc custom sync -split_sync directives. The
synchronization data path (WDATA to RDATA) is specified with two cdc custom sync data directives--one
for the -from port and one for the -to port--because they are on different modules.

Two hier port domain -sync directives indicate that the two ASYNC_IN ports drive synchronizers in their
respective domains (inside the synchronizer halves).

Two hier assume port -same_clock directives specify assumptions: WVALID/WRDY must connect to
signals in the same clock domain; and RVALID/RRDY must connect to signals in the same clock domain.
Two hier assume port -sync directives ensure inter-connectivity between the synchronizer halves. Both
WFLAG and RFLAG must drive only synchronizers. If these ports have the shown connections, then each
port only drives the other module's ASYNC_IN port. In this case, the hier port domain -sync directives
ensure these synchronizer assumptions are satisfied.

If the two half synchronizers are instantiated and WDATA/RDATA are connected to signals in different
clock domains, the handshake synchronizer instance is reported as one of:

    · A bus_custom_sync (handshake2) crossing--if all assumptions are satisfied.

       · A bus_custom_sync_mismatch (handshake2) crossing--if any assumption is not satisfied.

In this example, assumptions about the interconnection between halves of a split synchronizer are
ensured with hier assume port directives. The WFLAG-to-ASYNC_IN and RFLAG-to-ASYNC_IN
connections are checked that the flags drive only synchronizers (that is, the flag signals are synchronized
to the destination domains). A better check is that the ports are actually connected.

Example: FIFO Split Synchronizer

This 2-module example of a FIFO-style split synchronizer with inter-module connection assumptions has
this specification:

   cdc custom sync fifo3_write_sync -type fifo3 -split_sync
   cdc custom sync fifo3_read_sync -type handshake2 -split_sync
   cdc custom sync data -module fifo3_write_sync -from WDATA
   cdc custom sync data -module fifo3_read_sync -to RDATA
   hier assume connection \

     -from WPTR_GRAY -from_module fifo3_write_sync \
     -to WPTR_GRAY -to_module fifo3_read_sync
   hier assume connection \
     -from RPTR_GRAY -from_module fifo3_read_sync \
     -to RPTR_GRAY -to_module fifo3_write_sync

            hier assume connection

                        Specification Flow

Specification Flow

Specification flow moves away from the conventional template-based verification and provides you
enhanced control over design and verification.
Using this flow, you can specify control synchronizer modules and synchronizer enable signals, before
you run the CDC analysis on the design. The flow helps reduce noise as it produces cleaner results,
which decreases your efforts in specifying waivers and reviewing the CDC analysis results.

        Clockoff Specification
        Synchronizer Module Specification
        Synchronizer Clock Enable Specification
        Synchronizer Enable Specification

Clockoff Specification

Clockoff specification helps you filter out crossings where the clock at the Rx register is off when Tx
deassert. The specification further provides constraint options that you can use to narrow down the
results.

         Note:
         Using the clockoff specification, you can categorize the crossings as 'Evaluation' within
         async_reset_clockoff, stopping further processing on async_reset_clockoff crossings.

The specification filters three main types of clock domain crossings:
Use the cdc specification on directive to turn on the clockoff specification.

     cdc specifiction on -clockoff
The cdc specification clockoff directive specifies transmitter output and clock signal from the receiver
domain. The -reset and rx_clock options are mandatory with the directive and you must specify at least
one signal each. However, other arguments are optional and can be used to include more specific
constraints.

     cdc specification clockoff -reset signal_pattern... -rx_clock signal_pattern...
     [-module module...]

       · Clock domain crossings - Scenarios where the clock pin of the Rx register is off when its reset is
          deasserted.

            cdc specification clockoff ­reset TX ­rx_clock clk2

Questa® CDC User Guide  81
CDC Basics

Clockoff Specification                                                                                    

    · There can be scenarios where there is single reset and multiple clocks specified in directive.

         cdc specification clockoff ­reset TX1 ­rx_clock clk2 clk4

       To filter both the crossings, using the directive cdc specification clockoff ­reset TX1 ­rx_clock
       clk2 clk4 is same as specifying cdc specification clockoff -reset TX1 -rx_clock clk2 and cdc
       specification clockoff reset TX1 -rx_clock clk4.

    · For Rx clocks, you can also specify a list of clocks that eventually merge and that merged clock is
       connected to the clock pin of the Rx register.

82                      Questa® CDC User Guide
                        CDC Basics

                        Clockoff Specification

   cdc specification clockoff -reset TX -rx_clock clk1 clk2

  Output of gated clock can also be specified.

   cdc specification clockoff -reset TX -rx_clock AND_clk

  For this scenario, using the directive cdc specification clockoff -reset TX -rx_clock clk1 clk2
  works, while specifying it as cdc specification clockoff -reset TX -rx_clock clk1 and cdc
  specification clockoff reset TX -rx_clock clk2 will not work.
  In this scenario, there is a single reset and multiple clocks specified in the directive.

Support for HDM Scenarios

This feature enhances the handling of the clockoff specification in HDM scenarios. It ensures that clockoff
specifications are handled, and the corresponding crossings are successfully evaluated, when Tx and
Rx are in different HDM blocks. The specification must be applied in the top-run to evaluate "clockoff"
correctly, regardless of whether Tx/Rx is in a separate block or the top.

Questa® CDC User Guide                                                                             83
CDC Basics

Synchronizer Module Specification                                                                          

The -rx_clock and -reset options will evaluate clockoff specifications against signals that are present
outside HDM blocks and are not abstracted in the top-run. For the -reset option, you can specify the name
of the TX register as reported in the crossing, regardless of whether the TX is in an HDM block or the top
module.

Follow the above guidelines to ensure that the clockoff specification is correctly applied and reported in
HDM scenarios, providing clear and accurate evaluations in the top-run.

    Note:
    A conflict message is reported only if a clockoff specification is specified at the block level for a
    clock/reset pair but not in the top-run.

Examples

The following example demonstrates how clockoff specification is evaluated when Tx and Rx signals are
in different HDM blocks and the specification directive is mentioned in the top-level run.

Directives for top-run

   cdc specification on -clockoff
   cdc specification clockoff -reset Tx -rx_clock rx_clock

Sample Report

   Evaluations
   =================================================================
   Asynchronous reset deassertion synchronization with clockoff specification.

     (async_reset_clockoff)
   -----------------------------------------------------------------
   clk1 : start : tx_inst.Tx (../dut.v : 2)

                 clk2 : end : rx_inst.Rx (../dut.v : 3)
     (ID:async_reset_clockoff_62311) (Status : uninspected)

The evaluation async_reset_clockoff should then be correctly reported for the crossing Tx-->Rx.

Synchronizer Module Specification

Use this specification when you have designated synchronizer modules in your design. When you enable
the specification, any crossing that does not match the design requirements will be flagged as violation.

84                                 Questa® CDC User Guide

                                                                      Synchronizer Module Specification

Figure 28 shows a basic form of a synchronizer module specification.

                        Figure 28. Synchronizer Module Specification

Use the cdc specification on directive to turn on the synchronizer module specification. This preference is
specific to Control Signal Synchronizers.

     cdc specification on ­syncmodule
The cdc specification syncmodule directive specifies a user-specified name for the module that contains a
control signal synchronizer.

     cdc specification syncmodule module...
CDC crossings with control signal synchronizers inside the specified modules are reported as evaluation.

         Note:
         If you enable the synchronizer module specification and do not specify any module, the tool
         reports all control signal synchronizers as violations.

Example

The following design example defines two synchronizer modules, syncmod and Invalidsyncmod. Both
the modules contain synchronizers, however, only syncmod is specified using the cdc specification
syncmodule directive. So, the synchronized crossing in syncmod is reported in evaluation and the
crossing in Invalidsyncmod is reported as violation.

Design

  module syncmod(input tx_data, rx_clk,
    output rx_data);

  reg r1, r2;
  always@(posedge rx_clk)begin

      r1 <= tx_data;
      r2 <= r1; end
  assign rx_data = r2;
  endmodule

  module Invalidsyncmod(input tx_data,
   rx_clk, output rx_data_2);

  reg r1, r2;
  always@(posedge rx_clk) begin

     r1 <= tx_data;
     r2 <= r1; end

Questa® CDC User Guide                                                                             85
CDC Basics

Synchronizer Module Specification       

    assign rx_data_2 = r2;
    endmodule

    module dut(input tx_data, tx_clk,
     rx_clk, output rx_data);

    reg r1;
    always@(posedge tx_clk)
    r1 <= tx_data;
    syncmod S1(r1, rx_clk, rx_data);
    Invalidsyncmod S2(r1, rx_clk,

     rx_data_2);
    endmodule

Directive

  cdc specification on -syncmodule
  cdc specification syncmodule syncmod

Support for HDM Scenarios

This feature enhances the handling of synchronizer modules in different HDM scenarios. It ensures that
Questa CDC accurately verifies synchronizer modules against design requirements. When enabled, it
reports crossings with Rx within specified modules as evaluations and flags those with Rx outside as
violations or cautions. The feature also provides clear "Specification Passed" or "Specification Failed"
messages, improving the clarity and accuracy of synchronization issue identification.

  1. If syncmod_block is specified as a valid syncmodule:
       Directives for rx_block

  Cases for top-run reporting

   Specification turned on at the top with matching module name (syncmod_block):

   Specification turned on at the top with a mismatch in the module name:

     The crossing Tx-->Rx in the top run is reported as a Violation/Caution, converting
     "Specification Passed" to "Specification Failed".

     It disregards the syncmodule details from the block, and reports Tx-->Rx as a normal 2DFF
     family scheme without the "Specification Passed" message. An hcdc-98 message is also
     reported to notify the user of this mismatch.

       is specified with the cdc specification syncmodule directive:
       Directives for rx_block

        cdc specification on -syncmodule

Synchronizer Clock Enable Specification

A clock sync enables crossing is when the Rx enable clock can control the receiving clock. In addition, the
specification provide constraints that enable to refine the results further.
Figure 29 shows a basic form of a clock_sync_enable scheme.

                                           Figure 29. clock_sync_enable scheme

Use the cdc specification on directive to turn on the synchronizer clock enable specification.

     cdc specification on ­clockenable
Use the cdc preference clockenable directive to set preferences for the detection of the
clock_sync_enable scheme.

     cdc preference clockenable [-rx_enable_sync] [-disable_control_check]
The cdc specification clockenable directive specifies enable signals from the receiver domain. The
-rx_enable option is mandatory with the directive and you must specify at least one enable signal.
However, other arguments are optional and can be used to include more specific constraints.

     cdc specification clockenable -rx_enable rx_enable_pattern...
     [-module module_pattern...]

     [-from tx_signal_pattern...] [-to rx_signal_pattern...] [-tx_clock tx_clock_pattern...]

     [-rx_clock rx_clock_pattern...] [-disable_control_check]

The enable signals specified must be driven by a port, register or latch.

clock_sync_enable Scheme Detection

Figure 30 shows the clock_sync_enable scheme detection process. Clocksyncenable-style crossings are
analyzed as follows:

88                                       Questa® CDC User Guide
                        CDC Basics

                        Synchronizer Enable Specification

  1. Start with a crossing that has a combinational logic in RX clock.
  2. The crossing is identified as a valid clock_sync_enable scheme if it matches the following

       criterion:
         Enable signal in clock gate logic matches the enable signal specified.
         Crossing matches the constraints specified using the cdc specification clockenable directive.
         Crossing passes the functional check if the disable_control_check option is specified.
         Enable signal is driven by a synchronizer if the rx_enable_sync option is specified.
  3. Otherwise, the crossing can be partial_clock_gate_sync or clock_gate_sync.
  4. Otherwise, the crossing is reported as no_sync violation.

signal in the receiver domain. The specification further provides constraint options that you can use to

Unclocked Latch                                                                                                

Unclocked Latch

CDC determines a latch to be unclocked if no clock signal reaches the enable pin of the latch or, if the
clock that reaches the latch is constant or stable.

The enable pin is given higher priority. If enable is either constant or stable, then the latch is treated as
unclocked, irrespective of the domain of D-pin. The enable pin must have clock or clock divider in their
fanin then only these are considered as clocked, else these are categorized as unclocked.

The unclocked latches are further categorized as:

    · Single Domain: When D pin has the same domain as enable pin or only one of the pins has a
       domain, then the unclocked latch is part of the single domain list.

    · Mixed Domain: When D pin has different domain than enable pin or enable and D pin have
       multiple domains, then the unclocked latch is part of the mixed domain list.

    · Stable Enable: When enable pin is stable, the unclocked latch is always categorized as Stable
       Enable.

       · Constant Enable: When enable pin is constant, the unclocked latch is always categorized as
          Constant Enable.

In Table 7, the rows represent the clock domain and the columns represent the enable and D pin,
respectively.

Const 1          Clk1         Constant Enable                 Clk1

Const 1          Clk1, Clk2   Constant Enable                 Clk1, Clk2 (Multiple clocks)

Stable           Constant/Stable/Unspecified Stable Enable    Unspecified

Stable           Clk1         Stable Enable                   Clk1

Stable           Clk1, Clk2   Stable Enable                   Clk1, Clk2 (Multiple clocks)

Unspecified      Unspecified  Unspecified                     Unspecified

Unclocked Latch Crossings

CDC determines a latch to be unclocked if its enable is not a clock signal. To avoid metastability issues
at the latch and its destination registers, the enable signal, data input, and data output of the latch must
belong to the same clock domain. CDC assigns the domain of its enable signal to the latch and looks
for CDC paths from or to the latch. These CDC paths are flagged as data_latch and bus_data_latch
violations.

CDC infers the signals that drive clock pins of registers as clock nets. However, it does not infer the
enable signals of latches as clocks by default. In general, the enable signal of a latch may or may not be a
clock as it could be a part of the control logic. When the enable signal of a latch is not a clock signal, that
is, the enable signal is not inferred as a clock because it does not drive clock pins of registers, CDC infers
the domain of the latch from the clock domains contributing to the enable logic. Usually, the enable signal
of the latch is controlled by a single clock domain. Otherwise, the data in the latch can be latched to a mix
of clock domains, resulting in metastability at the latch output.

If the latch is not a CDC path, the data, the enable signal, and the output of the latch connect to the same
clock domain. Figure 36 shows such a latch operating in a single clock domain without a CDC path where
the enable signal of the latch is not inferred as a clock.

                                             Figure 36. Latch Without CDC Path

If the enable signal reaches a register or latch in a different clock domain, CDC flags this error as a
separate crossing. However, the part of the design shown in Figure 36 does not contain a CDC path so it
has no CDC issues.

Figure 37 shows a situation where signals from clock domain clk2 control when the latch captures data,
but the input and output of the latch are in clock domain clk1.

Questa® CDC User Guide             95
CDC Basics

Unclocked Latch Crossings                                

                           Figure 37. Latch On CDC Path

This can result in metastability at the latch and the rx register. If the input of the latch changes while its
capture edge is being triggered by the signal ctrl, the latch output can become metastable. Similarly, if the
output of the latch is changed by its enable signal while rx is capturing data, metastability can manifest at
the rx register. Therefore, CDC generates two crossings for the latch--one from tx to latch and another
from latch to rx.

In Figure 38, the enable signal of the latch is a combination of signals from two different clock domains
clk1 and clk2.

                                         Figure 38. Latch With Problematic Enable

Irrespective of the clock domain of the input of the latch, its enable signal can asynchronously latch
data while the input of the latch may be changing, causing metastability issue at the latch. Similarly, a
change in the output of the latch can be asynchronously triggered by a change in the enable signal. This
can happen due to a change in the ctrl2 output, thereby causing a change in the input of rx when it is
capturing data, resulting in metastability at register rx. The most likely cause of the issue is an incomplete
clock setup or inferencing. It could also be due to unspecified clock relationship between clk1 and clk2.
Or, it could be a design error, where a signal from the clk2 domain enables a latch operating in the clk1
domain.

As shown in Figure 37 and Figure 38, crossings from and to the latches that are not enabled by clocks
are flagged as data_latch crossings in case of single-bit signals and bus_data_latch crossings in
case of multiple-bit signals. You must review these errors and either fix the setup issues by grouping

96                                                       Questa® CDC User Guide
                        CDC Basics

                        Unclocked Latch Crossings

the appropriate clocks or fix the design issue if it is confirmed to be a design bug. As an alternative
to CDC analysis in the presence of unclocked latches, you can use the option cdc preference
-detect_pure_latch_clock so that the enable signals of unclocked latches are treated as new clocks and
are assigned new clock domains. This approach does not utilize the driving clock domains of the enable
signal of the latch. If all the enable signals of the latches in your design are clocks, this approach yields
results closer to your design intent.

Resolving Latches With Multiple Clock Domains In Their Enable Logic

Multiple clock domains in the enable logic of the latch can lead to metastability at the latch. This is
because irrespective of the clock domain of the input signal of the latch, the data may be latched
asynchronously with respect to its input. For such situations, CDC creates a virtual domain,
LatchEnCtrldBy_clk1_clk2, to represent the clock domains of the latch, so that crossings to and from such
latches can be reported. These latches are also reported under Unclocked Latches in the detailed CDC
report. An hdl-280 warning message is also generated if such latches are present in the design.

To resolve the multiple domains issue, resolve the clock domains of these latches to a single domain. The
following are some of the likely reasons behind the mixed domains:

  · The multiple clock domains involved in the enable logic are synchronous so you can group them
     into a single group. The latch automatically inherits the common domain.

  · The CDC clock propagation engine fails to propagate the clock to the enable pin of the latch
     because of combinational logic in the clock tree. In this case, guide CDC analysis to propagate
     the clock to the latch enable or define new clocks for the enable signals of such latches.

       · Due to design error, a signal from an incorrect clock domain enables the latch belonging to a
          different clock domain.

To debug the issue, trace the enable logic of such latches in the GUI. The GUI shows the driving clock
domains for each signal in the fanin cone of the enable logic.

Questa® CDC User Guide                                                                                  97
CDC Basics

Static CDC Analysis  

Static CDC Analysis

Static CDC analysis performs a sequence of critical functions for CDC verification.

     1. Identifies clock domain crossing logic.

          Static CDC analysis examines the design RTL and uses the user-specified and inferred clock
          groups to find the clock trees that determine the clock domains in the design. It then assigns each
          register to a clock domain. Static CDC analysis identifies the clock domain crossings by finding
          registers that drive registers from other clock domains and tracing associated crossing logic.

     2. Classifies crossing by CDC scheme.

          Static CDC analysis categorizes each crossing as one of a set of predefined CDC schemes.
          For example, one scheme contains all single-bit CDC signals that are synchronized by two-
          register data synchronizers. Another scheme contains all multiple-bit CDC signals that are not
          synchronized. Some schemes are identified as violations. For example, the following figure
          shows single-bit CDC signals with combinational logic driving, or within, the synchronizers.

         You can redefine the severities used for the different schemes. For example, you can make latch
         synchronization a violation.

    3. Verifies synchronizers.
         Static CDC analysis verifies that the expected synchronizers are used for the crossings..

    4. Verifies certain CDC protocols.
         If CDC formal verification is enabled, static CDC analysis includes static formal analysis of certain
         CDC protocols.

    5. Promotes CDC protocol checkers.

98                   Questa® CDC User Guide
                        CDC Basics

                        CDC Protocol Checker Promotion

    Static CDC analysis generates CDC protocol checkers for certain CDC schemes based on their
    scheme type, transmit clock, transmit signals, receive clock and receive signals. CDC checkers
    are not promoted for crossings that have severity proven or waived or for filtered crossings.
    Promoted checkers represent CDC protocols that need assertion-based analysis by the Questa
    Functional Verification tools and possibly simulation.

  CDC Protocol Checker Promotion

CDC Protocol Checker Promotion

Assertions are specifications of design behavior. They can be checked during simulation and they can act
as targets and constraints for formal verification. The CDC transfer protocol for a CDC synchronization
scheme is an assertion.

For example, consider a CDC signal synchronized by a two-register data synchronizer. This
synchronization scheme has the following implied CDC protocol:

       · The transmit signal remains stable until the synchronizer's output register has sampled the
          previous value.

This protocol can be checked with the following assertion using simulation with assertions and formal
verification:

       · The transmit signal must not change for at least N consecutive transmit-clock cycles, where N is
          a function of the transmit-clock and receive-clock frequencies.

If this assertion is violated, then a possible counterexample exists in which metastability on the CDC
signal can cause an incorrect result. In this case, the transmitted data is missed by the receiver logic.
In regular simulation (which is not subject to metastability unless it is a catastrophic violation of the
protocol), the signal reaches its goal and the problem is not detected. However, when using simulation
with assertions, an assertion fires. You can then examine the conditions under which the failure occurs
and correct the design problem.

Signal Stability Protocols

Single-bit CDC signals can be synchronized by various different types of synchronizers. However, such
synchronization must follow a signal stability protocol where each new value of a transmit signal is held
stable long enough for the receiving domain to sample it at least twice. Formal CDC tries to find proofs for
the signal stability protocols by analyzing the transmit signal pulse widths of the following types of CDC
schemes:

       · two_dff

       · four_latch

       · dff_sync_gated_clk

       · two_dff_phase

       · pulse_sync

Gray-Coding Protocols

Questa® CDC User Guide  99
CDC Basics

CDC Protocol Checker Promotion                                                                             

Multi-bit CDC signals (that is, data buses) can be synchronized by synchronizers typically used for
single-bit signals. However, such synchronization must follow a gray-coding protocol where only
one data bit changes at a time. Formal CDC tries to find proofs for the gray-coding protocols (that is,
hamming_distance_1) of the following types of CDC schemes:

· bus_two_dff

· bus_four_latch

· bus_dff_sync_gated_clk

· bus_two_dff_phase

       · reconvergence (if enabled by cdc preference protocol -promote_reconvergence).

Specifying Design Intent

The CDC protocol checkers contain SystemVerilog assertions (SVA) and are enclosed in a module that
also contains SVA cover statements and covergroups. The CDC protocol checkers are configured to
verify the CDC transfer protocol for a CDC synchronization scheme. The CDC protocol checkers provide
a simplified debug solution for your simulation and formal verification flows.

The CDC protocol checkers completely characterize associated synchronization schemes. A design that
does not violate any assertions conform to the associated CDC synchronization scheme. CDC protocol
assertions are available for the common CDC synchronization schemes. Static CDC analysis identifies
the synchronization schemes used for the CDC signals in the design. Based on this analysis, CDC
promotes instances of CDC protocol assertions depending on the synchronization scheme (although not
all schemes have associated promoted assertions). CDC also generates the cdc_protocol.rpt report file,
which contains details of promoted protocol assertions. The protocol checkers validate CDC behavior
during assertion-based verification.

Path and Protocol ID

Each CDC path has a unique path ID--derived from the path parameters--that remains the same
across multiple tool runs. Each CDC check is associated with the unique ID, which is also used to name
the associated promoted protocol checker. This path ID associates the CDC checkers in simulation to
their corresponding checks in the CDC report, which simplifies the correlation of the static and protocol
checking results. For example:

· CDC Checks window

CDC Analysis with DesignWare® Components                                                                  

CDC Analysis with DesignWare® Components

Questa CDC includes synthesizable version of DesignWare components. The default DesignWare
simulation components are encrypted, which cannot be directly used for CDC analysis. Moreover, CDC
also does not support remodeled DesignWare elements for simulation with CDC protocol monitors or
CDC-FX simulation.

Using Built-in DesignWare Components

For Questa CDC to understand the DesignWare components, a synthesizable version must be
referenced. Questa CDC includes this version in its installation package.
To pick up the built-in DesignWare libraries, use the cdc run -dw option. For example,

   prompt> qverify -c -do "cdc run -d DUT -dw"

The default DesignWare simulation libraries are encrypted. If you use these default libraries, which are
not included in the installation package, results in unresolved module warnings. For example,

   Warning : Unresolved module. Instance 'u_DW_bin2gray', Module
     'DW_bin2gray', File 'top.v', Line 27. [parser-47]

Remodeled DesignWare Components

When the remodeled version of the DesignWare components are not available, you can choose one of
the following options:

       · Infer missing DesignWare components as black box.
          Run CDC with -auto_black_box option, which turns all unresolved modules into black boxes.

            prompt> qverify -c -do "cdc run -d DUT -auto_black_box"

          Using the option turns all unresolved DesignWare components into black boxes. When the
          constraints are not specified for black box ports, tool does not report CDC crossings for paths to
          the inputs of a black box or for paths from the outputs of a black box.

       · Use the simulation definition.
          Run CDC with the simulation DesignWare models. Models with unsupported constructs are
          turned into inferred black boxes and tool reports the corresponding CDC black box schemes.
          For combinational DesignWare models, sometimes the simulation definition can be elaborated
          directly or with some small modifications. To run CDC directly on the simulation modules, use the
          following command:

            prompt> qverify -c -do "cdc run -d DW_bin2gray"

     · Define a black box model.

102                                       Questa® CDC User Guide
                                                                            CDC Basics

                        CDC Analysis with DesignWare® Components

  a. Black box for clocked DesignWare modules.

       Examples of clocked DesignWare modules include DW_fifo_s2_sf_MS and
       DW_fifoctl_s2_sf_MS.

       Sample of Tcl constraints for black box:

        netlist blackbox DW_fifoctl_s2_sf_MS
        netlist port domain <port list> -clock <clock port> /

                     -module DW_fifoctl_s2_sf_MS

  b. Custom synchronizer for DesignWare synchronizer modules.

       Examples of DesignWare synchronizer modules include DW_sync, DW_pulse_sync,
       DW_data_sync, DW_data_sync_1c, DW_data_sync_na, and DW_pulseack_sync. Specifying
       a custom synchronizer enables reporting of correct custom synchronizer usage.

       Sample Tcl constraints:

        cdc custom sync DW_sync -type dw_sync
        cdc custom sync data -from in -to out -module DW_sync
        hier port domain <port list> -clock <clock port> -module DW_sync

  c. HDM for non-clocked DesignWare modules.

       Examples of non-clocked DesignWare modules include DW_bin2gray, DW_gray2bin, and
       DW02_mult. Specifying an HDM enables forward propagation of clock signals and signal
       clock domains.

              Note:
              The HD must include an HDL definition. An HDL definition template can be generated
              with the cdc run -auto_black_box directive. This HDL definition must be compiled
              before specifying the HDM.

                Sample Tcl constraints:

                 hier block DW02_mult
                 hier port domain <output port> -combo_path <input port list> \

                            -module DW02_mult

Override User Defined DesignWare Libraries

When the cdc run -L option is used, -L option provides preference to user-defined DesignWare libraries.
You can override the behavior of L and give preference to internal DesignWare libraries by using the
override_user_dw_lib option with the netlist preference command. For example,
If you specify the cdc run -L option, user-defined DesignWare libraries (user_dw_lib) is given preference
over internal DesignWare libraries.

   cdc run -d dut -L user_dw_lib

Questa® CDC User Guide                                                      103
CDC Basics

CDC Analysis with DesignWare® Components                                                        

To change that, specify the -override_user_dw_lib option. This provides preference to internal
DesignWare libraries over user-defined DesignWare libraries.

netlist preference -override_user_dw_lib
cdc run -d dut -L user_dw_lib

Simulation                                                                                                  

Simulation

To simulate a design with CDC protocol checkers, use assertions in simulation and your standard HDL
simulator. During assertions in simulation, the CDC checkers verify the functionality of the CDC protocols.
A violation of a protocol assertion makes the associated CDC checker fire. To debug assertion firings and
review assertions coverage, run the GUI with the database from the simulation (cdc_sim.db).

A new CDC GUI window (Simulation) contains the simulation results (Figure 41).

                                                 Figure 41. Simulation Window

To invoke the waveform viewer with the assertion firing from simulation (Figure 42) right-click the Firing
in the Simulation window and select Show Firings to display the Firings window. Select all firings or an
individual firing to show the waveform.

106         Questa® CDC User Guide
                                                                     CDC Basics

                                                                     Custom Messaging

                        Figure 42. Show Simulation Firing Waveforms

        Custom Messaging

Custom Messaging

Enhance the reporting of CDC-FX metastability injection during simulation.

During CDC-FX analysis, the simulation run generates customized messages of CDC-FX firings. These
firings represent cases where metastability is intentionally injected into the CDC path to model hardware
behavior. This custom reporting includes details such as the timestamp of the firing, the type of CDC
violation (setup/hold violation), changes in data values observed at the input of the receive register, and
the implications of metastability injection on the output of the receive register.

As an example, below is a screenshot of the schematic depicting a CDC path of type combo_logic
and the custom report for a CDC-FX firing on this path. The message depicts a firing event at 224ns,
indicating a setup violation due to a change in data from 1111 to 0111, resulting in a one-cycle delay in the
data transition.

CDC Basics

 1)
     Check:cdc_fx, Scope:tb.U0.cdc_fx.combo_logic_5195.assert_cdc_fx,
 Message:Data changed from 1111 to 0111 in the 'setup'
                         metastability window at the data-pin of receive register
 'U0.U0.rx1[3:0]'. Metastability is injected on 'U0.U0.rx1[3:0]'
                         resulting in the transition to be delayed by 1 cycle.

                               Chapter 3
                          CDC Analysis

Questa CDC is a static analysis system that comprises a clock model compiler, a CDC analysis engine,
and a GUI debug environment. The qverify batch command and GUI run under the qverify shell.

The CDC analysis flow consists of running qverify in two phases in different modes:

  1. qverify in CLI mode

       Compiles a clock model of the design; runs CDC static analysis and generates a database file
       (cdc.db) containing the results. Static CDC analysis infers clock trees, identifies CDC signals and
       detects synchronization patterns.

  2. qverify in GUI mode

       Displays the CDC GUI with the results from cdc.db. This GUI has design data analysis windows
       and CDC verification tools--source code editor, schematics browser and waveform viewer--for
       debugging issues found by the analyzer.

    qverify Command
    Clock Tree Detection
    Static CDC Verification Flow
    CDC Protocol Verification
    CDC Constraints Verification
    CDC-FX Verification
    Modal CDC Analysis
    Hierarchical CDC Analysis
    Power Aware CDC
    CDC Analysis of FPGAs
    CDC Encryption
    CDC Analysis with CDC Assist Machine Learning
    SDC Native Analysis Flow
    CDC Waiver Guidelines

qverify Command                                                                                              

qverify Command

The Questa Formal verification flow starts with a compiled design library. The analysis portion of the flow
has two phases. Each phase runs the qverify command in a different mode: batch mode and GUI mode.

                                          Figure 45. Questa CDC Verification Flow

       Note:
       For more information about compiling a design library, see the Design Style Support chapter of
       the Questa Functional Verification Command Reference.

       Batch Mode: qverify -c -do
       GUI Mode: qverify cdc.db

Batch Mode: qverify -c -do

With a compiled design, the first phase of CDC analysis is to run the analyzer in batch mode.
Table 9 shows the batch mode syntax for qverify.

                                   Table 9. qverify Batch Mode Syntax

qverify ­c ­do {do_file | "commands"} [-od output_directory] [­l log_file] [-licq]

­c                                 Run a batch session.

­do {do_file | "commands"}         Execute the specified Tcl DO script.

­od output_directory               Path name of the initial output directory for the analyzer session.

­l log_file                        Name of the top-level session log.

-licq                              Enable license queueing for the top-level session.

112                                                                                 Questa® CDC User Guide
                                                                                    CDC Analysis

                                                                           Batch Mode: qverify -c -do

The analyzer executes Tcl commands in the DO file procedurally. The DO script can include different
procedural features such as looping and variable substitution and it can perform several CDC analysis
runs in the same session. But a basic qverify DO file flow has five steps (see the Tcl Commands chapter
of the Questa Functional Verification Command Reference).

  1. Add directives
       Use the general-purpose and cdc directives to configure the analysis run.

  2. Adjust settings
       Use the configure command to change basic settings for subsequent commands.

  3. Run CDC analysis
       Use the cdc run command to initiate a formal analysis run.

     4. Run post-session analysis
          Use the cdc utilities to generate reports and related files.

Steps 1 ­ 3 must be part of the same qverify session. Step 4 is optional.

need the .db file generated during the batch mode for analyzing the CDC results through the qverify shell.
Use the following command in the qverify shell to view and debug the CDC analysis results in the GUI:

   prompt> qverify cdc.db

CDC Checks Window

View the results of CDC analysis.

Description

The CDC Checks Window shows the results of Clock Domain Crossing (CDC) analysis. Each CDC
scheme instance has a status flag that indicates the status for the CDC instance. This window also shows
results merged from simulation and formal verification sessions. It provides various tools and options for
inspecting and managing CDC checks.

To view the CDC Checks Window, follow these steps:

     1. Choose View from the main menu.

     2. Select CDC Results.

     3. Click on CDC Checks.

                              Figure 47. CDC Checks Window

     Note:
     Each CDC scheme instance has a status flag that indicates the status for the CDC instance.
     Right-click a scheme instance to pop up commands for displaying various debug windows for
     inspecting the crossing. Also shows results merged from simulation and formal verification
     sessions.

Objects

    · Entries
      Each entry also has the following information:
