                        Clock Tree Detection

Clock Tree Detection

The report-clocks phase of CDC static analysis performs clock tree detection. CDC analysis finds all
signals that clock storage elements and tries to stitch the clocks together to identify the design's clock
trees. Accurate static CDC analysis requires that clock trees are identified properly and that clock trees
for the same clock domains are grouped together.

Only paths that cross clock domain boundaries are reported as clock domain crossings and are further
analyzed. So, all expected clock domains should match all the separate clock groups. If two expected
clock domains are combined in the same group, no CDC reporting and analysis occurs for paths between
the two (which makes analysis incomplete). Similarly, if what is expected to be a single clock domain is
split into two clock groups, CDC analysis reports paths between them as clock domain crossings and
analyzes them (which adds "noise" to the results and reduces performance). Having many more groups
than expected clock domains might even slow some GUI operations (such as expanding entries) so much
that the GUI becomes unusable (seems to "hang").

        Clocks Window

        User-Specified Clock Trees

        Inferred Clock Trees

Questa® CDC User Guide  137
CDC Analysis

Clocks Window  

Clocks Window

Shows how CDC analysis assumes the clock groupings specifying the clock domains are defined. To view
the Clocks window, choose View > Clocks.

                                                    Figure 60. Clocks Window

Description

The clock groups are color-coded: References to objects in a particular clock group (such as source code
and schematics objects) are displayed in the same color.

Objects

    · Clock levels

      The first level is the clock group classification (the specified type or one of the inferred types,
      described in subsequent sections). The second level lists the separate clock groups. The third
      level lists the clock trees that make up the group. The remaining levels show the various levels
      of the clock trees.

    · Clock group name

      The name of the clock group (cpu_clk_in, mac_clk_in, core_clk_in and check_en in the
      figure) is the top-level string. This name can be specified explicitly (using the -group <name>
      option of the netlist clock directive) or it can be derived. A derived clock group name is the
      hierarchical name of the originator clock in the group. If the group has multiple clock trees (and
      no explicit clock group name), the derived group name is the originator clock (root) of one of
      the clock trees.

    · Other information

      The Clocks window also shows the number of register and latch bits clocked in the
      corresponding domains. The Expression column shows gating expressions for gated clocks to
      help debug the CDC setup. Gated clocks need to be resolved to force their interpretation as
      nodes in real trees (gated clocks have multiple "roots").

138            Questa® CDC User Guide
                        CDC Analysis

                        User-Specified Clock Trees

User-Specified Clock Trees

You manually specify a clock tree by naming the originator clock (root) for the tree in a netlist clock
directive.
For example:

   netlist clock cpu_clk_in
   netlist clock core_clk_in
   netlist clock mac_clk_in

These three directives identify three trees with originator clocks cpu_clk_in,core_clk_in and mac_clk_in.
Each clock is a signal referenced hierarchically from the top level of the design. CDC clock tree detection
traces the tree down levels of hierarchy to its "leaf" clocks. For example, the clock tree for the originator
clock core_clk_in is:

   core_clk_in
     ­>core_clk
      ­>fifo_1_d.wr_clk
        ­>fifo_1_d.u0.Wclk
      ­>fifo_0_h.wr_clk
        ­>fifo_0_h.u0.Wclk

The core_clk_in signal drives core_clk in the top module. The core_clk then drives wr_clk in fifo_1_d,
which drives Wclk in u0, and so on. When the result is unambiguous, tree detection follows through
MUXed and combinational logic. For example, core_clk is defined with this MUX:

   assign cpu_clk = scan_mode ? scan_clk : cpu_clk_in;

The ambiguity is resolved by a netlist constant directive:

   netlist constant scan_mode 1'b0

Clock trees rooted in lower levels of hierarchy can be specified hierarchically or with the module option:

   netlist clock fifo_1_d.wr_clk

or

   netlist clock wr_clk -module generic_fifo

The first directive identifies one clock tree (in the mac.u0 instance).
The second directive identifies a tree per instance of generic_fifo. For example, if fifo_1_d and fifo_0_h
are instances of generic_fifo, the two trees have roots fifo_1_d.wr_clk and fifo_0_h.wr_clk. All trees
defined by the same netlist clock directive are grouped together, so all of the clocks in the two clock trees
are in the same group. If a name for the group is not specified (that is, with the -group <name> option),
one of the matching root clocks is selected as the name (for example, clock group fifo_1_d.wr_clk).
A single clock tree can be split by specifying roots in separate directives, for example:

Questa® CDC User Guide  139
CDC Analysis

User-Specified Clock Trees     

netlist clock core_clk_in
netlist clock fifo_1_d.wr_clk
netlist clock fifo_0_h.wr_clk

Clock Tree Grouping

A clock domain can have a single clock tree or it can have multiple clock trees. For example, the clock
domain might be clocked by several synchronous distributed clock trees. Or, a clock tree might be
"broken" into two pieces by going through a black box, MUX or combinational logic. Specifying multiple
trees in a single directive is one method:

   netlist clock cpu_clk_in core_clk_in

Specifying them in two directives (with the -group<name> option) is another:

   netlist clock cpu_clk_in
   netlist clock core_clk_in -group cpu_clk_in

Or:

   netlist clock cpu_clk_in -group master_clk
   netlist clock core_clk_in -group master_clk

Synchronous Clocks with Different Periods
Multiple clock trees in a design might be synchronous but have different clock periods--they might be
generated by clock dividers or similar logic. Typically, logic clocked synchronously is validated with static
timing analysis, including logic clocked between clock trees of different periods. Questa CDC is a tool for
verifying crossings between asynchronously clocked logic. To prevent CDC analysis from considering
paths between logic clocked synchronously to be clock domain crossings (which require synchronization),
the synchronous clock trees must be assigned to the same clock group. For example:

   netlist clock cpu_clk_in -group master_clk -period 100
   netlist clock core_clk_in -group master_clk -period 25

In some cases, paths between logic clocked by synchronous clocks with different periods should be
considered asynchronous. You must decide on a case-by-case basis whether or not such clock trees
should be members of the same clock group. If paths between two separately clocked circuits do not
require synchronization, their clock trees should be in the same clock group. Clock trees in different
clock groups are considered asynchronous and CDC analysis assumes synchronizers are required on
crossings between their domains.
hdl-77 Warnings
The required argument to a netlist clock directive is a repeatable clock name pattern, for example:

   netlist clock core_clk_in xyzzy xya*

Any pattern with no matching signal generates an hdl-77 warning:

140                            Questa® CDC User Guide
                                                                   CDC Analysis

                                                            Inferred Clock Trees

  # Warning : Signal specified for directive has no match.

  # Signal 'xyzzy', Module 'demo_top', Directive 'netlist clock',

  # File 'qs_files/directives.tcl', Line 5. [hdl-77]

  #  : Signal will be skipped.

  # Expanding Wildcard 'xya*', Module 'demo_top',

  # File 'qs_files/directives.tcl', Line '5'

  # Warning : Signal specified for directive has no match.

  # Signal 'xya*', Module 'demo_top', Directive 'netlist clock',

  # File 'qs_files/directives.tcl', Line 5. [hdl-77]

  #  : Signal will be skipped.

You should fix these directives because a pattern might be mis-typed.

Unused Clocks

After verifying the specified patterns match design signals, clock tree detection checks that the signals in
the tree are real clocks: they actually clock storage elements (register and latch bits). Those that do not
are classified as unused clocks.

Ignored Clock Groups

You can mark clock groups to be ignored. Their associated clock domains are removed from CDC
analysis: No crossings from/to the domains of ignored clock groups are analyzed. To mark a clock group
as ignored use the cdc clock attribute command:

  cdc clock attribute -group cpu_clk_in -ignore

The -group argument is the clock group name specified with a netlistclock -group <name> directive, or an
inferred name taken from one of the originator clocks in a tree in the group.

Inferred Clock Trees

Ideally, you define clock groups by specifying the top-level clock ports with individual netlist clock
directives; CDC clock tree detection traces the groups down to the leaf clocks; the entire design is
partitioned into the expected clock domains; CDC analysis works; you are done.

Resolving Inferred Clock Trees

Unfortunately, with complex clocking schemes in designs, this flow is not typical. A design might have
black boxes that originate clocks or that have clock trees pass through. Clock tree detection splits these
trees into separate clock groups. Combinational logic in clock trees and MUXed clocks complicate the
situation further. Grouping split trees helps, but might not be sufficient.

The initial user-specified clock trees typically do not cover all clocks. So, after performing clock tree
detection on the user-specified clock groups, CDC analysis runs clock tree detection on the remaining
clocks. The result is a set of clock trees, called inferred clock trees. CDC analysis considers these
individual trees to be individual clock groups. The process of adjusting the clock model specifications
to eliminate inferred clock trees and partitioning the design into user-defined clock domains is called
resolving the inferred clock trees.

Questa® CDC User Guide                                             141
CDC Analysis

Inferred Clock Trees                                                                                         

         CAUTION:
         You MUST resolve inferred clock trees before proceeding to full CDC static analysis. Otherwise,
         the inferred clocks trees are treated as defining separate clock domains. Much extra time is
         wasted analyzing "false" crossings among them and between them and the user-defined clock
         groups. In extreme cases, so many innocuous violations are reported that the GUI seems to slow
         down to the point of "freezing."

Two primary methods for resolving inferred clock trees are:

       · netlist clock
          Group inferred trees with other user-defined clock trees or with each other as new user-spefified
          clock groups.

       · netlist constant
          Get clock tree detection to properly group MUXed clocks by setting their MUX select signals to
          constants.

Clock Signal Classification
To help you resolve the inferred clock trees, clock tree detection classifies inferred clock trees into the
following classes: primary, black box, gate MUX, gated combo, undriven and other (Figure 61).

Inferring Combined Clock Trees

Some inferred clock trees are automatically combined into the same clock domain. For example, assume
clk1 and clk2 are in the same clock group. Then the tree rooted at clk_out1 is also grouped into the same
clock group (clk1):

assign clk_out1 = ~(clk1 || clk2);

Furthermore, if the port domains of en1 and en2 are not specified, then the tree rooted at clk_out2 is also
grouped in the clk1 clock group.

   assign clk_out2 = (clk1 && en1) || clk2 && en2);

HDM clock can be inferred as a gated clock. CDC analysis automatically identifies and handles HDM
clocks that show gated behavior. The clock tree report shows outclk as an HDM clock with gated
behavior.

   Directive

   cdc load hierdb Block/hcdc_block.hierdb;

Static CDC Verification Flow                                                                                 

Static CDC Verification Flow

Static CDC verification of a DUT is a three-phased flow.
As shown in Figure 62, the steps are:

     1. Compile the design.
     2. Run CDC analysis.
     3. Run GUI debug.

                                               Figure 62. Static CDC Verification Flow

Static CDC verification identifies the CDC signal paths (crossings) and their associated CDC schemes.
CDC schemes are ranked by severity, which are set by the cdc report scheme directive, or default to the
severity for the scheme. Typically, several cycles are spent adjusting the scheme identification attributes
and protocol promotion settings. Once you have properly configured static CDC verification, you can
enable the formal CDC analysis engine.

         Tip
         The following procedure uses the interactive OS shell to run the top-level commands. This
         method makes it easier to illustrate the various steps in the procedure. Typically, a Makefile,
         or other session management script is used instead. For examples of the Makefile method of
         scripting analysis sessions, see the CDC examples in <install_dir>/share/examples.

     Phase 1. Compiling the Design
     Phase 2: Running CDC Analysis
     Phase 3: Running GUI Debug
     Performance-Based Analysis Setup

148                                                                                     Questa® CDC User Guide
                        CDC Analysis

                        Phase 1. Compiling the Design

Phase 1. Compiling the Design

Use the compilation utilities to set up, compile and maintain the design libraries.

         Note:
         For more information, see the Design Style Support chapter of the Questa Functional Verification
         Command Reference.

Procedure

     1. Start from a working directory for the project.
         For example:

            prompt> cd /u/design/cdc

     2. Create a working library.

            prompt> vlib work

     3. Name the working library.

            prompt> vmap work work
            Copying /u/qstatic10.1/modeltech/../modelsim.ini to modelsim.ini
            Modifying modelsim.ini

         Note that a copy of the system modelsim.ini file is copied to the run directory and the local copy is
         modified to match the arguments of the vmap command.
     4. Compile the design files.
         Use vcom to compile the VHDL files and vlog to compile the Verilog/SystemVerilog files. For
         example:

            prompt> vcom -f pci.f
            prompt> vlog dut.v

         Check the warnings/errors messages and resolve any problems. To see more information about a
         message use the verror command.

            prompt> verror -full 2155

            MSG_IDX_GLBL_VARS_IN_VERILOG
            Global declarations are illegal in Verilog 2001 syntax.
            Global declarations are only legal in SystemVerilog. To enable
            SystemVerilog you can either use the -sv vlog command line switch
            or give the source file a .sv extension.

Questa® CDC User Guide  149
CDC Analysis

Phase 2: Running CDC Analysis  

Phase 2: Running CDC Analysis

You run CDC analysis by running qverify in batch mode (that is, with the -c -do options). In batch mode,
qverify runs the DO script specified by the -do argument. A DO script is a Tcl program that recognizes the
Questa Functional Verification extension to the standard Tcl commands.

         Note:
         For more information, see the Questa Functional Verification Command Reference.

The qverify command uses a Tcl interpreter internally. For example, you can run simple Tcl snippets with
qverify:

   prompt> qverify -c -do "exec date"
   # Questa Functional Verification System
   # Version 10.3x linux_x86_64 2012
   ...
   # Thu Apr 26 15:31:32 PDT 2012

Although the complete versatility of the Tcl scripting language is available, you need not be well versed in
Tcl to set up and run analysis sessions. The basic flows (and the flows shown in this manual) are simple
sequential scripts with no looping or branching.
The basic analysis session orchestrated by a typical qverify DO script follows the steps shown in Figure
63.

                                               Figure 63. CDC Analysis Session

150                            Questa® CDC User Guide
                                                                                      CDC Analysis

                                                                    Phase 2: Running CDC Analysis

Procedure

     1. Add directives.

         Directives are Questa Functional Verification Tcl commands that configure the subsequent analysis
         session. One method groups these commands in a separate DO file:

            prompt> cat cdc_directives.do
            # Define clocks
            netlist clock cpu_clk_in -period 50
            netlist clock core_clk_in -period 60
            netlist clock mac_clk_in -period 50
            # Define constants
            netlist constant scan_mode 1'b0
            # Add CDC constraints
            cdc reconvergence -depth 1 -divergence_depth 1
            cdc scheme on fifo handshake
            cdc port attribute in1 -combo_logic
            netlist blackbox pci_ctrl
            netlist port attribute cpu_in -no_combo

  The following are some example directive commands:

  · netlist clock -- Identify clocks' characteristics (including which clocks belong to the same clock
     groups).

  · netlist port attribute -- Identify primary ports' attributes for netlist checks.

  · netlist blackbox -- Identify modules/architectures that should be treated as "black boxes" for
     CDC analysis.

  · netlist constant -- Identify signals that should be considered constant for CDC analysis.

  · netlist memory -- Identify large memories that are modeled as single sequential elements for
     CDC analysis.

  · cdc preference -- Set the preferences for static CDC analysis.

  · cdc preference reset -- Define preferences for selecting which types of reset signals are
     included in reset trees.

  · cdc report scheme -- Set severities for CDC schemes.

  · cdc promote crossing and cdc promote scheme -- Set promotion attributes for CDC crossings
     and schemes.

      · cdc signal -- Override the classification of various signals and assign them certain CDC
         properties.

  2. Create the top-level DO script.

Questa® CDC User Guide                                                                              151
CDC Analysis

Phase 2: Running CDC Analysis                                                                             

     The script should run the directives, adjust the settings and execute cdc setup which detects clocks
     and resets, and identifies potential setup constraints.

     prompt> cat cdc.do
     onerror {exit 1}
     do cdc_directives.do
     configure error -inferred black_box
     cdc setup -d dut
     ### cdc run -d dut
     exit 0

        Notice the Questa Functional Verification onerror command. This command configures the session
        to exit when one of the Tcl commands encounters an error. For example, you want the session to
        end before running a long analysis session whenever a typo or other error occurs when running a
        directive. The last exit command is for future functionality, when a command line interpreter (CLI) is
        added. It prevents the session from dropping into the CLI at the end of a successful session.

        The do cdc_directives.do command runs the directives script created in step 1 (as if it were inline).
        The configure error -inferred black_box command adjusts the error condition by returning an error
        whenever clock model compilation processes an inferred black box (that is, one without a netlist
        blackbox directive).

        The cdc setup -d dut executable analyzes the design data and infers setup constraints that can
        be used for the CDC analysis. The command generates a CDC setup report (cdc.rpt) and CDC
        database (cdc.db) that includes the clock, resets, and port domain information. You can use the
        report or view the database in the GUI mode to review the CDC setup information.

     3. Perform CDC setup.

           prompt> qverify -c -do cdc.do -od cdc_results

     The -od cdc_results option sets the initial output directory to cdc_results.

     The cdc setup command also creates a directory (cdc_setup) with various templates. These
     templates list potential netlist directives (clock, resets, constant, and port domains) and stable
     signal directives. You can review these files and use the potential directives to create a separate
     directives file, which enables you to resolve the inferred clocks and resets before committing to a
     full CDC analysis run.

      a. Check for errors and warnings.

          Check the log file (cdc_setup.log) for errors and warnings. The Message Summary table gives
          the violation count of each type of error/warning.

     Message Summary

     -------------------------------------------------------------------

                     domains.

              bits

                     of port.

     Check cdc.rpt. This report shows clock, reset, and port domain information reported by cdc

     generate report directives.

     CDC static analysis resource requirements increase with the number of CDC signals identified
     in the design. Unconfigured CDC analysis can identify more CDC signals than the design
     actually has (for example because automatic clock grouping identifies more than the actual
     number of clock domains).

     Review and refine CDC setup to achieve the correct grouping. Adjust and add directives, then
     rerun CDC setup. The following clock data must be accurate before advancing to step 4:

  · Clocks are identified correctly -- Clocks not needed for CDC analysis can be removed
     from the clock list.

  · Clock groups are identified correctly -- Clocks can be added and removed from the
     different clock groups.

           · Ports are assigned to the correct clock domains -- Clock domains of DUT ports are
               inferred, but you can override these assignments. Clock domains of black box outputs must
               be identified.

  4. Change the DO script to run full CDC analysis.

     Once the design is compiled and the cdc setup results are verified, adjust the CDC session DO
     script:

Questa® CDC User Guide                                                                 153
CDC Analysis

Phase 3: Running GUI Debug                                                                         

           prompt> cat cdc.do
           onerror {exit 1}
           do cdc_directives.do
           configure error -inferred black_box
           ### cdc setup -d dut
           cdc run -d dut
           exit 0

        The cdc run ­d dut command runs full CDC analysis. Because the analysis is performed post
        the CDC setup, the clock setup is skipped which improves analysis performance. You can iterate
        the setup phase and then incrementally run the analysis step. Each analyzer and analysis model
        compiler tracks whether or not the setup is current or is different.

        If CDC setup is not performed before the CDC analysis, the analyzer runs the setup automatically.
        Otherwise, the analysis session is significantly faster because the setup is ready.

        The analysis updates the database (cdc.db) file with the CDC analysis, and the file can be read by
        qverify in GUI mode.

     5. Run a full CDC analysis session.

           prompt> qverify -c -do cdc.do -od cdc_results

     6. Check for errors and warnings.

        Check the log file (cdc_run.log) for errors and warnings.

     The default tuning of the CDC attributes provides a balance between performance and the effort
     spent to provide a high level of detail. You can adjust the exact balance by specifying a CDC
     attribute profile targeted to specific needs. For example, the following directives file creates a
     profile that has the minimum compute time and memory consumption. This profile is useful for very
     large designs, especially when working iteratively to fine-tune results at early stages of verification.

        # high_performance.do -- High-performance CDC profile
        # Turn off reconvergence checking.

          cdc reconvergence -check off
        # Turn off exact memory modeling for large memories.

          netlist memory -abstract mem1 mem2
        # Disable generation of CDC protocol assertions

          cdc promote scheme * -off
        # Define custom synchronizer modules and identify the clock domains
        # of the custom synchronizer module pins.

      cdc synchronizer custom cust_2sync
      netlist port domain in1 out2 -clock clk1 -module cust_2sync
      netlist port domain in2 out1 -clock clk2 -module cust_2sync
     # Black box modules that are not required for CDC analysis
      netlist blackbox modX

     For extremely large designs, use a hierarchical CDC verification flow (see "Hierarchical CDC
     Analysis" on page 231).

     The following example directives file creates a profile that provides a higher level of detail in the
     checking and reporting of CDC data.

     # high_accuracy.do -- High-accuracy CDC profile
     # Enable single-source reconvergence and set reconvergence checking
     # to a greater depth (default is 0). Start with a depth of 1.

      cdc preference reconvergence -divergence_depth 1 -depth 1
     # Enable reconvergence reporting for paths thru DMUX synchronizers.

      cdc preference reconvergence -dmux_as_recon_start
     # Enable FIFO and handshake scheme checking:

      cdc scheme on fifo handshake
     # Report disabled CDC paths.

      cdc preference -filtered_report
     # Enable constant propagation through registers with non-constant
     # enables

      netlist constant propagation -enable

     Also, consider the following:

     · Turn on reporting of paths to dead-end nodes using the cdc run argument process_dead_end.

     · Use modal analysis to check all modes of clocking (see "Modal CDC Analysis" on page 219).

Performance-Based Analysis Setup

CDC analysis sessions must trade off between performance and completeness. For initial analysis
phases, you set up CDC analysis for high performance, yet incomplete results. This helps you quickly set
up the analysis parameters before running "complete analysis" sessions. Various directives disable the
more complex checking and analysis--you can fine tune how performance-based analysis works in your
environment.
A performance session script (cdc_performance.do) in the installation tree runs directives that configure
CDC analysis for high-performance operation:

   install_directory/share/tcl/cdc_performance.do

An example directory contains an example showing how to use cdc_performance.do:

   install_directory/share/examples/cdc_performance

The cdc_performance.do script (Figure 72) increases performance by:

164                                 Questa® CDC User Guide
                        CDC Analysis

                        Performance-Based Analysis Setup

       · Ignoring inferred clocks.

       · Disabling complex schemes.

       · Disabling reconvergence checking.

       · Reporting single paths per Tx signals (cdc path -single_tx).

The cdc_performance.do script is updated with new performance enhancements as they are developed,
so you can point to this file in the installation tree to create a performance session environment.

                                                Figure 72. cdc_performance.do

      #------------------------------------------------
      # Script to run Questa CDC in performance mode
      #------------------------------------------------
      # Only perform CDC analysis on user-specified clocks
      cdc preference -ignore_inferred_clock
      # Turn off all DMUX templates, except simple_dmux
      # Also turn off multi_sync_mux_select
      cdc scheme off dmux
      cdc scheme off partial_dmux
      cdc scheme off and_gate_dmux
      cdc scheme off mux_lock_dmux
      cdc scheme off forward_simple_dmux
      # Turn off reconvergence scheme
      cdc reconvergence off
      # Only report one CDC path per TX signal
      cdc path -single_tx

CDC Protocol Verification  

CDC Protocol Verification

CDC protocol verification is a dynamic extension of static CDC analysis. It has two parallel components:
Simulation with CDC protocol assertions and formal analysis with CDC protocol properties.

        CDC Protocol Flow
        CDC Protocol Checker Library
        CDC Protocol Verification Setup
        CDC Protocol Formal Analysis
        CDC Protocol Simulation
        Correlate Protocol and Static Results

CDC Protocol Flow

CDC protocol flow is a dynamic functional analysis process using two parallel analysis methods: formal
verification and simulation.

Figure 73 shows the flow for CDC protocol verification. The flow starts with a common setup, where
the design is compiled and static CDC analysis is run. With final static CDC analysis results, the CDC
protocol checkers are promoted: instances of Questa Protocol Library checker models are instantiated for
specific crossings, a bind file binds the checker inputs to the design logic and simulation arguments files
are created for running simulations. Two independent separate processes verify that the design obeys its
CDC protocols:

       · simulation of the design with standard testbenches

       · formal verification of the design in a standard environment

166                        Questa® CDC User Guide
                                                      CDC Analysis

                                                      CDC Protocol Checker Library

                        Figure 73. CDC Protocol Flow

CDC Protocol Checker Library

CDC protocol verification uses protocol checkers automatically "promoted" from results of static CDC
analysis. Promotion instantiates instances of checker types from the CDC Protocol Checker Library,
binds them to nodes in the design and generates formal analysis and simulation environments for running
dynamic CDC verification of crossing protocols.

The installation software includes the CDC protocol library of standard protocol checker types, located
here:

   install_dir/share/CDC_PROTOCOL

This library defines the checker types for the various standardized CDC protocols available to Questa
CDC (Table 13). Checkers (instances of protocol checker types) are instantiated outside the design logic
and are bound to the internal design logic to monitor activity during simulation and to act as targets for
formal analysis. The protocol library includes a cdc_sample checker model that is more generalized than
the one described in our example.

Questa® CDC User Guide                                167
CDC Analysis

CDC Protocol Checker Library                                                                    

                    Table 13. Questa CDC Protocol Checker Library

Protocol            Properties

cdc_dsel            Verifies that a multi-bit Tx signal synchronized by a DMUX-style
                    synchronizer remains stable long enough for the Rx logic to properly
                    sample the signal's value.

cdc_fifo            Verifies that a FIFO-style crossing synchronizes a multi-bit Tx signal so
                    that Rx logic correctly samples the Tx values.

cdc_glitch          (Simulation only) Verifies that a single-bit input to Rx logic changes
                    value at most once each Rx clock cycle.

cdc_hamming_one     Verifies that when a multibit Tx signal changes value, it only changes
                    value by hamming distance 1 and the value remains stable for a
                    specified number of Tx clock cycles.

cdc_handshake       Verifies that a handshake-style crossing synchronizes a multi-bit Tx
                    signal so that Rx logic correctly samples the Tx values.

cdc_sample          Verifies that when a multi-bit Tx signal is sampled in the Rx domain, its
                    Tx value remains stable in the setup period before the value is sampled
                    and the hold period after the value is sampled, or both.

cdc_sync            Verifies that a single-bit signal crossing from a faster to a slower clock
                    domain is stable long enough for the Rx logic to correctly sample the
                    signal's value.

cdc_clockoff        Verifies that a signal crossing through an async_reset_clockoff style
                    synchronizer is not deasserting within the receiver clock metastability
                    window.

cdc_clockgate_sync  Verifies that a signal crossing through clockgate sync style synchronizer
                    is stable or is not changing when receiver clock is active.

CDC Protocol Checkers

A CDC protocol property is a statement about the behavior of a clock domain crossing subcircuit in its
intended operating environment. If the statement is expected to be true for all legal states of the design,
the property is an assert type property (an assertion). You can check whether or not design logic avoids or
tolerates the effects of metastability that can corrupt a data path or signal that crosses a domain boundary
--by specifying a set of CDC protocol assertions for the crossing. CDC protocol verification assures that
the CDC protocol assertions are not violated.

For example, Figure 74 shows a crossing from tx_clk domain logic to rx_clk domain logic. The circuit
has no synchronizer to mitigate metastability effects for the transmitting signal as it crosses the domain
boundary (it is a no_sync or multi_bits crossing).

                                   Figure 74. Signal Crossing with No Synchronizer

168                                                                Questa® CDC User Guide
                                                            CDC Analysis

                                                            CDC Protocol Checker Library

But, suppose this circuit can avoid metastability if: whenever tx_sig is sampled by the rx_sig register, its
value remains stable for at least one whole tx_clk cycle before the value is sampled until one whole tx_clk
cycle after it is sampled. That is, the crossing does not violate the setup and hold requirements for the Rx
input. This cdc_sample protocol ensures that the data value transitioning the two domains is stable (and
not prone to metastability) when it is loaded into the Rx logic.

Example Checker Type: cdc_sample

A module containing the protocol properties, coverage modeling logic and protocol cover point definitions
for the no_sync example comprises a verification unit for validating the CDC protocol, called cdc_sample
(Figure 75). Such an SVA module is called a CDC protocol checker type.

                        Figure 75. cdc_sample Checker Type

Protocol Properties

The cdc_sample protocol is expressed by two SVA properties:

       · setup check
          Tx value does not change during the setup time of an Rx sample.

            property setup_check_prop(tx_clock, rx_clock, data, areset, rx_en);
              logic data1;
              @(posedge rx_clock) disable iff(areset)
               (rx_en, data1 = data) |=>
                 @(posedge tx_clock) (data1 === $past(data));

            endproperty

       · hold check
          Tx value does not change during the hold time of an Rx sample.

            property hold_check_prop(tx_clock, rx_clock, data, areset, rx_en);
              logic data1;
              @(posedge rx_clock) disable iff(areset)
               (rx_en, data1 = data) |=>
                 @(posedge tx_clock) (data1 === data) and
                 @(posedge rx_clock) (data1 === data);

            endproperty

Assert and Cover Properties
Each checker property has two variants:

Questa® CDC User Guide                                                           169
CDC Analysis

CDC Protocol Checker Library                                                                                

       · assert property

          Property always holds (is true).

       · cover property

          Property "passes" at least once.

For an assert property (i.e., an assertion), the property should hold under any legal stimulus. If a
simulation test puts the design into a state in which the assertion fails, the simulator reports the assertion
failure. Formal analysis tries to find a proof that the property always holds for any "legal" stimulus (i.e.,
stimulus that does not violate the design's environmental assumptions).

For a cover property, the property is expected to "pass" at least once. For a sequence, its series of
events should occur as specified at some point. For an implication, the predicate must occur (be true)
at lease once, followed by the consequent sequence of events. If a simulation test creates a series of
states in which the property passes, the cover property is covered. If formal analysis discovers a stimulus
sequence that results in the cover property passing, the property is covered--the coverage waveform for
the property has the stimulus and the cover property's "firing" (passing).

CDC protocol properties are implications. Both assert and cover instances of each protocol check are
available. But, a CDC protocol's cover properties are used for advanced analysis, so by default they are
turned off (see cdc preference protocol -cover_properties_on).

Simulation Coverage

Typically, each checker has two kinds of simulation coverage metric:

       · Checker coverage

          Percentage of included assert properties (checks) that are activated during simulation.

       · Cover points

          Interesting events that might occur during standard operation.

         Note:
         Checker coverage is saved to the cdc_sim.db for viewing in the CDC GUI when loaded with the
         results of simulation. Cover point coverage is saved in the simulation coverage database (for
         example, for viewing with vcover). In addition, CDC protocol cover group coverage is saved in the
         simulation UCDB (which can be analyzed by Questa Cover Check).

Checker Evaluation

Each included check (assert property) is evaluated, if it is active at some point during simulation. The
activation condition for a check is the predicate of the property's implication. For example, here is the
cdc_dsel checker's tx_data_stable check description:

     tx_data_stable (default Off)

     Value of tx_data is stable when tx_select is active in the Tx domain.

     Eval: @(posedge tx_clk) !tx_reset && tx_select

This check is evaluated if and only if at some rising edge of tx_clk: tx_reset is not active and tx_select
is asserted. That is, the Tx data stable property has been tested at least once. If the check is not an

170                           Questa® CDC User Guide
                                                                              CDC Analysis

                                                              CDC Protocol Checker Library

implication (i.e., it is the glitch check of cdc_glitch), the implied predicate is 1. In particular, the check is
evaluated for every simulation.

If any included check is evaluated, the checker itself is considered evaluated. In the GUI, the Evaluated
icon indicates an evaluated checker:

                Evaluated

Put another way, another way: if no included checks are evaluated, the checker itself is considered
unevaluated. In the GUI, the Unevaluated icon indicates an unevaluated checker:

                Unevaluated

Checker Coverage

A checker's coverage goal equals the number of included checks. The default coverage goal--when no
checks are turned on/off (with cdc protocol on or cdc protocol off)--is shown in the checker data sheet
reference. For example:

  · Default Coverage Goal = 1

   rx_data_stable (@(posedge rx_clk) !rx_reset && rx_select)

  · Extra Coverage Items (2)

   tx_data_stable (@(posedge tx_clk) !tx_reset && tx_select)

             tx_select_stable (@(posedge tx_clk) !tx_reset && $rose(tx_select))
Checker's coverage is the ratio of the number of evaluated checks to the checker goal.

Evals column shows the number of times one of the checker's evaluation condition was met.

goal for the checker. Run Show >Coverage for the checker's coverage metrics.

CDC Analysis

              Figure 77. Details of a Checker's Coverage

Cover Points
In addition to assert and cover properties, some CDC protocol checkers include cover points to ensure
that simulation covers metastability-producing behavior for the crossing. Cover points also track the
number of times certain conditions are encountered in simulation (for example: number of times a FIFO
fills or empties). Such statistics help fine-tune simulation tests and discover simulation coverage "holes."
In the no_sync example, the following Rx register tracks cycles when the data value is sampled:

   reg incr_values_sampled = 0;
   always @(posedge rx_clock)

     incr_values_sampled <= rx_enable;

A wire indicating when the data value is known and driven is used in a cover group activation condition:

   wire xz_detected = ((^rx_enable) === 1'bx);
   wire cg_active = ((areset === 1'b0) && (xz_detected === 1'b0));

With this modeling logic, a cover group is defined for the cdc_sample protocol:

   covergroup cg_cdc_sample @(posedge rx_clock);
     cp_values_sampled : coverpoint incr_values_sampled iff
      (cg_active === 1'b1) {
      bins cpb_values_sampled = { 1'b1 };
     }

   endgroup

CDC Protocol Verification Setup

CDC protocol verification extends static verification to dynamic analysis. To set up protocol verification,
first run a static analysis session with the final preferences for CDC protocol analysis. Subsequently,
configure and promote analysis environments for targeted dynamic verification sessions.

CDC protocol verification is an extension of static CDC analysis. Static CDC analysis finds and classifies
the design's clock domain crossings. Before proceeding to CDC protocol verification, the results of static
analysis must agree with the expected architecture of the design. Sometimes design logic is changed.
For example, missing synchronizers are added or synchronizers are modified to specification. Sometimes
static analysis environment is changed. For example, analyzer preferences are adjusted, or specified
clock domains are merged or split.

Once static CDC analysis results agree with design specifications, you can move to verifying CDC
protocols for crossings. A final CDC analysis session followed by protocol promotion generates the

172                                                       Questa® CDC User Guide
                                                 CDC Analysis

                                                 CDC Protocol Verification Setup

setup for CDC protocol verification. CDC protocol verification results are viewed in the same CDC GUI
environment as that used to view static analysis results.

Configuring Protocol Checker Promotion

Protocol checker promotion is the automated process of identifying crossings that need protocol
verification, generating appropriate protocol checkers for the verification and creating a bind module that
binds the checker instances to nodes in the design logic. Configuration of protocol checker promotion
is controlled by two collections of qverify directives: directives that set the default configuration and
directives that override the default.

Default promotion environment directives set the general way CDC analysis promotes protocol checkers:

  · cdc scheme on -- Turn on CDC scheme checks.

   To improve performance, detection of certain schemes is default off. Following options
     turn on detection for these schemes: dff_sync_with_enable, reg_enable_no_sync,
     pulse_single_edge, handshake, dmux_no_hold, fifo and functional_false_path.

   If promotion of DMUX style crossings is on, a cdc_dsel on page 626 checker is promoted
     for each crossing.

   In addition, the following options affect the configuration of CDC protocol promotion:
     promote_reconvergence, sample_data_stability, promote_unnamed_block_signal,
     protocol_nopli and promote_async_reset.

  · cdc promote scheme -- Change the promotion attribute for the specified CDC scheme.

     Each CDC scheme has a factory default promotion attribute: promote protocol and FX checkers;
     promote just protocol checkers; promote just FX checkers; and do not promote checkers. This
     directive overrides the factory default promotion for crossings of the specified scheme and sets
     a default promotion attribute for the scheme. Some schemes do not support protocol promotion.
     See the cdc promote scheme description in the Command Reference.

  · cdc protocol on -- Promote the specified types of CDC protocol checkers and checks for
     simulation and formal verification.

     Some protocol checkers have some of their checks defined, but by default they are not turned on
     for promotion. This directive turns on checks that are default off.

  · cdc protocol off -- Turn off specified checks for a CDC protocol checker type or do not promote
     checkers of that type.

     Sometimes a protocol does not need to have certain checks turned on. This directive turns off
     those checks in the promoted checkers. You also can use this directive to turn off promotion for
     all protocol checkers of a specified type.

       · cdc protocol -- Identify a CDC protocol checker type to promote for one or more custom
          synchronizers.

          Directive specifies a Questa CDC Protocol Library checker type to promote for crossings to
          instances of a set of specified custom synchronizers.

One type of override directive changes promotion for individual crossings or groups of crossings:

Questa® CDC User Guide                                                                                 173
CDC Analysis

CDC Protocol Verification Setup                                                                               

     · cdc promote crossing -- Change the promotion attribute of specified clock domain crossings.

        Directive to override the default scheme promotion attribute (on, off, promote or fx) for individual
        crossings.

      Tip
      Specify cdc preference directives before running cdc run. The cdc protocol * and cdc promote
      * directives can be specified after cdc run, but must be specified before cdc generate protocol.
      This way, you can re-configure protocol verification sessions or create parallel protocol verification
      session environments without re-running static CDC analysis.

Promoting Protocol Checkers

Creating a setup for performing CDC protocol verification with a particular environment is called CDC
protocol checker promotion. Protocol checker promotion starts with the results of static CDC analysis:
a cdc.db. Promotion creates a CDC protocol report and a cdc_protocol directory in the output directory
(Figure 78).

                              Figure 78. Setup from CDC Protocol Checker Promotion

A data generator executable promotes the CDC protocol checker environment:

     cdc generate protocol [-vcs | -nc | -nc3 | -xm | -xm3]

     Generate properties, bind and simulation arguments files for CDC protocol verification.

Output from cdc generate protocol are a cdc_protocol directory with the CDC protocol verification
setup and a CDC protocol report (Figure 79). The cdc_protocol directory has a simulation subdirectory
containing the setup for running simulation with CDC protocol assertions, a formal subdirectory containing
the setup for running formal analysis with CDC protocol properties, and a bind file (Figure 80) connecting
protocol checkers to the design.

       Note:
       The qft_prefix macro definition has been added to the bind file, allowing you to bind CDC
       protocols to all instances of the DUT or to specific instances. Default: The checkers will bind to
       the DUT (top module) if no specifications are provided.

To verify the protocols associated with each crossing, use the cdc generate report command with the
-protocol option. The directive generates the cdc detailed report, cdc_detail.rpt (Figure 81), with the
protocol information for each crossing.

Simulation setup matches the simulator specified by the last session configure simulator command.

CDC Protocol Formal Analysis

CDC protocol SVA properties can be verified using the Questa Verify Property formal verification platform.
This platform applies a suite of formal analysis engines running as multicore processes to prove the CDC
protocol assert properties and find coverage waveforms for cover properties.

Prerequisites

To perform formal verification of the promoted protocol assertions for the clock domain crossings you
need a formal verification environment with CDC protocol properties. This environment is created from
the static CDC analysis database using the cdc generate protocol command. The environment is located
at: <output_directory>/cdc_protocol/formal. The command also creates a file (<output_directory>/
cdc_protocol/cdc_protocol_bind.sv) specifying the bind module that instantiates the promoted protocol
checkers and connects them to crossing logic.

You have two options for setting up the environment for formal verification.

       · Use the formal environment "as is."

          Generated formal setup has no formal assumptions. Formal analysis tries to violate asserted
          properties, which is often easy without constraints on stimulus considered for producing
          counterexamples. So, checker firings are not particularly meaningful--they are typically "false
          firings" produced by illegal stimulus (stimulus that cannot occur in the design's environment).
          Alternatively, proofs are valid.

       · Port the environment to an existing setup for formal analysis of the design.

          An environment already set up for formal verification already has assumptions defined. Porting
          the generated formal environment to the existing one configures analysis to be effective. Not only
          are proofs valid, but firings are meaningful. If a protocol checker's assert property fires:

180                                         Questa® CDC User Guide
                                                                                  CDC Analysis

                        CDC Protocol Formal Analysis

             Either the firing is false: setup needs additional assumptions to prevent formal analysis from
                considering the stimulus as a counterexample.

             Or, the property's counterexample is valid: checker's crossing logic allows its transfer protocol
                to be violated.

          Both results are actionable. If additional constraints are needed, firing waveform helps determine
          how to define them. Here, debugging the firing helps you fine tune the setup, which can improve
          formal analysis in general.

          If the transfer protocol is violated, either the logic has a bug or the protocol is not necessary.
          Promotion for that checker (or perhaps just the property) can be turned off.

Formal verification with CDC protocol properties flow:

Procedure

     1. Check the Makefile created for formal verification.
         Open the Makefile in your text editor, for example, Notepad++ or gedit:
            output_directory/cdc_protocol/formal/Makefile

         Makefile

Results

By default, the generated formal environment performs formal verification of the promoted CDC SVA
protocol properties. Such an environment has no constraints, so most firings are "false" and are produced
by illegal stimulus. Same holds for covered properties. A covered property might be covered by applying
illegal stimulus.

Alternately, proven properties are valid. They do not need verification in simulation.

If your design already is set up for formal verification, you can merge your environment with the one
generated for the promoted protocol checkers. Here, firings are meaningful, as they represent one of
these two situations:

       · Firing stimulus is illegal.

          Setup is incomplete (under-constrained).

       · Design can violate the property's clock domain crossing transfer protocol.

          Design has a bug.

CDC Protocol Simulation

CDC protocol SVA properties are verified using the Questa SIM simulation platform. CDC protocol
assertions and cover properties supplement the test suites used for standard verification. CDC protocol
checkers' cover groups provide protocol-related coverage data from simulation to supplement design
coverage metrics.

190                      Questa® CDC User Guide
                                                                             CDC Analysis

                                                                             CDC Protocol Simulation

Prerequisites

After generating a CDC protocol simulation environment using the cdc generate protocol command,
include the promoted protocol checkers in your simulation tests. As described in "CDC Protocol
Checkers" on page 168, for simulation, checkers are packages of:

  · Assert properties
     Properties that should pass every time they are evaluated.

  · Cover properties
     Properties that should pass at least once.

       · Cover points
          Events related to the crossing that are counted.

Flow for simulation of a testbench with the promoted CDC protocol checkers:

Procedure

     1. Check the files in the generated simulation environment.

            prompt> ls Output_Results/cdc_protocol/simulation
            cdc_protocol_exclude_assertion.sv cdc_protocol_vlog_files.arg

              cdc_protocol_vsim_2step.arg cdc_protocol_waveform.do
            cdc_protocol_vlog.arg cdc_protocol_vopt.arg

              cdc_protocol_vsim_3step.arg

  2. Port the protocol simulation environment to your simulation setup.

     Since all simulation environments are different, following procedure assumes the generated
     environment is left intact.

  3. Compile the testbench. For example:

Questa® CDC User Guide                                                                           191
CDC Analysis

CDC Protocol Simulation  

           prompt> vlog testbench_dir/tb.v

        or

           prompt> vcom testbench_dir/tb.vhd

     4. Compile the protocol checkers.
        The checker models and bind module are SystemVerilog modules, so you use vlog. The simulation
        directory has the argument file cdc_protocol_vlog.arg:

           //+define+CDC_PROTOCOL_NOPLI
           -mfcu -cuname CDC_PROTOCOL_PROPS_CUNAME
           -f output_Results/cdc_protocol/simulation/cdc_protocol_vlog_files.arg

        Script for cdc_protocol_vlog_files.arg file:

           incdir+install_dir/share/QFT_CHECKER
           Output_Results/cdc_protocol/cdc_protocol_bind.sv
           Output_Results/cdc_protocol/simulation//
           cdc_protocol_exclude_assertion.sv
           install_dir/share/QFT_CHECKER/rst_clk_aligned.sv
           install_dir/share/CDC_PROTOCOL/cdc_protocol_dsel.sv
           install_dir/share/CDC_PROTOCOL/cdc_protocol_hamming.sv
           install_dir/share/CDC_PROTOCOL/cdc_protocol_sync.sv
           install_dir/share/CDC_PROTOCOL/cdc_protocol_sample.sv
           install_dir/share/CDC_PROTOCOL/cdc_protocol_glitch.sv
           install_dir/share/CDC_PROTOCOL/cdc_protocol_fifo.sv
           install_dir/share/CDC_PROTOCOL/cdc_protocol_handshake.sv
           install_dir/share/CDC_PROTOCOL/cdc_protocol_clockgate_sync.sv
           install_dir/share/CDC_PROTOCOL/cdc_protocol_clockoff.sv

        Checker models are defined in the share/CDC_PROTOCOL directory in the install
        directory. Bind file is in the cdc_protocol directory. Modules are compiled as the
        CDC_PROTOCOL_PROPS_CUNAME compilation unit. The compilation unit is created from
        multiple files, so the -mfcu switch is needed (multi-file compilation unit). Uncomment the +define
        to disable PLI generation. This mode is used when only simulation output is needed, such as for
        regressions or simulation with third-party tools. PLI is needed to create the cdc_sim.db database.

           prompt> vlog -f output_Results/cdc_protocol/cdc_protocol_vlog.arg

     5. Run optimization step using vopt command. The simulation directory has the argument file
        cdc_protocol_vopt.arg:

           CDC_PROTOCOL_PROPS_CUNAME
           -suppress 3009
           -suppress 2262
           -assertdebug

        The compilation unit CDC_PROTOCOL_PROPS_CUNAME created is optimized as follows:

        prompt> vopt tb -o tb_vopt

  6. Run simulation with the compiled testbench and protocol checkers.

     Two generated files are used in the vsim invocation:

      · cdc_protocol_vsim_3step.arg

           -suppress 3009
           -suppress 12027
           -pli install_dir/lib/lib0InLoadMTIPLI-g.so
           -assertdebug
           +qhome+install_dir

         The -pli argument is critical. It has the PLI library for creating the cdc_sim.db database.
         Generated vsim arguments might change in future releases and you can include custom
         arguments.

      · cdc_protocol_waveform.do

           # CDC Protocol Waveform util file
           #---------------------------------------------------------------
           if {![info exists cdc_protocol_waveform_prefix]} {

                         # Specify Prefix here
                         set cdc_protocol_waveform_prefix ""
           }
           add log $cdc_protocol_waveform_prefix/gclk
           add log $cdc_protocol_waveform_prefix/data_reg
           add log $cdc_protocol_waveform_prefix/rst
           add log $cdc_protocol_waveform_prefix/en_reg
           add log $cdc_protocol_waveform_prefix/clk1
           add log $cdc_protocol_waveform_prefix/clk2

         Waveform creation DO file for protocol signals. Set cdc_protocol_waveform_prefix to the path
         to the DUT--either by modifying this file or using a set command before running the DO file.
         These signals are logged during simulation to display their waveforms from the CDC GUI. This
         script changes as checkers are added to the CDC SVA protocol library.

     Table 14 shows additional simulation arguments you can add to control the simulation session.
                                      Table 14. CDC Protocol Simulator Arguments

     ­f sim_arg_file              File (generated by cdc generate protocol) with the simulator
                                  arguments for running simulation with assertions.

     +qft_db+file                 Name of the generated database. Default: cdc_sim.db.

     +qft_firing_limit+limit      Maximum number of firings in the .db database. Default: 10.

     +qft_signature_limit+limit   Maximum number of signatures per check in the .db database.
                                  Default: 10.

     +qft_no_violation_limit      Remove the limits on firings per signature and signatures per check in
                                  the .db database.

     +qft_firing_keyword+keyword  Add keyword to each firing message, so each firing message begins
                                  with: Questa CDC keyword Firing. Default: Each firing message
                                  begins with: Questa CDC Firing.

     +qft_no_statistics           Turn off statistics computation and reporting during simulation. *
                                  disable coverage tracking/reporting to the db.

     +qft_simulation_message_li   Number of firings per signature reported to the simulation log and
     mit+limit                    STDOUT. Default: 1. Currently the system reports only one firing per
                                  signature. This argument can help to change this limit.

     ­version                     Report the software release version and copyright information and
                                  exits.

   Synchronizer length : 2

Results

Simulation with CDC protocol assertions fits into a wide range of site simulation environments. This
procedure shows how to merge the generated protocol simulation environment into a suite of simulation

Questa® CDC User Guide                                               195
CDC Analysis

Correlate Protocol and Static Results                                                                     

tests. Tests are augmented to track CDC protocol assertions and to gather checker cover point statistics
during simulation.

This procedure shows the flow for the Questa SIM simulation and coverage environment. But the process
is easily adapted to third-party simulators. See install_dir/share/examples/design_solutions/samples/
cdc_protocol_3rd_party_sim for a sample setup and more information.

But the full capability of dynamic analysis of CDC protocols with Questa CDC lies in the ability to correlate
protocol verification results with the static analysis results. Matching results of crossings' protocol
verification with the crossings themselves is done by loading the CDC GUI with the cdc_sim.db database.
This database is generated by simulation configured with the CDC protocol PLI. This is the topic of the
next procedure.

Correlate Protocol and Static Results

Each CDC protocol checker verifies the transfer protocol for its clock domain crossing. Once protocol
verification is complete, you can view these dynamic analysis results merged into the results from the
original static CDC analysis. In addition to correlating dynamic with static results, this process provides a
unified debugging environment.

Prerequisites

Static analysis identifies logic straddling clock domain boundaries and partitions this logic into individual
crossings that match specific patterns called CDC schemes. CDC static verification is the process of
iterating this analysis, adjusting the design or the analysis setup until the results satisfy the desired
implementation specification. Included in this process is the assignment of status values to the crossings
--including waivers for crossings that are examined, meet specification and are signed off.

Some schemes are naturally tolerant of metastability effects resulting from signals traversing domain
boundaries. Other schemes might or might not have metastability issues, depending on the crossings'
driving logic and the design's operating environment. Many of these crossings cannot be waived per se,
because design logic is complex, it changes with development and operating environment is in flux. To be
safe, the crossings' associated transfer protocols must be verified dynamically.

Checker models from the CDC SVA Protocol Library are designed to verify many of these transfer
protocols. Checkers are automatically instantiated and bound to the design in a process called promotion.
Although the protocol checkers' default configurations are typically sufficient, they also can be configured
to match the unique requirements of their corresponding crossings.

Promoted checkers and their protocol verification environments are ready for dynamic formal verification
and simulation. Combining results from dynamic CDC protocol verification with results from static CDC
analysis has two advantages:

       · correlate static and protocol results

          Each protocol checker is associated with its clock domain crossing, so viewing the protocol and
          static results on a per-crossing basis helps you understand the issues for the separate crossings.

       · unified debugging environment

          CDC GUI with the correlated protocol and static CDC results provides a single debug
          environment for debugging issues with both static and dynamic methods. The entire static CDC
          GUI platform, plus most of the formal verification GUI tools and simulator verification tools are
          accessible in one package.

This procedure describes correlating the following results with static CDC results.

196                                    Questa® CDC User Guide
                        CDC Analysis

                        Correlate Protocol and Static Results

       · Multiple simulation with CDC protocol assertions tests.

       · A formal analysis with CDC protocol properties session.
Procedure is easily adapted to variations where only simulation results, only formal results or simulation
results are from a single simulation.
Flow for correlating CDC static and protocol results:

Procedure

     1. If multiple simulation tests are used, merge their cdc_sim.db databases.

         Command cdc sim merge merges the databases. Database paths can be listed in the command
         or you can use the -f <filelist> option to specify them from a file. Default name for the merged
         database is cdc_sim_merged.db.

         Here is a sample Make target that creates a cdc_sim_tb<tb_id>.db database.

            set tb_id = 1
            sim_with_checkers: compile

              ${VLOG} src/vlog/tb$(tb_id).v
              ${VLOG} -f $(CDC_SIMFILE)

                   -voptargs="-designfile ./design$(tb_id).bin" \
               -do "set cdc_protocol_waveform_prefix {path_to_dut}; \
               do $(CDC_SIMWAVE); run -all; exit" \
               -f $(CDC_VSIMFILE) \
               +qft_db+cdc_sim_tb$(tb_id).db \
               -l sim_with_checkers_$(tb_id).log

     ·        Unevaluated -- At least one of the checker's properties has an evaluation condition

     9. Check simulation assertion coverage.

        Most checker types have multiple assert properties. Associated with each property is its evaluation
        condition. Each cycle at which one or more of a checker's evaluation conditions are satisfied, the
        Evals count for the checker increments by that number.

        Coverage Goal is the same as the number of assert properties. A checker property is covered
        if the property's evaluation condition is satisfied at least once. Coverage is the number of the
        checker's properties that are covered. Coverage % is the ratio of covered properties to coverage
        goal.

Results

Loading a CDC protocol simulation database into the CDC GUI and annotating the formal analysis
results combines static and dynamic protocol verification data into one platform. CDC Checks window
shows correlation of results of static and dynamic analysis. Simulation window provides quick access to
simulation assertion and coverage data on a per-checker basis, which corresponds to the clock domain
crossings the protocol checkers validate. Property window shows formal results on a per-property basis.

All windows provide quick access to debugging and analysis tools--preloaded with the relevant views
pertaining to the crossing being inspected.

                        CDC Constraints Verification

CDC Constraints Verification

CDC constraints verification is a dynamic extension of static CDC analysis. The objective is to validate the
assumptions and constraints specified for the static CDC analysis.

Design constraints are specifications of designer's intent. During CDC analysis, constraints are used
to specify ports and signals as constant and stable, and to declare gray-coding signal relationships.
Constant constraints affect netlist synthesis, whereas stable constraints disables CDC analysis on stable
paths. Gray-code constraints identifies reconvergence logic and reports them as reconvergence_gray
schemes.

If the constraints are not verified and they propagate through the CDC analysis, the results can be
incorrect and misleading. Questa CDC automates the constraints verification process by generating
SVA assertions from CDC constraints. The process generates scripts to run these assertions in formal
verification and simulation.

        CDC Constraints Flow
        CDC Constraint Checker Library
        CDC Constraints Verification Setup
        CDC Constraint Formal Analysis
        CDC Constraint Simulation

CDC Constraints Flow

CDC constraints flow is incorporated into the standard Questa protocol verification flow where the
constraints assertions are generated after the CDC static analysis.

Figure 82 shows the flow for CDC constraints verification. The flow starts with a common setup, where
the design is compiled and static CDC analysis is run. With final static CDC analysis results, the
CDC constraint checkers are promoted: instances of Questa Constraint Library checker models are
instantiated, a bind file binds the checker inputs to the design logic and simulation arguments files are
created for running simulations. Two independent separate processes verify that the CDC constraints are
valid:

       · simulation of the design with standard testbenches

       · formal verification of the design in a standard environment

The constraints assertions are verified with the Questa Formal model checker. When formal proves an
assertion, it indicates that the assertion can never be violated and does not need further verification. All
formally proven constraints are automatically removed from the list of assertions passed to simulation.

All non-proven assertions are run in the design simulation environment. During simulation, any violated
assertion indicates that the constraint is incorrect and must be further reviewed to determine if the
constraint is incorrect and if it must be removed from CDC analysis. If assertions are not violated,
the assertion coverage is reviewed to confirm the assertion verification. If coverage indicates that an
assertion was not verified, the current simulation tests can be improved or new simulation tests may be
created to improve the assertion verification.

Questa® CDC User Guide  203
CDC Analysis

CDC Constraint Checker Library                                                                                

                                Figure 82. CDC Constraints Flow

CDC Constraint Checker Library

CDC constraint verification uses constraint checkers automatically "promoted" from results of static CDC
analysis. Promotion instantiates instances of checker types from the CDC Constraint Checker Library,
binds them to nodes in the design and generates formal analysis and simulation environments for running
dynamic CDC verification of constraint.

The installation software includes the CDC constraint library of standard constraint checker types, located
here:

install_dir/share/CDC_PROTOCOL/cdc_constraint_*

This library defines the checker types for the various standardized CDC constraints available to Questa
CDC (Table 15). Checkers (instances of constraint checker types) are instantiated outside the design
logic and are bound to the internal design logic to monitor activity during simulation and to act as targets
for formal analysis.

                                   Table 15. Questa CDC Constraint Checker Library

Constraint    Related Directive            Properties

constant      netlist constant             (Simulation only) Verifies that a signal is always
                                           constant.

stable        cdc signal <signal> -stable  Verifies that a signal is always stable. CDC
                                           analysis considers a stable signal (and its
                                           propagated values) as properly synchronized.

204                                                              Questa® CDC User Guide
                                                                         CDC Analysis

                                                            CDC Constraints Verification Setup

            Table 15. Questa CDC Constraint Checker Library (continued)

Constraint  Related Directive                   Properties

gray-coded  cdc signal <signal>                 Verifies that a signal is changing it's value in
            -gray_coded                         gray-coded manner, which is, one bit at a time at
                                                its associated clock edge.

mutually exclusive cdc signal <signal>          Verifies that a signal is always mutually
                           -mutually_exclusive  exclusive. Signals that are the receiving
                                                signals of the first register of synchronizers are
                                                considered as mutually exclusive.

tx_stable   cdc signal <signal> -tx_stable      Verifies that a signal when used as Tx of a
                                                crossing is stable with respect to the rx clock of
                                                that crossing.

rx_stable   cdc signal <signal> -rx_stable      Verifies that a signal when used as Rx of a
                                                crossing is stable with respect to the tx clock of
                                                that crossing.

CDC Constraints Verification Setup

CDC constraint verification extends static verification to dynamic analysis. To set up constraint
verification, first run a static analysis session with the final preferences for CDC constraint analysis.
Subsequently, configure and promote analysis environments for targeted dynamic verification sessions.

CDC constraint verification is an extension of static CDC analysis. Static CDC analysis finds and
classifies the design's clock domain crossings. Before proceeding to CDC constraint verification, the
results of static analysis must agree with the expected architecture of the design.

Once static CDC analysis results agree with design specifications, you can move to verifying CDC
constraints. A final CDC analysis session followed by constraint promotion generates the setup for CDC
constraint verification. CDC constraint verification results are viewed in the same CDC GUI environment
as that used to view static analysis results.

Configuring Constraint Checker Promotion

Constraints checker promotion is the automated process of identifying assumptions that need constraints
verification, generating appropriate constraints checkers for the verification and creating a bind module
that binds the checker instances to nodes in the design logic. Configuration of constraints checker
promotion is controlled by two collections of qverify directives: directives that set the default configuration
and directives that override the default.

Default promotion environment directives set the general way CDC analysis promotes constraint
checkers:

       · cdc preference protocol -promote_constraints-- Turn on SVA generation only for constraints
          verification.

       · cdc preference protocol -promote_protocol-- Turn on SVA generation only for protocol
          verification. This option can be avoided if you only want to perform protocol verification. By not
          specifying any preference for cdc peference protocol directive, you imply that you only want to
          perform protocol verification.

Questa® CDC User Guide                                                   205
CDC Analysis

CDC Constraints Verification Setup                                                        

     Note:
     If you want to perform both constraints and protocol verification, specify both
     -promote_protocol and -promote_constraints options with the cdc preference protocol
     directive.

       · cdc promote constraint -promotion on -- Promote the specified types of CDC constraint checkers
          and checks for simulation and formal verification. By default, all constraint checkers are turned on
          for promotion.

       · cdc promote constraint -promotion off-- Turn off specified checks for a CDC constraint checker
          type or do not promote checkers of that type.

Promoting Constraint Checkers

Creating a setup for performing CDC constraint verification with a particular environment is called CDC
constraint checker promotion. Constraint checker promotion starts with the results of static CDC analysis:
a cdc.db. Promotion creates a CDC constraint report and a cdc_protocol directory in the output directory
(Figure 83).

                             Figure 83. Setup from CDC Constraint Checker Promotion

A data generator executable promotes the CDC constraint checker environment:
     cdc generate protocol [-vcs | -nc | -nc3]

     Generate properties, bind and simulation arguments files for CDC constraint verification.

Output from cdc generate protocol are a cdc_protocol directory with the CDC constraint verification
setup and a CDC constraint report (Figure 84). The cdc_protocol directory has a simulation subdirectory
containing the setup for running simulation with CDC constraint assertions, a formal subdirectory
containing the setup for running formal analysis with CDC constraint properties, and a bind file (Figure 85)
connecting constraint checkers to the design.

Simulation setup matches the simulator specified by the last session configure simulator command.
Unless configured for another simulator, the default is Questa SIM (vsim). The -nc and -nc3 options

checkers' cover groups provide constraint-related coverage data from simulation to supplement design
