CDC-FX Verification                                                                            

CDC-FX Verification

Simulation tests used for simulation with CDC protocol assertions can be re-used for CDC-FX
metastability analysis. For these simulations, the compiled design is extended with CDC-FX metastability
injection logic, which causes the simulated design to behave like a hardware implementation with random
metastability effects. End-to-end tests that pass under normal simulation can fail when simulated with
metastability effects, unless the design is "metastability hardened."

A clock domain crossing is metastability hardened if transmit values are always held stable around
receive clock edges whenever the active edges of the transmit and receive clocks "align." Here, the two
clocks are considered aligned if the active transmit clock edge falls in a "metastability window" around
an active receive clock edge. By default, the start and end of this window are set at 25% before and 10%
after the receive clock edge, respectively. The sizes and skews of metastability windows can be adjusted
to accommodate clocking and physical design characteristics. Crossings that are guaranteed to be stable
when active clock edges align, do not produce metastable values, so these paths are simulated the same
in both regular simulation and simulation with CDC-FX injectors. The injectors on these paths are never
activated and therefore never simulate metastability.

However, clock domain crossings that can legally become metastable can be considered metastability
hardened. In these cases, the receive logic must account properly for the random delays and advances
that can occur as a result of the metastability effects exhibited by the crossings and their reconverging
logic. For these crossings, CDC-FX simulation randomly injects metastability by delaying or advancing
various value changes that occur when transmit and receive clocks align in their metastability window.

Simulating the design with random metastability in this way tests that all clock domain crossings are
metastability hardened. If these simulation tests adequately exercise the design to cover the various
possible signal crossing situations, a truly metastability hardened design will pass--indicating a high level
of confidence that the design's hardware implementation will not exhibit faults arising from metastability.
Alternatively, a well-constructed test suite simulated with metastability effects will detect unhardened
CDC paths and logic by producing end-to-end test failures. You debug the test failures the same way as
with standard simulation by analyzing backward from the miscompared outputs using your simulation
waveforms and debug environment.

        Running Simulation with CDC-FX Metastability Injection

                        Modal CDC Analysis

Modal CDC Analysis

Modal CDC analysis configures the design as a set of operational modes and runs CDC analysis on each
modal version of the design.

Modal CDC analysis accomplishes two things:

       · Reduces complexity and pessimism

          Using a divide-and-conquer approach, CDC analysis is split into smaller pieces. Rather than have
          a huge number of violations and cautions for the general design, CDC analysis returns results
          in groups relevant to the legal operational modes of the design. Running regular CDC analysis
          on such a design returns pessimistic results because the design has more clock domains. Modal
          CDC analysis eliminates these pessimistic results.

       · Captures the modal nature of the design

          An artifact of modal CDC analysis is that a design's various legal operational modes become
          well-defined. Understanding these operational modes helps designers and verifiers grasp the true
          nature of the design's functionality.

The CDC analysis flow for modal CDC analysis is the same as for regular CDC analysis, except with
some additional steps:

       · Phase 1: Design compilation

          This phase is the same for both flows.

       · Phase 2: CDC analysis

          Run CDC report clocks and ensure the clock domain partition is correct. Before running full CDC
          analysis, run CDC report modes. This extra step infers the various operational modes recognized
          by the analyzer. You can manually adjust the modal setup as with setting up the clock domains.

          Once the clock domains and operational modes are established properly, run full CDC analysis
          for each mode. An automatically-generated run script helps you configure and run this stage of
          modal CDC analysis.

       · Phase 3: GUI debug

          This phase is similar for both flows. However, the GUI has several modal indicators that are not
          relevant to non-modal designs and are not visible when viewing regular CDC analysis results.
          The results of all the modal CDC runs are combined in a single database. Therefore, the GUI has
          an additional separation of results based on the various operational modes.

        CDC Modal Analysis
        Modal GUI Debug

CDC Modal Analysis

Run report clocks as with regular CDC analysis. Then run report modes and adjust until the operational
modes are correct. Then run modal CDC analysis on each of the various modal versions of the design.

Questa® CDC User Guide  219
CDC Analysis

CDC Modal Analysis                                                                             

Report Modes

CDC report modes finds the design's clock configuration registers and determines the design's
operational modes by examining the clock multiplexing circuits. Consider circuit A:

Assume that clkA, clkB and clkC are asynchronous and X0/X1 are clock signals. Unless X0 or X1 are
grouped with clkA, clockB or clkC, regular CDC analysis considers this circuit as having five clock groups.
CDC report clocks shows this is the case. When you examine this circuit, you see that as a non-modal
circuit, simplifying CDC analysis by grouping some of these clock signals is not correct. Yet, regular CDC
analysis results are pessimistic.

For cases such as these, you can use modal analysis to remove the pessimism. First, run CDC report
modes with -report_modes option.

   cdc run -report_modes

For circuit A, CDC report modes finds four operational modes and generates the following mode
definitions in a generated Tcl file (cdc_mode_ctrl.tcl):

   cdc mode cdc_mode_0 -set {ctrl[0]} 1'b0 -set {ctrl[1]} 1'b0
   cdc mode cdc_mode_1 -set {ctrl[0]} 1'b0 -set {ctrl[1]} 1'b1
   cdc mode cdc_mode_2 -set {ctrl[0]} 1'b1 -set {ctrl[1]} 1'b0
   cdc mode cdc_mode_3 -set {ctrl[0]} 1'b1 -set {ctrl[1]} 1'b1

These modes correspond to the following assignments for X0/X1:

     Mode           ctrl[0]  ctrl[1]  X0    X1

     cdc_mode_0     0        0        clkA  clkB

     cdc_mode_1     0        1        clkA  clkC

     cdc_mode_2     1        0        clkB  clkB

     cdc_mode_3     1        1        clkB  clkC

Each of these modal circuits is less complex than the non-modal circuit. In particular, they have two clock
domains rather than five. Results of modal CDC analysis of each modal circuit are less pessimistic.

Adjusting CDC Modes

220                                         Questa® CDC User Guide
                                                               CDC Analysis

                        CDC Modal Analysis

If the inferred modes found with the initial CDC report modes run is not accurate and complete, you can
adjust the mode specification by creating user-specified cdc mode directives. You can make the following
types of adjustments:

  · Specify all modes

     One important rule: when specifying cdc mode directives to define a particular mode, the
     definition must be complete. Every mode possibly configured by the various combinations of
     mode control signal values must be specified before the CDC report modes step is complete. So,
     if you add the cdc mode directive, you must also add the missing modes:

  cdc mode cdc_mode_0 -set {ctrl[0]} 1'b0 -set {ctrl[1]} 1'b0
  cdc mode cdc_mode_1 -set {ctrl[0]} 1'b0 -set {ctrl[1]} 1'b1
  cdc mode cdc_mode_2 -set {ctrl[0]} 1'b1 -set {ctrl[1]} 1'b0
  cdc mode cdc_mode_3 -set {ctrl[0]} 1'b1 -set {ctrl[1]} 1'b1

  · Skip a particular mode

     An inferred mode might not be interesting for CDC analysis. You can identify such a mode
     by adding the -ignore argument to its corresponding set mode directive. Do not edit the
     cdc_mode_ctrl.tcl file, as this file is overwritten each time you run CDC report modes. Instead,
     copy the directive to a directive file called by the CDC report modes run. For example, if you
     want to skip analysis of cdc_mode_2, add the following directive (the mode name is changed for
     readability):

       cdc mode clkB_only -set {ctrl[0]} 1'b1 -set {ctrl[1]} 1'b0 -ignore

  · Identify additional modes
     Since the initial CDC report modes infers operational modes controlled by MUX selections of
     clocks, some modes might be missed. You can specify these modes manually with user-defined
     cdc mode directives. For example:

       cdc mode fast_mode -set tm 1'b0 -set sel 1'b1
       cdc mode scan_load -set tm 1'b1 -set scan_en 1'b1 -ignore
       cdc mode scan_test -set tm 1'b1 -set scan_en 1'b0 -ignore

     Each -set argument specifies a register, port or black box output and its corresponding constant
     value for the mode.

  · Identify mode control signals
     You can identify signals that contribute to the configuration of the design's operational modes with
     the cdc mode control directive. For example:

       cdc mode control config dut.clkgen.ctrl0 dut.clkgen.ctrl1

     CDC report modes uses this information to generate the cdc mode directives for the correct
     operational modes. When specifying mode control signals this way, you can mimic the behavior
     of the -ignore argument. The syntax for the cdc mode control directive is:

Questa® CDC User Guide                                         221
CDC Analysis

CDC Modal Analysis                                                                                      

              cdc mode control signal... [-values value...]

          Only modes for which each specified signal assumes one of the specified values is analyzed.
          CDC report modes creates cdc mode directives with -ignore arguments for the other modes.

After adjusting the CDC modes, you must re-run CDC report modes. Check the Modal Analysis
Information table in cdc.rpt for the complete description of the defined CDC modes. For example:

All Mode Reporting

You can configure the CDC analysis run to produce a consolidated report that contains information of all
the modes using the -modal argument to the cdc generate crossings executable. Generate this report
after the completion of analysis. For example:

   qverify -c -do "cdc load db cdc.db; cdc generate crossings -modal"

Upon completion of this step, an all-mode report is generated with the default name cdc_detail_mode.rpt.
Report Contents
The cdc_detail_mode.rpt contains the following sections:

       · CDC Mode Report Section -- List each mode with summary totals. For example:

     · CDC Path Report Section -- This section contains three the following subsections:

           Paths that exist in all modes (Number of paths: <number>).

               · Paths that are consistent (Number of paths: <number>).

                     Paths (Tx, Rx pair) that exists in all modes and have the same Tx, Rx, Tx clock, Rx
                        clock, severity, status.

               · Paths that are inconsistent (Number of paths: <number>).
                   Paths (Tx, Rx pair) that exists in all modes but have any of Tx, Rx, Tx clock, Rx clock,
                   severity, status different. Within this section, the paths are ordered by worst severity first,
                   with violation, caution, evaluation, proven, and resolved/waived listed in that order.

           Paths that exist in some modes (Number of paths: <number>).

               · Paths that are consistent (Number of paths: <number>).
                   Paths (Tx, Rx pair) that exists in some modes (not all) and have the same Tx, Rx, Tx
                   clock, Rx clock, severity, and status.

               · Paths that are inconsistent (Number of paths: <number>).
                   Paths (Tx, Rx pair) that exists in some modes (not all) and with any of Tx, Rx, Tx clock,
                   Rx clock, severity, or status different. Within this section, the paths are ordered by worst
                   severity first, with violation, caution, evaluation, proven, and resolved/waived listed in that
                   order.

                        Hierarchical CDC Analysis

Hierarchical CDC Analysis

Hierarchical CDC analysis is a methodology for analyzing large designs with faster run times, less
memory, and clearer results. It is the only feasible methodology for analyzing large, complex designs with
many clocks and clock domain crossings. Hierarchical methodologies complement IP-based SoC design
flows.

Hierarchical CDC analysis enables both top-down and bottom-up flows. Project teams should use the
methodology that best matches their project design flow. For some IP-based SoC projects, the block
design and verification are started before the top-level design and constraints are available, so a bottom-
up flow is most effective. However, some projects start CDC analysis after the top-level design and
constraints are available, so a top-down flow is most effective.

In the bottom-up flow, the CDC analysis is run on selected lower-level blocks individually to target intra-
block CDC problems and generate abstract models for the top-level analysis. With hierarchical CDC
analysis, IP design groups set up and run parallel block-level CDC flows. The block-level CDC verification
includes the review and debug of block-level results and the automatic generation of abstraction models
(hierarchical databases). To run CDC analysis at the top-level, the SoC integration team includes the
hierarchical databases for the IP blocks. The hierarchical block databases abstract the intra-block design
information, so the SoC integration team can focus on top-level inter-block CDC results as shown in
Figure 90.

                                               Figure 90. Hierarchical CDC Flow

In the top-down flow, the full SoC design and top-level constraints are provided for CDC analysis. The
top-down analysis is run on the top level and the constraints for selected lowerlevel blocks are extracted
from the top-level design and constraints. The top-level analysis also automatically generates a script to
run the complete analysis which includes block-level and top-level CDC analysis. Similar to the bottom-

Questa® CDC User Guide  231
CDC Analysis

Hierarchical Data Model                                                                                    

up flow, the block-level CDC analysis may be run in parallel to target intra-block CDC problems. The
block-level CDC verification includes the review and debug of block-level results and the automatic
generation of abstraction models (hierarchical databases). For the top-down flow, the top-level CDC
analysis includes the hierarchical databases for the IP blocks. The hierarchical block databases abstract
the intra-block design information, so the SoC integration team can focus on top-level inter-block CDC
results as shown in Figure 90.

Hierarchical CDC methodologies are used for CDC sign-off in most SoC design projects. These
methodologies improve design team productivity and enable design projects to reduce their time to
implementation and produce CDC bug-free SoC designs.

Hierarchical CDC analysis is static analysis only and does not support the promotion of protocol
assertions or the generation of CDC-FX injectors.

Advanced level settings for hierarchical analysis let you customize settings based on your design
requirements. For more information, see the Advanced Hierarchical CDC Analysis Methods section.

     Hierarchical Data Model

Hierarchical Data Model

A Hierarchical Data Model (HDM) is a concise, portable abstraction model for capturing the CDC intent of
a block. An HDM for a block is generated automatically during block-level analysis. It is a binary-format
hierarchical database that contains all the information about the block internals that is required to detect
CDC issues in the top-level analysis.

An HDM is a binary database, but text and Tcl versions also are created during block-level analysis. The
Tcl version contains a sequence of hier directives that constrain the block and are equivalent to the HDM
constraints. Block designers should review HDM constraints and modify them if necessary--the hier
directives can be edited to override corresponding HDM constraints. This HDM approach is IP friendly. An
IP vendor can distribute the HDM for an IP block without including an implementation model.

                        CDC Analysis

                        CDC Hierarchical Analysis Methods

CDC Hierarchical Analysis Methods

CDC hierarchical analysis can primarily be performed using two available methods--the bottom-up
analysis method and the top-down analysis method. In the bottom-up analysis method, you perform full
static CDC analysis on selected lower-level blocks first, and then run static CDC analysis on the top level
and the remaining design logic.

Figure 91 shows the flow of the CDC hierarchical bottom-up method.

                                    Figure 91. CDC Hierarchical Bottom-up Analysis

In the top-down analysis method, you run static CDC analysis on the top level first and then run static
CDC analysis on the lower-level blocks. Figure 92 shows the flow of the HDM top-down method.

              Figure 92. CDC Hierarchical Top-down Analysis

        HDM Bottom-up CDC Analysis
        HDM Top-Down CDC Analysis

HDM Bottom-up CDC Analysis

In the bottom-up analysis method, first, run CDC analysis for each block and then load the generated
HDMs and run top-level CDC analysis. Typically, various design verification teams analyze their blocks
separately--and only need the hierarchical databases when analyzing the top-level.

                                       Figure 93. HDM Bottom-up Analysis Method

234                                                          Questa® CDC User Guide
                        CDC Analysis

                        HDM Bottom-up CDC Analysis

Prerequisites

       · Ensure that the specified block instances do not have hierarchical references to objects in
          the top-level module or to other block instances and vice versa. That is, when you analyze a
          hierarchical block, all of its hierarchical references must be resolved within the block and when
          you analyze the top-level, all of its hierarchical references must be resolved to objects that are not
          in any block analyzed.

       · Ensure that the RTL provided for the block module matches with respect to port names,
          sequence, or count in the block- and top-level runs. Otherwise, CDC run aborts by default.
          However, if the -ignore_mismatch option is specified with the cdc load hierdb directive, CDC run
          continues after displaying the error message, and the block schematic and reconvergence check
          inside the HDM are disabled.

Procedure

     1. Run block-level CDC analysis on the hierarchical blocks with block-level constraints. For example:

            qverify -c -od OutputResults
            do constraints_block1.tcl
            cdc run -d block1 -hcdc
            do constraints_block2.tcl
            cdc run -d block2 -hcdc
            do constraints_block3.tcl
            cdc run -d block3 -hcdc

     The -hcdc option generates the hierarchical databases for each block in the specified directory, for
     example: hcdc_block1.hierdb, hcdc_block2.hierdb, and hcdc_block3.hiedb hierarchical databases
     are created in the OutputResults directory.

     Repeat this step for each hierarchical block and analyze the CDC results for each block.

  2. Review the results of the hierarchical CDC analysis of the blocks. Hierarchical analysis results
     are provided in the hierarchical constraints report, hcdc.rpt. Example HDM Bottom-up CDC
     Analysis11 shows the sample hcdc.rpt for block1.

  3. Resolve the conflicts before using the hierarchical data at the next level. For more information on
     Conflict checks, see "Conflict Checks" on page 243.

  4. Load the hierdb files for all the hierarchical blocks of the design and run CDC analysis on the top-
     level module. You must add cdc load hierdb directives to the top-level directives file. For example:

        cdc load hierdb OutputResults/block1/hcdc_block1.hierdb
        cdc load hierdb OutputResults/block2/hcdc_block2.hierdb
        cdc load hierdb OutputResults/block3/hcdc_block3.hierdb
        cdc run -d demo_top

     5. Verify the CDC analysis results. The whole design is available for debugging in the GUI.

Results

View the results in the GUI schematic by specifying the following command:

   qverify TOP/cdc.db &

HDM Top-Down CDC Analysis

In the top-down CDC analysis method, you provide the complete design, the top-level constraints and the
list of hierarchical blocks and invoke CDC analysis.

Questa CDC automatically infers the block-level constraints for each hierarchical block and generates
an hcdc_run.Makefile for block-level and top-level analysis. The Makefile contains the individual Make
targets for running each block-level analysis session followed by top-level CDC analysis. Figure 95 shows
the steps to be performed for the top-down analysis method.

         Note:
         The HDMs generated for sub-blocks using the top-down setup will be instance-independent and
         can be used across different hierarchies, irrespective of the instance name. These HDMs will also
         support conflict checks, similar to the HDMs generated by the bottom-up flow.

238                        Questa® CDC User Guide
                                                                 CDC Analysis

                                                      HDM Top-Down CDC Analysis

                        Figure 95. HDM Top-Down Analysis Method

Prerequisites

Ensure that the specified block instances do not have hierarchical references to objects in the top-level
module or to other block instances and vice versa. That is, when you analyze a hierarchical block, all of
its hierarchical references must be resolved within the block and when you analyze the top level, all of its
hierarchical references must be resolved to objects not in any block analyzed.

Procedure

     1. Specify the hierarchical blocks and the top-level constraints as follows:

            qverify -c -od OutputResults
            hier block block1 block2
            do top_ctrl.tcl

  2. Run top-level CDC analysis as follows:
        cdc run -d top

  The following files and directories are generated:

  · hcdc_run_setup/constraints/directory -- Entries for this directory are Tcl hierarchical
     constraint files for the unique instances of each specified block, that is generated by
     propagating the top-level constraints to the block instances and the top-level constraints
     file. Names of the constraint files for blocks with homogeneous instances have the
     hcdc_consctraints_block.tcl format. Names for heterogeneous instances of a block have
     counter suffixes, such as: hcdc_constraints_block-i.tcl, hcdc_constraints_block-j.tcl. Comments
     in each constraints file indicate the instances of block to which the constraints apply. The top-
     level constraints file naming format is hcdc_constraints_top.tcl, where top is the top-module
     name, these constraints are sourced in the top-level run.

  · hcdc_run.Makefile file -- Makefile contains the command-line arguments that run each block-
     level analysis (generating a hierdb for the block) and the top-level CDC analysis. The Makefile
     contains the individual Make targets for running each block-level analysis session separately,
     for example to run sessions in parallel. Edit the Makefile to create a setup that fits your work
     environment. The default environment uses the top-level output directory hcdc_run. Each

Questa® CDC User Guide                                           239
CDC Analysis

HDM Top-Down CDC Analysis                                                                             

block CDC session uses an output directory in hcdc_run with the same unique block name that
matches its constraints file. The output directory for the top run is the -d <design> name. For
example:

prompt> ls hcdc_run

hcdc_run/block1-1
hcdc_run/top

3. Execute the hcdc_run.Makefile.
   The results of the block and top-level run CDC analysis are available at:

· hcdc_run/block1-0

· hcdc_run/block1-1

         · hcdc_run/top

Block-Specific Constraints in Top-Down Flow                                                                     

Block-Specific Constraints in Top-Down Flow

In top-down CDC analysis, you can specify block-specific constraints and waivers using the -setup_file
option with the hier block command. This ensures that constraints are applied only to the intended
hierarchical blocks without affecting the top-level analysis.
To apply waivers and directives to specific hierarchical blocks, you can define a custom Tcl file with
necessary directives. Use the following command:

   hier block <module_name> -setup_file <Tcl directives file>

Example:

   hier block generic_fifo_dc_gray -setup_file blk_setup.tcl

Sample Setup:

   qverify -c -od Output_Results -do " \
          sdc load demo_top.sdc; \
          hier block generic_fifo_dc_gray -setup_file blk_setup.tcl; \
          cdc run -d demo_top; \"

Makefile Integration:
The HDM top-down flow integrates block-specific directives through setup files generated during the
analysis. These directives are included in the setup files generated for each block.
When integrating setup files in the Makefile, the specified Tcl file must be processed with -use_directives
option to ensure proper validation and prevent execution of invalid commands. The setup file is included
in a block-specific Tcl file that is generated during the flow.
Sample Makefile entry:

   blk1:
              qverify -c -do "do Output_Results/../hcdc_run_blk.tcl"

Generated block-specific Tcl file (hcdc_run_blk.tcl):

   do Output_Results/../hcdc_constraints_blk.tcl
   do blk_setup.tcl -use_directives

The setup files are processed only for their specified sub-blocks, supporting multiple blocks in a single
command. This prevents unmatched crossing warnings at the top level and ensures proper constraint
application.

         Note:
         Consider the following:
          · When specifying multiple blocks, the same setup file applies to all listed blocks: hier block blk1

            blk2 -setup_file blk_setup.tcl.
          · The -setup_file option cannot be used in conjunction with the -user_specified option.

242                                          Questa® CDC User Guide
                                                                      CDC Analysis

                                                        Hierarchical CDC Constraints

Hierarchical CDC Constraints

Each block port can have two sets of constraints--the top-down constraints and the bottom-up
constraints.

Top-down constraints are the attributes on the block's ports that are imposed by the top-level logic.You
can apply these directives manually during block-level CDC analysis. These constraints can be specified
as netlist or cdc directives. For example: netlist clock, netlist reset, netlist port domain, netlist constant, or
cdc signal.

Bottom-up constraints are the attributes on the block's ports that are imposed by the internal logic of the
block. These constraints are embodied in the hierarchical database (hcdc_<block>.hierdb). CDC infers
and saves them in HDM during the block-level analysis. They are reported in the form of hier directives,
for example, hier clock, hier reset, hier port domain, hier stable, and hier constant among others.

Figure 97 shows the relationship between top-down and bottom-up hierarchical port constraints.

                                          Figure 97. Hierarchical Port Constraints

Conflict Checks

When performing hierarchical CDC analysis, you need to ascertain that block-level and top-level
constraints are set correctly. The constraints to the block should be compatible with the constraints
between the top-level run and the block-level run.

During block-level CDC analysis, constraints for the block ports are inferred and they can at times differ
from the user-specified constraints present in the top-level CDC analysis. This leads to mismatches
between the inferred constraints and the user-specified constraints.

Table 17 shows the list of conflicts that Questa CDC detects.

                                             Table 17. HDM Integration Conflicts

  Conflict Check        Block-level Constraint  Top-level Constraint

  hcdc-2                Block port is not inferred or specified Block port driven by clock
                        as a clock signal

  hcdc-3                Block port is inferred or specified as Block port is not driven by a clock
                        a clock signal          signal

Hierarchical CDC Assumptions

Assumptions are external block connection properties that should validate during the block integration in
SoC. Specify these assumptions through directives during the block run or top run of the hierarchical CDC
analysis. During CDC analysis at the SoC level, Questa CDC checks the assumptions for each instance
of the block and generates a warning if the assumptions do not match.

When using hierarchical CDC analysis, use the hier assume port directive and hier assume connection
directive to specify the assumptions related to the HDM. You can specify assumptions in the block run
and top run of the hierarchical CDC analysis.

Table 18 explains all the available hier assumption directives along with their options. all these
assumption directives are applicable for a custom synchronizer module as well.

                                            Table 18. Hier Assumption Directives

Assumption Directives                  Description

hier assume port <port> -no_combo -module Checks if the specified port of the HDM module is not
<HDM module>                           connected to combo logic outside the HDM module.

hier assume port <port> -clock         Checks if the specified port of the HDM module is driven
<top_clk_name> -module <HDM module>    by top_clk_name signal outside the HDM module.

hier assume port <port> -sync -module  Checks if the specified port of the HDM module is driven
<HDM module>                           by a synchronizer outside the HDM module.

Advanced Hierarchical CDC Analysis Methods

Questa CDC analysis provides the flexibility to make certain adjustments to the hierarchical analysis
methods to meet your specific design requirements.

        Overriding HDM Information

Overriding HDM Information

When using the Bottom-up method, you have the flexibility to override the block port constraints for the
top-level CDC analysis using the hier directives.

In the Bottom-up CDC hierarchical method, you run block-level CDC analysis on the specified blocks
along with the block constraints and then load the generated HDMs for the blocks. For example:

  qverify> cdc load hierdb OutputResults/block1/hcdc_block1.hierdb
  qverify> cdc load hierdb OutputResults/block2/hcdc_block2.hierdb
  qverify> cdc load hierdb OutputResults/block3/hcdc_block3.hierdb

Run the top-level CDC analysis:

  qverify> cdc run -d demo_top

Hierarchical constraints report (hcdc.rpt) contains the hierarchical analysis results. Here, the top-
level analysis uses the bottom-up port constraints saved in the HDMs, which also are reported in the
hcdc.rpt file. However, you can override the block port constraints for the top-level analysis using the hier
directives described in Table 19.

                                     Table 19. Block Constraint Override Directives

  Directive                      Description

  hier clock                     Specifies that a hierarchical block port is a clock port with the
                                 specified attributes.

  hier reset                     Specifies that a hierarchical block port is a reset port with the
                                 specified attributes.

  hier constant                  Specifies that a hierarchical block port is held at the specified
                                 constant value.

  hier stable                    Specifies that a hierarchical block port is stable.

  hier port domain               Specifies the port domain attributes o a hierarchical block port.

To override constraints for a particular block, you must edit the override template file for the block.
The override template file is created during the block-level analysis and the file naming format is:
hcdc_<block>.tcl. Sample hierarchical constraint template is shown in Example 4.

Questa® CDC User Guide                                                                                   247
CDC Analysis

User-Specified Tcl HDM                                                                                

                                      Example 4. Hierarchical Constraint Template

      ######################################################################
      ###
      #
      # Hier-CDC Constraints
      #
      ######################################################################
      ###
      # hier port domain {clr} -multiple_clocks -module {blk2}
      # hier clock {core_clk_in} -module {blk2}
      # hier port domain {addr} -clock {cpu_clk_in} -combo_logic -module

       {blk2}
      # hier clock {cpu_clk_in} -module {blk2}
      # hier port domain {din} -clock {core_clk_in} -module {blk2}
      # hier constant {scan_mode} 1'b0 -module {blk2}
      # hier reset {rst} -module {blk2}
      # hier port domain {we} -clock {core_clk_in} -combo_logic -module {blk2}

The hier directives for the constraints saved in HDM in the override template file are commented
out. Uncomment and fix the desired commands and save the file to a different name, for example:
hcdc_<block>_override.tcl to prevent a future block run from overwriting it. Perform the steps as follows to
load and source the override template file:

     1. Load the hierarchical databases for the blocks. You must load the hierdb for the block you are
          overriding.

            qverify> cdc load hierdb OutputResults/block1/hcdc_block1.hierdb
            qverify> cdc load hierdb OutputResults/block2/hcdc_block2.hierdb
            qverify> cdc load hierdb OutputResults/block3/hcdc_block3.hierdb

     2. Source the override template file as follows:
           qverify> do OutputResults/block2/hcdc_block2_override.tcl

     3. Run top-level analysis as usual.
           qverify> cdc run -d demo_top

     Tip
     To recover a lost override template file from a block's HDM, use the hier generate tcl command.

User-Specified Tcl HDM

There can be instances when you may not wish to include HDMs with the IP blocks for use in hierarchical
analysis. In such scenarios, load the HDMs individually through Tcl commands. Based on your
requirements, specify both module-specific HDMs and instance-specific HDMs using the Tcl commands.

248                                       Questa® CDC User Guide
                                              CDC Analysis

                                              User-Specified Tcl HDM

To specify Tcl HDM, either reuse the override template by uncommenting the hier directives or create
a new file and specify the hier directives. When performing CDC analysis of the top level with a block
without a hierdb--replace the cdc load hierdb step with a hier block -user_specified command as follows:

  qverify> hier block -user_specified block1
  qverify> do hcdc_block1.tcl
  qverify> cdc run -d demo_top

Here, hier block -user_specified directive identifies the hierarchical block for which there is no
corresponding hierdb provided. Subsequent hier directives--in this case, the hcdc_block1.tcl file--specify
the HDM model in Tcl format instead of hierdb.

To specify the different HDMs for different instances and modules of the same HDM module, use the
-instance and -module arguments.

The following example shows how to set different behavior for the two instances (M1.inst1 and M1.inst2)
of the block1 module by using the -instance argument.

   qverify> hier block ­user_specified block1 ­instance M1.inst1
   qverify> hier port domain P1 ­clock clk1 ­module block1 ­instance M1.inst1
   qverify> hier assume port P1 ­nocombo ­module block1 ­instance M1.inst1
   qverify> hier clock clk1 ­module block1 ­instance M1.inst1
   qverify> hier clock clk2 ­module block ­instance M1.inst1

   qverify> hier block ­user_specified block1 ­instance M1.inst2
   qverify> hier port domain P1 ­clock clk2 ­module block1 ­instance M1.inst2
   qverify> hier clock clk1 ­module block1 ­instance M1.inst2
   qverify> hier clock clk2 ­module block1 ­instance M1.inst2
   qverify> cdc run ­d top

Here,

Questa® CDC User Guide                        249
CDC Analysis

Modifying Parameter Configurations for HDMs  

       · For the M1.inst1 instance, the P1 port is connected to the clk1 domain inside the HDM module
          whereas, for the M1.inst2 instance, the P1 port is connected to the clk2 domain inside the HDM
          module.

       · For the M1.inst1 instance an assumption is specified through the hier assume directive that the
          P1 port should not be connected to combo logic outside the HDM module. However, since this
          assumption is not specified for the M1.inst2 instance, in the top-run analysis the assumption will
          only be applicable for the M1.inst1 instance.

If the design contains multiple instances of the HDM module, then you must specify the HDMs for all the
instances through the Tcl commands. If you do not specify the HDMs for any instances, a warning will be
generated.

Modifying Parameter Configurations for HDMs

Typically, while generating HDM, the parameter configurations of the block during the block-level analysis
should match the parameter configurations of the block instance during top-level analysis. However, if
you want to use hierdb with different parameters, use the hier parameter directive. The hier parameter
directive enables you to modify the parameters based on your requirements. If you need to use the HDM
with different parameter configurations during the top-level analysis, you can load the hierdb file with the
-ignore_parameter_check option.

To integrate an HDM in the top-level analysis with different parameter values, the following hier parameter
options are available:

       · Specify legal parameter value range for the hierarchical blocks using the following command:

            hier parameter <parameter_name> -range <parameter value range>

          When the block is used in the top-level analysis, instances of the block must have parameter
          values that satisfy the hier parameter specifications.

       · Specify that all the values for a parameter are legal by using the following command:

            hier parameter <parameter name> -ignore <parameter name>

       · Specify that all the values for all the parameters are legal by using the following command:

            hier parameter <parameter name> -ignore

          The hier parameter -ignore directive with no parameters specified indicates that all values are
          legal for all parameters.

       · Specify the parameter match to be ignored while loading hierdb by using the following command:

            cdc load hierdb

For example, the following Tcl script creates an HDM model of block1 with the specified ranges of legal
values for parameters WIDTH1 and WIDTH2.

250                                          Questa® CDC User Guide
                        CDC Analysis

                        CDC HDM Models

   configure output directory Block1
   hier parameter WIDTH1 ­range 0 32
   hier parameter WIDTH2 ­range 0 16
   cdc run ­d block1 ­hcdc

A subsequent top-level run loads the HDM model of block1 and performs CDC analysis:

   cdc load hierdb Block1/hcdc_dut.hierdb
   cdc run ­d top ­hcdc

However, if any instance of block1 in top has values of WIDTH1 and WIDTH2 outside the legal ranges,
the top-level run terminates with an hcdc-11 error:

   Error: Parameter mismatch between module and specified hierdb. Module
     'dut', Instance 'inst3', Hierdb(s)',

   Block1/hcdc_dut.hierdb(Mismatching Parameter(s) WIDTH1) [hcdc-11]:
     Processing will abort.

CDC HDM Models

CDC supports three different models of HDM: standard, interface, and abstract.

Standard HDM

If your design has a standard HDM of a block, you can load the HDM using the cdc load hierdb directive.
This instance of standard HDM is available in the GUI.

   block:
   qverify> vlog block.v
   qverify> cdc run -d block -hcdc -od BLOCK
   top:
   qverify> vlog top.v
   qverify> cdc load hierdb BLOCK/hcdc_block.hierdb
   qverify> cdc run ­d top -od TOP

The following apply to each instance of an standard HDM when analyzed at the top level:

       · RTL reference to block HDM is available.

       · Block schematic is available in the GUI.

       · In case of multiple CDC crossings on a port, single crossing with multi_clock is reported in the
          cdc_detail.rpt.

Interface HDM

Interface HDM is similar to the standard HDM that contains the block interface logic. During interface
HDM creation, a complete CDC analysis takes place and all the crossings internal to the block are
reported. Any information related to the block internals is not saved in the interface HDM. However, the
following apply to each instance of an interface HDM when analyzed at the top level:

Questa® CDC User Guide  251
CDC Analysis

CDC HDM Models                                                                                              

       · RTL reference to block HDM is available.

       · Block schematic is available in the GUI.

       · In case of multiple CDC crossings on a port, single crossing with multi_clock is reported in the
          cdc_detail.rpt.

To load the standard HDM, use the cdc load hierdb directive.
Examples

     1. This example illustrates the use of the -use_interface_hdm option:
          Block:

            qverify> vlog block.v
            qverify> cdc run ­d block -hcdc -od BLOCK

          Top:

            qverify> vlog top.v
            qverify> cdc load hierdb BLOCK/hcdc_block.hierdb -use_interface_hdm
            qverify> cdc run ­d top -od TOP

     2. This example illustrates the impact of the -use_interface_hdm option while loading the hierdb.
          It shows that the TX indicated at the interface of the HDM block (refer to the figure below) may
          correspond to the actual TX within the HDM block.

     The crossing is reported as combo_logic since the actual TX is inside the HDM block. However,
     when the hierdb is loaded as interface_hdm, the reporting of the TX signal occurs at the HDM
     block's output port. For instance, as shown in the figure below, the actual TX signal is t1.TX, but
     the tool reports the TX as t1.out when the HDM is loaded as an interface HDM.

Abstract HDM

Abstract HDM model is similar to the interface HDM model with the following differences:

  · In case of multiple CDC crossings on a port, multi_clock crossings are expanded for individual
     clock domain in the cdc_detail.rpt.

  · RTL reference to block HDM is not available at the top.

             Note:
             If the compiled library of block is available during the top run, the RTL reference of block
             will be available at the top.

To create an abstract HDM, specify hier preference -create_abstract_hdm directive along with the -hcdc
option for HDM:

  block:
  qverify> vlog block.v
  qverify> hier preference ­create_abstract_hdm
  qverify> cdc run ­d block -hcdc -od BLOCK

Load the abstract HDM using the cdc load hierdb directive. This instance of abstract HDM appears as a
black box in the GUI.

   top:
   qverify> vlog top.v
   qverify> cdc load hierdb BLOCK/hcdc_block.hierdb
   qverify> cdc run ­d top -od TOP

Auto-Import of Block Waiver to Top Run

Auto-import of block run waivers to the top run, allow crossings in the top run to be waived using waivers
specified in the block run.

If a crossing from a block input port to a sequential element or from a sequential element to the block
output port is waived in a block run, corresponding crossings reported in the top run across the block
boundary will also be waived. The block waiver directives (cdc report item) are modified and saved inside
the block HDM. While using this HDM in top run, these are applied. For all waivers migrated from the
block run and filtering any crossing in the top run, a message indicating that the waiver is migrated from

Questa® CDC User Guide                                                                                     253
CDC Analysis

Auto-Import of Block Waiver to Top Run                                                                      

the block is added in the comment of the waiver. This message can be seen in the CDC status report.
The waivers are internally generated from block waivers and follow the normal course as other waiver
directives in the top run.

Examples

     1. Consider the following example to illustrate the feature:
          Block run directive:

     cdc report item -status waived -from r_in -message "Validating"

     Top run directive:

      cdc report item -status waived -message {waiver imported by the tool
        from block HDM; Validating} -module block -through {out} -from {r_in}
        -tx_clock {clk2} -rx_clock {clk1}

     In this example, the waiver specified in the block run is modified and saved in the HDM. The
     modified waiver is then automatically applied in the top run. The related directive view and status
     report in the top should point to the original directive.

     2. Consider the following example where netlist port domain is specified in the block. It illustrates
          assigning a domain to the ports and translating waivers in the block run.

     netlist port domain out -clock clk1
     cdc report item ­from in -status waived

     Sample Block Design:
      module block (input in, clk1, clk2, output out);
      reg r_in;
      always @ (posedge clk2) r_in <= in;
      assign out = r_in;
      endmodule

     Specify the clock and the clock domain in the top and, load the hierarchical block:

                        Power Aware CDC

Power Aware CDC

Power aware CDC (CDC-PA) is an extension to the CDC analyzer that handles HDL designs augmented
with power control logic. Whereas standard design logic is specified through an HDL (SystemVerilog or
VHDL), power control logic is commonly specified with a powerintention specification written in Unified
Power Format (UPF).

The UPF definition of the power architecture for a design applies to the entire design process--from
abstract functional model through its physical implementation. So, the abstract logic associated with
a UPF definition can be considered both a functional specification and a physical implementation.
A design's power architecture partitions the design into regions (called power domains) that have
independent power supplies. It defines how interaction among the logic in different power domains is
managed and mediated.

Figure 98 shows a subcircuit with and without the power control logic added by its UPF definition.

                              Figure 98. UPF Adds Power Control Logic to HDL Design

CDC-PA handles UPF-extended HDL designs by doing two things:

       · Static verification of the UPF logic.

       · Analysis of clock domain crossings involving UPF logic.
Static verification of the UPF logic consists of a series of checks performed by the Questa SIM vopt
command (see the "PA Static Checks" table). These focus on two power-management logic structures:
isolation cells and level shifters. The CDC analyzer calls vopt in the background to perform these static
checks--for details of these checks and how to debug them, see "UPF Static Checks".

Questa® CDC User Guide  257
CDC Analysis

Dynamic Voltage and Frequency Scaling                                                              

CDC analysis of the design with UPF logic can uncover clock domain crossing issues where both power
domains and clock domains are involved. For example, a design without power logic might have a clock
domain crossing that is properly synchronized. But, adding power control logic adds combinational logic
to the crossing, which makes the crossing unsynchronized. Adding a synchronizer after the combinational
logic (that is, in the Tx clock domain, but in the sink power domain) can restore proper synchronization.

Table 21 lists the CDC Schemes that are reported by CDC analysis of UPF-extended designs. These
schemes have the prefix pa_ and are violations by default.

                                                   Table 21. CDC-PA Schemes

Scheme                   Description

pa_combo_logic           UPF adds combinational logic to a crossing.
pa_fanin_different_clks  When UPF logic is added, synchronizer has fanin from multiple clock
                         domains.
pa_iso_en_no_sync        UPF isolation cell enable signal does not have a proper synchronizer.
pa_retention_restore     UPF retention register restore port does not have a proper synchronizer.
pa_retention_save        UPF retention register save port does not have a proper synchronizer.

Dynamic Voltage and Frequency Scaling

CDC-PA handles new techniques adopted for low power designs, such as the presence of dynamic
voltage scaling, that may adversely affect CDC design logic. Advanced low power designs take
advantage of dynamic voltage frequency scaling (DVFS) to improve power savings and maximize
performance. By reducing the voltage and/or frequency, designs can reduce power consumption and heat
dissipation when performance is not needed.

However, new metastability issues between registers in the same synchronous clock group may be
introduced in designs that implement DVFS techniques. Moreover, paths to or from variable voltage
domains behave the same way as paths to or from asynchronous clock domains. So synchronous clocks
on a variable voltage domain do not have a synchronous relationship with other clocks in the design
and CDC-PA treats these clocks as new asynchronous clocks. As the voltage level for a specific voltage
domain changes, the clock in that voltage domain does not maintain a deterministic phase relationship
to the synchronous clocks in other variable voltage groups. CDC-PA considers every control and data
signal that runs to or from DVFS voltage domains as CDC paths including signals between synchronous
registers, as shown in the following example.

By default, CDC-PA does not create a CDC violation for a level shifter, since in general, there is a static
delay. For DVFS, CDC-PA treats the clocks between voltage domains as asynchronous, causing signals
between voltage domains to become asynchronous to each other. This behavior can be enabled using
the following command:

cdc preference clock -voltage_domain_async

Example:                                    Questa® CDC User Guide
258
                        CDC Analysis

                        Dynamic Voltage and Frequency Scaling

  # Create power domains.
  create_power_domain TOP
  create_power_domain PD_I0 -elements {i0}
  create_power_domain PD_I1 -elements {i1}

  # Create supply ports.
  create_supply_port VDD_HIGH
  create_supply_port VDD_HIGH_1
  create_supply_port VDD_HIGH_2
  create_supply_port VSS

  # Create supply nets.
  create_supply_net VDD_HIGH -domain TOP
  create_supply_net VDD_HIGH_1 -domain TOP
  create_supply_net VDD_HIGH_2 -domain TOP
  create_supply_net VSS -domain TOP

  # Connect supply nets to ports.
  connect_supply_net VDD_HIGH -ports VDD_HIGH
  connect_supply_net VDD_HIGH_1 -ports VDD_HIGH_1
  connect_supply_net VDD_HIGH_2 -ports VDD_HIGH_2
  connect_supply_net VSS -ports VSS

  # Declare primary power and ground nets for the power domains.
  set_domain_supply_net TOP -primary_power_net VDD_HIGH -primary_ground_net

   VSS
  set_domain_supply_net PD_I0 -primary_power_net VDD_HIGH_2

   -primary_ground_net VSS
  set_domain_supply_net PD_I1 -primary_power_net VDD_HIGH_1

   -primary_ground_net VSS

  Figure 99. Synchronous Registers on Different Voltage Domains Considered New CDC Paths

Insertion of only level shifters on paths between voltage domains is insufficient to handle the
asynchronous behavior of the synchronous clocks between variable voltage domains. CDC-PA checks if
a CDC synchronizer is present on the receiver side of the data transfer between these voltage domains,
thus ensuring correct handling of DVFS crossings, as shown in Figure 100.

UPF Support

CDC-PA supports the UPF 3.0 standard (IEEE 1801-2015).

There are two types of UPF versions:

       · UPF version or UPF syntactic version -- This version is mentioned in the UPF files and is used
          for syntax checking. To change the UPF syntactic version, specify the new version in the UPF file.
          By default, Questa supports version 2.0.

       · UPF semantic version -- Questa supports version 2.0, by default. To change the UPF
          semantic version, use the vopt command with the -pa_upfversion option. The PA design report
          (pa_design_detail.rpt) shows the UPF semantic version, which is either set by the pa_upfversion
          option or is UPF Semantics 2.0, by default.

For different UPF semantic versions, the definition of some command and options varies. Questa PA is
designed to handle the varied implementation of these commands and options, and the tool automatically
considers the required functions based on the semantic version specified.

If a new command or option is added in a newer UPF version:

       · you must specify the command or option along with the new UPF version in the UPF file. If you
          fail to specify the commands or options in the UPF file, vopt generates a syntax error.

       · the tool considers and processes the command or option as per the new UPF semantic version,
          which was not present in the UPF semantic version 2.0.

       · the tool considers the commands and options of the new UPF semantic version in the default run
          regardless of whether the new version is specified with vopt -pa_upfversion and the default UPF
          semantic version is set to 2.0.

For example, if a new command is added in UPF version 3.1, you must specify the UPF version 3.1 and
the new command in the UPF file. However, if you don't specify vopt -pa_upfversion 3.1, the tool still
considers the semantic version 3.1 and its commands for the default run.

The following points must be noted while using UPF files:

260           Questa® CDC User Guide
                                                                  CDC Analysis

                                                                  UPF Support

  · If the UPF version specified in the top level UPF file is UPF Semantic 2.1 but the vopt
     pa_upfversion does not specify any version, then the PA design report includes the default
     version, which is UPF Semantics 2.0.

  · If there are multiple UPF files with different UPF versions specified but the vopt pa_upfversion
     does not specify any version, then the PA design report includes the default version, which is
     UPF Semantics 2.0.

Running CDC-PA Analysis

The CDC-PA flow is the same as the static CDC analysis flow. The flow has three steps: compile HDL;
run CDC analysis; debug results. The same method is used for both flows; the only addition for power
aware CDC analysis is to compile the UPF files.

This is done automatically by the cdc run command. You indicate which UPF files to compile with the
pa_upf <file> option:

  qverify -c -do " \
   onerror {exit 1}; \
   cdc run -d top -pa_upf my.upf; \
   exit 0"

Without this option, cdc run performs only static CDC analysis; with the option, cdc run performs PA-
extended CDC analysis.

Questa® CDC User Guide                                                                                 269
CDC Analysis

Running CDC-PA Analysis  

Generating Reports

Typical CDC sessions are configured to generate a crossings report (cdc generate crossings). Another
useful report applicable only to CDC-PA is the PA design report. Use netlist generate pa design to create
this report (default: pa_design_detail.rpt). For example:

   qverify -c -do " \
      onerror {exit 1}; \
      cdc run -d top -pa_upf my.upf; \
      cdc generate crossings crossings.rpt; \
      netlist generate pa pa_design_detail.rpt -design; \
      exit 0"

Hierarchical CDC-PA Analysis

CDC-PA is compatible with hierarchical CDC analysis using HDMs as shown in the following example.
The design top has only one hierarchical block: interleaver. The following session runs CDC analysis of
hm_shift_ram, and generates the HDM for, the interleaver block:

   qverify -c -od blk_interleaver -do " \
      onerror {exit 1}; \
      netlist clock vclk -virtual; \
      netlist port domain iso_en -clock vclk; \
      cdc run -d hm_shift_ram -process_dead_end \
        -pa_upf interleaver.upf -hcdc; \
      cdc generate crossings crossings.rpt; \
      netlist generate pa pa_design_detail.rpt -design; \
      exit 0"

The following session runs CDC analysis of top:

   qverify -c -od top -do " \
      onerror {exit 1}; \
      netlist clock vclk -virtual; \
      netlist port domain iso_en -clock vclk; \
      cdc load hierdb blk_interleaver/hcdc_interleaver.hierdb; \
      cdc run -d top -process_dead_end -pa_upf top.upf ; \
      cdc generate crossings crossings.rpt; \
      netlist generate pa pa_design_detail.rpt -design; \
      exit 0"

Typically, UPF files are organized hierarchically, so the hierarchical UPF is compatible with the
hierarchical CDC structure. Here, top.upf loads interleaver.upf:

   prompt> more top.upf
   ...
   set_design_top top
   set upf_dir .
   ...
   load_upf_protected $upf_dir/interleaver.upf

     -params { hm_shift_ram_scope intl_io_scope glue_logic_scope upf_dir }
     -hide_globals

270                      Questa® CDC User Guide
                                                                 CDC Analysis

                        CDC-PA Results Analysis

Since hm_shift_ram is the module in the block run, load_upf_protected sets the scope to
hm_shift_ram_scope.

Note that hierarchical UPF is supported whether or not the blocks are analyzed hierarchically by CDC.
In this example, interleaver.upf loads another UPF file (shiftmem.upf) which loads another UPF file
(sram.upf):

  prompt> more interleaver.upf
  set_design_top interleaver
  create_power_domain PD_intl -include_scope
  load_upf_protected $upf_dir/shiftmem.upf -scope { shift_ram }
  prompt> more shiftmem.upf
  set_scope hm_shift_ram
  set upf_dir .
  ...
  load_upf_protected $upf_dir/sram.upf -scope { hm_sram }

CDC-PA Schemes

All the clock domain crossings of an HDL subcircuit might be properly synchronized. However, adding
power management logic to the subcircuit can result in extra un-synchronization. For CDC-PA, additional
CDC schemes are added to identify these crossings.

pa_iso_en_no_sync Crossings

The pa_iso_en_no_sync crossings are cases where the isolation enable signal crosses from a power
control cell in a clock domain to the isolation cell in another clock domain without proper synchronization
(Figure 108).

276                                                         Questa® CDC User Guide
                                                                 CDC Analysis

                                                                 CDC-PA Results Analysis

                        Figure 108. pa_iso_en_no_sync Violation

                 Violations
                 =================================================================
                 Isolation enable signal does not have proper synchronizer.
                 (pa_iso_en_no_sync)
                 -----------------------------------------------------------------
                 clk2 : start : pwr_ctrl.out1 (top.v : 11)

                             clk1 : end : Rx.out1 (top.v : 11) (ID:iso_en_no_sync_40515)

pa_fanin_different_clks Crossings

A pa_fanin_different_clks crossing is a crossing that is synchronized in the HDL logic--but, the power
management logic adds logic that results in a synchronizer's fanin logic coming from two clock domains
(Figure 109). Without the power-aware logic, the crossing might be properly synchronized. You should
change the clock for the isolation enable register to match the clock for the transmit signal.

                                      Figure 109. pa_fanin_different_clks Violation

  Violations
  =================================================================
  Power-aware fanin logic from multiple clock domains.
  (pa_fanin_different_clks)
  -----------------------------------------------------------------
  rx_clk: end : Rx.s1 (.../cdc_pa_fanin_diff_clks/top.v : 11)

                                                        (ID:pa_fanin_different_clks_73486)

Questa® CDC User Guide                                                                      277
CDC Analysis

CDC-PA Results Analysis                                                                                     

                        pwr_iso_clk: start : Pwr_ctrl.out
                                                         (.../cdc_pa_fanin_diff_clks/top.v : 23)

                                     via : Rx.in
                        tx_clk: start : Tx2.out (.../cdc_pa_fanin_diff_clks/top.v:
              19)

                                     via : Rx.in

pa_combo_logic Crossings

A pa_combo_logic crossing is a crossing that is synchronized in the HDL logic--but, the power
management logic adds an isolation cell before the synchronizer. The crossing path travels through
combinational logic in the isolation cell, which makes the crossing unsynchronized when the isolation cell
is not clamped (Figure 110). The fix is to add a Tx domain register after the isolation cell.

                                           Figure 110. pa_combo_logic Violation

     Violations
     =================================================================
     Power aware combinational logic before synchronizer.
     (pa_combo_logic)
     -----------------------------------------------------------------
     clk1 : start : Tx.out1 (top.v : 12)

                 clk2 : end : sync.out1 (top.v : 12)
      (ID:pa_combo_logic_71618)

               Base Type : TWO DFF SYNCHRONIZER

pa_retention_restore Crossings

A pa_retention_restore violation occurs when UPF logic adds a retention register, but the signal driving
the register's restore port and the retention register are in different clock domains. Without the power-
aware logic, no crossing exists. But, when the UPF retention logic is added, the unsynchronized retention
restore signal spawns a pa_retention_restore violation.

The following example shows an instance of a pa_retention_restore scheme. UPF for the design:

   set_design_top interleaver
   create_logic_port ret_en
   create_logic_port sw_en
   create_logic_port clamp_mem

   ## Top-level PD_intl which is always on
   create_power_domain PD_intl -include_scope
   create_power_domain PD_gluelogic -elements { }

278                      Questa® CDC User Guide
                        CDC Analysis

                        CDC-PA Results Analysis

   create_power_domain PD_intl -update \
        -supply { mem_ssh } \
        -supply { perif_ssh } \
        -supply { sram_ssh } \
        -supply { primary }

   set_retention glue_ret -domain PD_gluelogic -update \
        -save_signal { save posedge } \
        -restore_signal { restore negedge }

The UPF logic inserts a retention register (INTERNAL_restore1) between two DFFs in the clk1 domain.
However, the retention restore signal (restore1) comes directly from domain clk2 (unsynchronized). So
the HDL logic has no clock domain crossing. However, the UPF logic adds a control signal with a missing
(or invalid) synchronizer, which is identified as a pa_retention_restore crossing (violation).

  Violations
  =================================================================
  Power-aware retention restore.(pa_retention_restore)
  -----------------------------------------------------------------
  clk2: start: Pwr_ctrl.restore1 (top.v: 11)

           clk1: end: Rx.restore1 (top.v:
   11)(ID:pa_retention_restore_4494)

pa_retention_save Crossings

The pa_retention_save violation occurs when UPF logic adds a retention register, but the signal driving
the register's save port and the retention register are in different clock domains. Without the power-aware
logic, no crossing exists. But, when the UPF retention logic is added, the unsynchronized retention save
signal spawns a pa_retention_save violation.

The following example shows an instance of a pa_retention_save scheme. UPF for the design:

   set_design_top interleaver
   create_logic_port ret_en
   create_logic_port sw_en
   create_logic_port clamp_mem

   ## Top-level PD_intl which is always on
   create_power_domain PD_intl -include_scope
   create_power_domain PD_gluelogic -elements { }

Questa® CDC User Guide                                               279
CDC Analysis

CDC-PA Results Analysis                                                                                  

create_power_domain PD_intl -update \
     -supply { mem_ssh } \
     -supply { perif_ssh } \
     -supply { sram_ssh } \
     -supply { primary }

set_retention glue_ret -domain PD_gluelogic -update \
     -save_signal { save posedge } \
     -restore_signal { restore negedge }

The UPF logic inserts a retention register (INTERNAL_save1) between two DFFs in the clk1 domain.
However, the retention save signal (save1) comes directly from domain clk2 (unsynchronized). So the
HDL logic has no clock domain crossing. However, the UPF logic adds a control signal with a missing (or
invalid) synchronizer, which is identified as a pa_retention_save crossing (violation).

     Violations
     =================================================================
     Power-aware retention save.(pa_retention_save)
     -----------------------------------------------------------------
     clk2 : start : Pwr_ctrl.save1 (top.v : 11)

               clk1 : end : Rx.save1 (top.v : 11)(ID:pa_retention_save_3194)

                        CDC Analysis of FPGAs

CDC Analysis of FPGAs

CDC analysis of an FPGA design requires special handling. The standard FPGA source libraries are
designed for simulation and in particular, they are not completely synthesizable. Synthesizable libraries
are needed because CDC analysis (unlike simulation) is based on a netlist of the design. Building a netlist
requires synthesizable code for compiling the design and for compiling the FPGA source libraries.

Questa CDC/Formal distribution software comes with synthesizable versions of the unisim/simprim
Xilinx and the Altera source libraries in <install_dir>/../../share/fpga_libs. Included in the Xilinx and Altera
subdirectories of fpga_libs are Makefiles and control files for running the flows.

         CAUTION:
         Recommended method for using FPGAs is to download pre-compiled synthesizable libraries
         as described in section Installing FPGA Libraries (Installation Instructions) and use the netlist
         fpga and netlist fpga directory commands to identify the required FPGA libraries for analysis. The
         following instructions are used for manually compiling FPGA libraries when the recommended
         procedure is not available.

        Phase 1: Compile FPGA Libraries
        Phase 2: Compile Design
        Phase 3: Create Clock Domain Model
        Phase 4: Run GUI Debug

Phase 1: Compile FPGA Libraries

If you have compiled your FPGA source libraries already for Questa simulation, you can use them
for CDC analysis if these statements are true--the libraries' RTL is synthesizable VHDL, Verilog, or
SystemVerilog code; and the libraries were compiled using the versions of Questa vcom/vlog commands
that match those shipped with the Questa CDC/Formal distribution software.

If these statements are true, skip to Phase 2. If not, compile the FPGA source libraries into resource
libraries. First create a directory to hold the compiled FPGA resource libraries:

   prompt> mkdir qstatic_libs

Then, set up and compile the FPGA source libraries. If FPGA library elements are instantiated in VHDL
code, you must compile a resource library for that. The logical library name for this library has no _ver
suffix. If FPGA library elements are instantiated in Verilog code, you must compile a resource library for
that. The logical library name for this library has a _ver suffix.

Xilinx

       · unisim

          Used for library elements instantiated in VHDL. Compile the VHDL files containing the component
          and package declarations from the standard Xilinx simulation library. Then compile the
          synthesizable Verilog models of the library. The vlog -convertallparams option is needed to
          convert the Verilog parameters to match the generic types in the VHDL component definitions.

     vcom -work unisim $XILINX/vhdl/src/unisims/unisim_VPKG.vhd
     vlog -work unisim -convertallparams \

Logical-Physical Library Mappings

The vmap command creates a logical-to-physical library mapping. For example, in the previous
examples, vmap mapped the logical name altera_mf to the physical location qstatic_libs/altera_mf. The
command also updates the modelsim.ini file with the logical-physical mapping. The command creates
a new modelsim.ini file if one does not exist. This example shows the library mappings for a VHDL-only
Xilinx design:

Questa® CDC User Guide                                            283
CDC Analysis

Phase 2: Compile Design                       

[Library]
unisim = ./qstatic_libs/unisim
XilinxCoreLib = ./qstatic_libs/XilinxCoreLib
work = ./qstatic_libs/work

Phase 2: Compile Design

You likely have created one or more filelists that identify the source code files for your design. The files
within each individual library must be compiled in the correct order. Also, different libraries that depend on
each other must be compiled in the correct order. Using filelists from simulation handles this.

With the filelists for your design, run the design compilation commands. The following example compiles a
VHDL-2002 design into the work library.

   vlib qstatic_libs/work
   vmap work qstatic_libs/work
   vcom -f vhdl_files.list -work work -skipsynthoffregion

The -skipsynthoffregion argument directs the compiler to obey synthesis-off regions. These are regions
of code surrounded by synthesis_off/synthesis_on (or translate_off/translate_on) pragmas. The compiler
parses this code to pick up declarations, but otherwise ignores it. One reason to use -skipsynthoffregion is
to ignore VHDL library and use statements for libraries needed for simulation only.

Rather than using a filelist to compile files with one invocation, you can set up a script to compile the file
one-by-one:

   vcom vhdl_file1.vhd -work work
   vcom vhdl_file2.vhd -work work
   vcom vhdl_file3.vhd -work work -skipsynthoffregion

The following example shows the compiler invocation for a Verilog design:

   vlog -f verilog_files.list -work work +incdir+src/verilog

Phase 3: Create Clock Domain Model

The target design is the top-level block for CDC analysis. This can be a VHDL entity (or configuration)
or a Verilog module. The -d <design> argument to the cdc run command is a required argument that
identifies the target design.

The cdc run command creates a CDC logic model for CDC analysis after the FPGA resource libraries and
design library are ready. Here is an example:

   cdc run -d DUT_top -work work

Creates a CDC model for the target design DUT_top from work library. The tool calls netlist create
automatically with the correct configuration arguments to use the library mappings from the default
modelsim.ini file in the current directory.

284                                           Questa® CDC User Guide
                        CDC Analysis

                        Phase 3: Create Clock Domain Model

Procedure

     1. Set up the directive files.

         A directives file is a Tcl-based file of Questa Functional Verification directives. Directives set up
         operating conditions, define clocks, define black boxes, specify custom synchronizers, modify
         reported results, create waivers, and so on. You apply significant effort creating and adjusting the
         directives files because this is how you fine tune CDC analysis. Here is an example:

            netlist constant scan_mode '0'
            netlist clock CLK_1 -group clk_grp_A -period 4
            netlist clock CLK_2 -group clk_grp_A -period 8
            netlist clock CLK_3 -group clk_grp_B -period 11
            netlist port domain input_port1 -async
            netlist port domain input_port2 -clock CLK_1
            netlist port domain -output -clock CLK_2
            cdc reconvergence -depth 1 -divergence_depth 1
            netlist blackbox syncA* cdi_master
            cdc preference -black_box_empty_module

         In addition to standard CDC directives, the following directives are particularly useful for CDC
         analysis of FPGA designs.

  · netlist constant

     Applies a constant value to input ports (and sometimes to internal nodes) so the cdc compiler
     can prune irrelevant logic from the design logic and the CDC model. This technique makes
     the memory footprint smaller, improves performance and ensures only relevant results are
     returned.

  · cdc preference reconvergence

     Sets the sequential levels that define how deep paths diverge and reconverge to be considered
     instances of reconvergence and single_source_reconvergence schemes. The deeper the
     analysis, the greater the decrease in performance. Initially, set the reconvergence depth to 1
     and the divergence depth to 1.

  · netlist blackbox

     Identifies specific modules/entities/architectures as user-defined black boxes. Use netlist
     portdomain directives to identify the clock domains for the black boxes' ports (even
     asynchronous ones) so the logic outside the black box instances can be analyzed properly.
     Fanin/fanout logic of ports of user-defined black box instances that are not assigned port
     domains is ignored for CDC analysis.

  · cdc preference -black_box_empty_module

     Turns empty modules/entities/architectures into inferred black boxes instead of treating them as
     regular models. Some elements in a synthesizable FPGA library are "stubs" containing only the
     port declarations. Specifying the black_box_empty_module option makes it easier to identify
     these elements so you can add netlist port domain directives for their ports.

     · cdc.db -- .db database of the CDC results for loading into the CDC GUI.

     4. Check the cdc_design.rpt file again.

          a. Check the port domains:

     Port Domain Information

     =======================

     Port Direction Constraints Clock Domain           Type

     ----------------------------------------------------------------

     rst input     Reset            {clk[1]}           Questa CDC

        Check the inferred port domains (clock domains assigned to the ports). By default, each input
        port is assigned to the clock domain of its first fan-in register. Any primary inputs or outputs that
        connect to multiple clock domains or are not assigned to a clock domain are listed. Use netlist
        port domain directives to make adjustments.

     b. Check for black boxes.

     Black Boxes:

     ------------

     Module        Instance Count File (Line)

     ----------------------------------------------------------------

     cdi_master    1                /home/cdc/blackbox/cdi_master.v (2)

     Black boxes may indicate that a design block is not verified by CDC analysis. Black boxes
     occur when a design block is not synthesizable or when an implementation model is not
     found for a design block. Internal logic of the black boxes is unknown and in particular, the
     connectivity between a black box's inputs and outputs is unknown. So, black boxes can mask
     some CDC problems. Check that the port domains of the user-defined black boxes (blackbox
     in the report) are all specified.

     VITAL models, FPGA library elements that are not synthesizable and design blocks with
     unsynthesizable constructs are inferred black boxes (inferred in the report), unless explicitly
     specified with netlist blackbox directives. Check the inferred black boxes in the GUI CDC
     Setup Checks window or in the cdc.rpt. If an inferred black box affects CDC results, at least
     one associated black box CDC scheme is reported:

     Black Box Crossing. (blackbox)
     ----------------------------------------------------------------
     tx_clk: start: tx_sig2 (/u/zin/blackbox/dut.v : 25)

            <clock N/A>: end: dut.Di2 (/u/zin/dut.v: 40)(ID:blackbox_12944)
