  It is recommended to specify the black box as a user-defined Hierarchical Data Model or HDM
  (with hier block) and specify the port domains for the HDM I/O ports (with hier port domain).

  The following example directives do this for an Altera dual-port RAM block:

  hier block -user_specified altdpram
  hier port domain wren -clock inclock -module altdpram
  hier port domain data -clock inclock -module altdpram
  hier port domain wraddress -clock inclock -module altdpram
  hier port domain wraddressstall -clock inclock \
  -module altdpram
  hier port domain inclocken -clock inclock -module altdpram
  hier port domain byteena -clock inclock -module altdpram
  hier port domain rden -clock outclock -module altdpram
  hier port domain rdaddress -clock outclock -module altdpram
  hier port domain rdaddressstall -clock outclock \
  -module altdpram
  hier port domain outclocken -clock outclock -module altdpram
  hier port domain q -clock outclock -module altdpram
  hier port domain aclr -async -module altdpram

  Alternatively, declare the black box as a user-defined black box (with netlist blackbox) and
  specify the port domains for the black box's I/O ports (with netlist port domain).

  The following example directives do this for an Altera dual-port RAM block:

  netlist blackbox altdpram
  netlist port domain wren -clock inclock -module altdpram
  netlist port domain data -clock inclock -module altdpram
  netlist port domain wraddress -clock inclock -module altdpram
  netlist port domain wraddressstall -clock inclock \
  -module altdpram
  netlist port domain inclocken -clock inclock -module altdpram
  netlist port domain byteena -clock inclock -module altdpram
  netlist port domain rden -clock outclock -module altdpram
  netlist port domain rdaddress -clock outclock -module altdpram
  netlist port domain rdaddressstall -clock outclock
  -module altdpram
  netlist port domain outclocken -clock outclock -module altdpram
  netlist port domain q -clock outclock -module altdpram
  netlist port domain aclr -async -module altdpram

  You might be able to obtain or write synthesizable models of various black boxed elements. For
  example, using the Xilinx CoreGen tool: choose Project > Project Options; select the Generation
  tab; and set Simulation Files: Structural. Structural models are synthesizable. Be sure to keep the
  structural models and behavioral models in different locations to prevent overwriting previously-
  generated files.

CDC Encryption

CDC analysis supports the encryption of source IP code and hides all information related to the encrypted
logic in the schematic. Warning/error messages, policy checks, crossings, clock/reset trees, and other
information in reports related to the encrypted portion of the design are hidden. CDC analysis labels
encrypted elements in the schematic, messages, and text reports as <protected>.

Encrypted design elements are labeled as <protected> in all the GUI windows. Figure 111 shows
encrypted elements in a schematic, the Design window, the Modules window, and the CDC Checks
window.

                                          Figure 111. CDC Encryption GUI Display

A snippet from the cdc_details.rpt report file:  Questa® CDC User Guide

   =================================================================

   =================================================================
   Violations (1)
   -----------------------------------------------------------------
   Single-bit signal does not have proper synchronizer. (PROTECTED) (1)
   ...
   ...

     (Status : uninspected)

CDC analysis also supports encryption in the hierarchical CDC flow. If a hierarchical data model (HDM)
is generated from a module containing encrypted elements, the elements are saved in the HDM with the
<protected> tag and reported as <protected> in the hcdc.rpt report file.

The encryption solution works with all CDC flows. CDC analysis supports all encryption standards
supported by the Questa simulator. Refer to the chapter Protecting Your Source Code in the Questa SIM
User's Manual for more information.

CDC Analysis with CDC Assist Machine Learning                                                             

CDC Analysis with CDC Assist Machine
Learning

CDC violations often have a common cause, and CDC analysis utilizes data mining and machine
learning to help you identify the cause for CDC violations and errors. CDC Assist utilizes machine
learning to analyze the CDC results to detect patterns, then builds on this learning to provide setup
recommendations that will reduce the number of unsynchronized crossings detected.

        CDC Assist Overview
        CDC Assist Step-by-Step Flow

CDC Assist Overview

CDC Assist machine learning will leverage results from previous designs to automate and accelerate
causality analysis and identify the cause of CDC violations.

CDC Assist machine learning will learn from previous design results to prioritize the highest return
violations, filter false violations and recommend constraints or waivers. Machine learning will identify
common violations to isolate the causes and reduce the redundant effort in repeatedly reviewing multiple
examples of the same violation. In general, CDC Assist will improve designer productivity and provide
faster CDC verification closure.

By reducing the number of unsynchronized crossings detected and automatically identifying the cause
of CDC violations, CDC Assist will improve designer productivity. CDC Assist prioritizes violations and
recommends constraints to enable faster CDC verification closure.

         Note:
         For crossings categorized as Evaluation type, such as async_reset, which are considered good
         crossings, no suggestions would be provided.

292                                            Questa® CDC User Guide
                        CDC Analysis

                        CDC Assist Step-by-Step Flow

CDC Assist Step-by-Step Flow

The CDC Assist flow utilizes both the CDC batch tool and the CDC GUI.
The steps of this flow are as follows:

        Step 1: Design Setup
        Step 2: Setting Up CDC Assist
        Step 3: Running CDC Assist
        Step 4: Reviewing CDC Results in the GUI
        Guide to Interpreting CDC Assist Analysis
        Step 5: Running CDC Analysis and Reviewing the Results

Step 1: Design Setup

The design setup includes compiling design files and specifying design constraints including CDC
preferences.

Step 2: Setting Up CDC Assist

You enable CDC Assist analysis with the cdc preference -assist directive to qverify.

Prerequisites

       · Refer to cdc preference assist.

Procedure

     1. To enable CDC Assist analysis, add the following directive to your qverify dofile or Makefile:

            cdc preference -assist

         For example:

            qverify -od Output_Results -c -do " \
                 do qs_files/directives.tcl; \
                 cdc preference -assist; \

            ...
                 cdc run -d $(DUT); \
                 cdc generate report cdc_detail.rpt; \
                 exit"

     2. Optionally, add additional options to specify thresholding. Refer to cdc preference assist for details.
         For example:

Questa® CDC User Guide  293
CDC Analysis

Step 3: Running CDC Assist                                                                                

     qverify -od Output_Results -c -do " \
          do qs_files/directives.tcl; \
          cdc preference -assist; \
          cdc preference assist -min_stable_signal_fanout 2; \
          cdc preference assist -min_impacted_crossings 2; \
          cdc run -d $(DUT); \
          cdc generate report cdc_detail.rpt; \
          exit"

Step 3: Running CDC Assist

Running CDC analysis with the assist preference generates the assist report.

Procedure

     1. In a shell, run the CDC Assist analysis using the cdc run executable.
         For example:

            cdc run ­d <DUT>

     2. Generate the detailed assist report using the cdc generate report executable.
         For example:

            cdc generate report ­assist

         The tool generates the following report: cdc_assist_detail.rpt
         You can also generate the detailed report during the assist analysis. For example:

            % qverify ­c ­do "cdc preference ­assist; \
                   cdc run ­d top_module; \
                   cdc generate report ­assist"

         Another variation is generating the detailed report after the assist analysis. For example:

            % qverify ­c ­do "cdc load db cdc.db; \
                     cdc generate report ­assist"

Results

Guide to Interpreting CDC Assist Analysis

The section provides a guide for you use to interpret the CDC Assist results contained in the CDC Assist
report.

296                                        Questa® CDC User Guide
                                                                             CDC Analysis

                        Guide to Interpreting CDC Assist Analysis

Constraint suggestion is generated for each possible cause suggested by the tool in report. You can apply
suggested constraints through GUI by clicking the right-mouse button and selecting the Edit Directive
menu after reviewing the suggested cause.

Review Suggested Synchronous Clocks

When CDC paths between two clocks only result in violations, the two clocks will be suggested as
"possible synchronous clocks". You should review the possible synchronous clocks and specify these
clocks as synchronous where appropriate.

For example:

If clk1, clk2 and clk3 are synchronous, you should specify the following constraints:

   netlist clk1 ­group clk1_group ­module top netlist \
      clk2 ­group clk1_group ­module top netlist clk3 \
      ­group clk1_group ­module top

Review Suggested Stable Signals

When a signal is the source of multiple missing synchronizer violations, these signals will be suggested

SDC Native Analysis Flow

The CDC tool provides a mechanism to use native SDC as input for analysis.
        SDC Native Analysis Use Case

SDC Native Analysis Use Case

Use this process to input SDC files and perform CDC analysis on these SDC design files.

Flow Overview

You use SDC files for the following related purposes:

       · Certain SDC directives set netlist attributes (of clocks, for example) and CDC constraints.

       · Tcl directive counterparts to the loaded SDC directives are exported as a Tcl file that can be
          loaded in a subsequent session.

Specifically, you can load the SDC data directly. Or, you can load the SDC data; generate a Tcl version
of the effective directives; edit the Tcl version, if necessary; and use that Tcl file to set up analysis
parameters for subsequent sessions.
Use the following SDC-specific executables in your CDC scripts:

       · sdc load

       · sdc generate tcl
For example:

   qverify -od Output_Results -c -do " \
              sdc preference -sta_mode; \
              sdc load sdc_files/my_design.sdc; \
              cdc setup -report cdc.rpt; \
              cdc run -d $(DUT); \
              exit"

SDC access commands can be used only after design elaboration. To process SDC access commands,
you must run CDC analysis.

Native SDC Flow Usage Notes

       · Clocks having same async relationship are grouped together

       · In native SDC mode, the logically exclusive relationship of clocks extends to gated clocks. As a
          result, the crossings between logically exclusive clocks and their gated clocks are not reported.
          You can view detailed information on paths excluded from CDC analysis due to exclusive clock
          relationships, in the sdc_exclusive_path.rpt report.

Questa® CDC User Guide                                                      305
CDC Analysis

SDC Native Analysis Use Case                                                                             

     · set_false_path not supported by default

      Only supported under preference sdc preference -infer_false_path_domains

      Unidirectional async clock relationship specified by set_false_path is considered bidirectional
        and treated in the similar manner as set_clock_groups

      The direction in which async relationship was not given is considered inferred false path.
        These are stored in m_resolvedInferredFalsePathDirection. The CDC crossing in this
        direction is filtered because this direction is synchronous

      Example: set_false_path -from CLK1 -to CLK2

        · Here, CLK1 and CLK2 will be considered async in both direction. The crossing will be
           waved in CLK2 CLK1 direction

       · Synchronous clock groups are saved in sdc context db and then restored to be used in 'cdc run'
          to filter boundaries between synchronous clock groups

       are not reported.

        create_clock -name CLK2 [get_ports clk2] -period 40

Questa® CDC User Guide                                   307
CDC Analysis

SDC Native Analysis Use Case                                                                            

     3. Logically exclusive relationships propagate through gated clocks.

          When CLK1 and CLK2 are defined as logically exclusive, the gated clock gc inherits this
          relationship, causing CDC analysis to suppress crossing reports between these clock domains.
          A subsequent CDC crossing from rx2 to rx3 (CLK3 domain) is reported since CLK3 has no
          exclusive relationship defined.

     Sample Design:

      module dut(input in, clk1, clk2, clk3, output q1, q2, q3);
         reg tx1, tx2, rx1, rx2, rx3;
         assign q1 = rx1;
         assign q2 = rx2;
         assign q3 = rx3;
         always@(posedge clk1)
             tx1 <= in;
         always@(posedge clk2)
             tx2 <= in;
         assign gc = clk1 & clk2;
         always@(posedge gc) begin
             rx1 <= tx1;
             rx2 <= tx2;
         end
         always@(posedge clk3)
             rx3 <= rx2;

      endmodule

                                                                             CDC Analysis

  create_clock -name CLK1 [get_ports clk1] -period 40
  create_clock -name CLK2 [get_ports clk2] -period 40
  create_clock -name CLK3 [get_ports clk3] -period 40

CDC Waiver Guidelines

While using waivers (such as cdc report item directives), follow these guidelines to avoid performance
challenges and unexpected filtering of any crossings.

       · Avoid Wildcard Pattern Matching Recursively: Use cdc preference ­match_local_scope
          {cdc_report_item} to avoid wildcard pattern matching recursively down the hierarchy. If such
          a need arises, write separate waiver commands with wildcards representing each hierarchy
          explicitly.
          For example, to waive a crossing with a Tx object starting with the character a1 inside the
          instance inst1 and its submodules, use inst1.a1*, inst1.*.a1*, inst1.*.*.a1*, and so on.

       · Avoid Wildcards in '­through' Argument: Avoid using any wildcard in the ­through argument
          of cdc report item directives, as using ­through itself is performance-intensive due to the potential
          for too many matches. Using a wildcard makes it even more aggressive.

       · Specify More Arguments: Try to specify as many arguments as possible in the waiver command
          to reduce the search scope while matching the different arguments.

       · Avoid Using Only * for Any Argument: Do not specify only '*' for any argument of the waiver
          command, as it puts pressure to match the pattern for all possible matches. It is better to omit that
          argument. For example:

            cdc report item ­scheme "*" ­to xyz ­tx_clock clk1

     · Minimize Wildcards in Multiple Arguments: Avoid using wildcards in multiple arguments of a
        waiver command. If complete removal is not feasible, try to minimize the use of such waivers. For
        example:

          cdc report item ­to "inst1.inst2.*.*.xyz" ­tx_clock "m1.m2.*.*/clk1"

     · Avoid Using Outdated Waivers: Avoid using waivers from previous versions of designs that are
        no longer applicable to the current design. Although they would not waive any crossing for the
        current design, processing those waivers consumes memory and runtime. To find such waiver
        commands, refer to Section 2 of the waiver.rpt generated through the cdc generate report ­status
        command, as it contains all waivers that are unused (not filtering any crossing).

310                    Questa® CDC User Guide
                        CDC Analysis

                        CDC Waiver Guidelines

  · Be Cautious with Waivers for Different Designs: Waivers written for one design might not be
     as aggressive as they are for another design. Be aware when using extensive waiver commands
     for any designs.

     Waiver commands showing good performance for a design with an older version of the tool but
     giving poor performance for another design with a newer version do not necessarily indicate
     an issue with the newer tool version. It is possible that the waivers are more aggressive for the
     newer design than the older design.

                        CDC-FX Metastability Injection

Metastability injected simulation is an extension to normal RTL simulation that injects random
metastability into the circuit's behavior. CDC-FX metastability injected simulation is similar to simulation
with assertions. But, it compiles special cdc_fx and cdc_mfx checkers to inject metastability into the circuit
at strategic clock domain crossings during simulation. These checkers also monitor the metastability logic
and report coverage of metastability effects during simulation.

                  Figure 113. Compiling CDC-FX/MFX Checkers with Metastability Injection

The cdc_fx checkers are generated for clock domain crossings that originate from single Tx clock
domains. These checkers inject delays that model metastability in both the setup and hold regions of
registers in Rx clock domains. The cdc_mfx checkers are generated for clock domain crossings that
originate from multiple Tx clock domains. These checkers inject delays that model metastability only in
the setup regions of registers in the Rx clock domains.

         Note:
         The checkers are also generated for CDCs across standard HDMs.

Running cdc generate fx command creates the cdc_fx and cdc_mfx checker logic and the simulation
arguments files that run simulation with CDC-FX metastability injection.

        Setting Up CDC-FX Metastability Injection
        Running Metastability-Injected Simulation
        Metastability Injector Simulation Methodology

Questa® CDC User Guide    313
CDC-FX Metastability Injection

Setting Up CDC-FX Metastability Injection  

Setting Up CDC-FX Metastability Injection

To compile CDC-FX metastability injection logic for use in simulation, run a CDC analysis session and
then run FX by executing the cdc generate fx command. But before running FX, ensure these preferences
are set up for compiling the metastability checkers--specify metastability windows; adjust CDC-FX
checker promotion; and control FX checker checks.

        Specifying Metastability Windows
        Adjusting CDC-FX Checker Promotion
        CDC-FX Cover Points
        Controlling CDC-FX Checks

Specifying Metastability Windows

The two metastability injection checker types (cdc_fx and cdc_mfx) have different metastability injection
logic and associated metastability windows. The cdc_fx checkers are automatically created for crossings
from sources in single Tx clock domains. They model delays involving both setup and hold violations.
The cdc_mfx checkers are automatically created for crossings from sources in multiple Tx clock domains.
They model delays involving only setup violations.

Configuring cdc_fx metastability windows is more complex than configuring cdc_mfx metastability
windows. This section describes them and how they are specified. See the details of the cdcfx mfx
window command for how cdc_mfx metastability windows are configured.

Setup and Hold Periods

Figure 114 shows setup and hold time periods around a register's clock edge along with sample
waveforms for an input to the registers. The input signal is stable if it is held at a constant 0 or 1 value
during the setup and hold periods. The signal is unstable if it changes during these periods. If the signal
input to a register is unstable, then the register can become metastable.

                                Figure 114. Setup and Hold Times for a Register Input

Metastability Windows

The setup and hold times determine receive clock cycles for which a register can become metastable--
based on the active edge of the receive clock and the value of the signal at the input port of the register.
In hardware, however, this input port switches value after the output port driving the signal (in the transmit
clock domain) switches and the new value propagates to the input port (in the receive clock domain). This
propagation delay (tprop) has the following physical bounds:

314                                        Questa® CDC User Guide
                        CDC-FX Metastability Injection

                        Specifying Metastability Windows

     min tprop  tprop  max tprop

Accounting for propagation delay identifies a metastability window relative to each active edge of the
receive clock, as shown in Figure 115. A metastability window defined this way assumes the worst case
events as follows:

       · CDC signal propagates as slowly as possible (max tprop) and violates the setup time (tsetup).

       · CDC signal propagates as quickly as possible (min tprop) and violates the hold time (thold).

                                                   Figure 115. Metastability Window

The start value is the number of time units before the active edge of the receive clock that the
metastability window "opens." The stop value is the number of time units after the active edge of the
receive clock that the metastability window "closes."

Note the following information about metastability windows:

       · Except for the default case, the metastability windows are not set automatically by software. The
          user sets up metastability windows based on the knowledge of the hardware technology and
          characteristics of the design by specifying their start and stop values. However, the user does not
          need to specify setup/hold times or propagation delay ranges.

       · Each pair of transmit/receive clocks has its own metastability window (either specified or default).
          In particular, a receive clock might have multiple windows.

       · If the duration of a metastability window is sufficiently large, then every active edge of the
          corresponding transmit clock falls inside the window. In this case, simulation with metastability
          injectors randomly inserts metastability effects every clock cycle the register changes value.

       · A common metastability verification methodology is to start with large metastability windows
          (for example, the default case). Then, successively narrow the windows and focus analysis on
          select CDC paths. This way the user can analyze the worst case scenario (so no bugs might be
          missed). Then, after eliminating "false" violations, the user can identify real problems caused by
          metastability intolerance.

       · Metastability windows are used for metastability injected simulation. They have no counterpart
          in hardware. In hardware, a changing CDC signal either does or does not result in the receive
          register going metastable, and the hardware value either does or does not agree with the value
          used in plain simulation.

clks_aligned[65:0]

Questa® CDC User Guide  315
CDC-FX Metastability Injection

Specifying Metastability Windows                                                                           

When the assertion compiler instantiates a cdc_fx checker, it also creates clock monitor logic that
determines when the transmit clock is within the metastability window of the receive clock (for that
transmit clock). Whenever this occurs, the receive register is prone to metastability if its input value also
changes in that receive clock cycle. The clks_aligned output from the clock monitor is used to pass this
information to the cdc_fx checker.

The clks_aligned output is a 66-bit value that is 0 throughout normal cycles. When the clock monitor
detects an active transmit clock edge in the corresponding metastability window of the receive clock edge,
one of the clks_aligned bits asserts a pulse that begins at the second active clock edge and stops at the
first subsequent inactive clock edge (see Figure 116).

Note the following:

     · clks_aligned[0] -- 1 if tx_clk is before rx_clk.

     · clks_aligned[1] -- 1 if tx_clk is after rx_clk.

     · clks_aligned[33:2] -- metastability window start time.

     · clks_aligned[65:34] -- metastability window stop time.
                                      Figure 116. clks_aligned Input to cdc_fx Checker

cdcfx fx window
The cdcfx fx window directive specifies metastability windows for specified receive register clocks. This
directive is used by the cdc generate fx command to configure the injection logic for single-Tx domain
crossings.

     cdcfx fx window
     {-start value -stop value [-percent] | -small | -medium | -large}
     [-tx_clock clock_group] [-rx_clock clock_group]
     Window size is specified two ways:

316                                                            Questa® CDC User Guide
                        CDC-FX Metastability Injection

                        Specifying Metastability Windows

       · Preset ranges corresponding to the following duty cycle percentages: -small is (start=25%,
          stop=10%); -medium is (start=35%, stop=30%); -large is (start=50%, stop=50%).

       · Custom ranges. Unless the directive includes the -percent option, the -start and -stop values
          specify metastability using directional time units as follows:

             The -start value is the number of time units before the active receive clock edge that the
                associated metastability window opens.

             The -stop value is the number of time units after the active receive clock edge that the
                associated metastability window closes.

          If -percent is specified, the -start and -stop values instead are percentages of the receive clock
          duty cycle.

The -tx_clock <clock_group> and -rx_clock <clock_group> options restrict the directive to cdc_fx
checkers on crossings from, and to, the specified clock groups (default: all clock groups). As the cdcfx
fx window directive obeys the last-one-wins rule, you should specify a global (default) cdcfx fx window
directive before other cdcfx fx window directives.

         Note:
         The -tx_clock and -rx_clock arguments do not allow wildcards. The cdcfx metastabilitywindow
         directive does not support bussed clocks.

If any cdcfx metastability window directive is specified, a cdc_fx checker with no applicable window
specification has the default window size of 0. It is instantiated, but never injects metastability and never
fires.
Special Default for Metastability Windows
If no cdcfx metastability window directives are specified, special default metastability windows for all
cdc_fx checkers are set as follows (see Figure 117):

       · Start time is 25% of the receive clock cycle before the receive clock edge.

       · Stop time is 10% of the receive clock cycle after the receive clock edge.

                                        Figure 117. Metastability Window Special Default

For example, if rx_clk has period 100 time units, then the default metastability window is the same as the
window set by the following:

Questa® CDC User Guide  317
CDC-FX Metastability Injection

Adjusting CDC-FX Checker Promotion                                                                          

   cdcfx metastability window
     -start 25 ­stop 10 -tx_clock tx_clk -rx_clock rx_clk

cdcfx mfx window

The cdcfx mfx window directive specifies metastability windows for receive register clocks. This directive
is used by the cdc generate fx command to configure the injection logic for multiple-Tx domain
crossings.

     cdcfx mfx window percent_value

Window opens at the specified percentage of the receive clock period, before the clock edge and closes
at the clock edge. Metastability injectors for multiple-Tx domain crossings are instances of cdc_mfx
checkers, which only detect setup violations.

Adjusting CDC-FX Checker Promotion

CDC-FX checkers are "promoted" for clock domain crossings. Promoted checkers are compiled by
vlog and then are activated during vsim simulation. When active, CDC-FX checkers inject random
metastability at the Rx registers of the crossings.

You can adjust the selection of crossings to promote CDC-FX checkers at the scheme level, and at the
crossing level, with two commands: cdc promote scheme and cdc promote crossing.

cdc promote scheme

The cdc promote scheme directive sets the promotion attribute for schemes.

     cdc promote scheme scheme -promotion {off | on | protocol | fx}

The -promotion attribute specifies what to promote for scheme: no checkers (off), both protocol and fx
checkers (on), only protocol checkers (protocol) or only fx checkers (fx).

By default, CDC-FX promotion for the following schemes are On: and_gate_dmux,
bus_dff_sync_combo_clk, bus_dff_sync_gated_clk, bus_dff_sync_with_enable, bus_sync_gray,
bus_two_dff, bus_two_dff_phase, combo_logic, dff_sync_combo_clk, dff_sync_gated_clk,
dff_sync_with_enable, dmux, dmux_no_hold, fanin_different_clks, forward_simple_dmux, handshake,
multi_bits, multi_sync_mux_select, mux_lock_dmux, no_sync, partial_dmux, pulse_single_edge,
pulse_sync, simple_dmux, two_dff, and two_dff_phase.

By default, CDC-FX promotion for the dmux_no_hold scheme is off.

Promotion of CDC-FX checkers for other schemes is not supported.

cdc promote crossing

The cdc promote crossing directive sets the promotion attribute for individual crossings. If a crossing has
no matching cdc promote crossing directive, the promotion attribute for the crossing is the promotion
attribute for the crossing's scheme, which is set by cdc promote scheme or is otherwise the default
promotion attribute for the scheme.

     cdc promote crossing [-scheme scheme] [-from var_pattern...] [-to var_pattern] [-through
     var_pattern...]... [-from_signals var_pattern... ] [-tx_clock clock_group] [-rx_clock clock_group]
     [-module module_pattern] [-promotion {off | on | fx | waived}] [-owner owner] [-reviewer reviewer]
     [-check check]

The -promotion attributes specify what to promote for matching crossings: no checkers (off), both protocol
and fx checkers (on), only protocol checkers (protocol) or only fx checkers (fx).

318                                 Questa® CDC User Guide
                        CDC-FX Metastability Injection

                        CDC-FX Cover Points

Limitations with CDC-FX Promotion

Following situations can cause a cdc_fx checker not to be promoted:
       · Individual signals from multibit registers.
       · Signals from registers with different transmit clocks fan into a receive register.
       · The tx_reg or rx_reg register is a latch.
       · The tx_reg or rx_reg register is not a real register and custom_fx is not on. For example, it is a
          memory or FIFO.
       · The tx_clk or rx_clk is missing. For example, the transmit register is an asynchronous input port.
       · There are latches between tx_reg and rx_reg.
       · Promotions are turned off.
       · Clock logic for one of the clocks has a UDP.
       · RX logic uses a custom synchronizer.

CDC-FX Cover Points

When a CDC-FX/MFX checker is instantiated for a clock domain crossing, the crossing signal bypasses
the Rx register and drives an input port of the checker. The checker's rx_q output replaces the output
of the Rx register. This instantiation allows the checker to control the Rx signal and model random
metastability injection by introducing delays and advances on the crossing data. Problems arising from
metastability intolerance might be detected by simulation end-to-end tests and by the design's assertions
during simulation.

In addition to the metastability injection logic, a CDC-FX/MFX checker has assertion specifications
and cover points. The cover points are the corner cases and statistics output from the checker. Corner
cases reflect functional coverage monitored by the checker. One goal of the CDC-FX method is to have
100% coverage of the corner cases. Statistics monitor special events during testing. But rather than
just detecting whether or not a particular event is covered, a particular statistic counts the number of
times that event occurred. For example, the simplest statistic is the evaluation statistic, which counts the
number of cycles the checker is active. Checking a CDC-FX checker statistic that is too low or zero might
indicate holes in simulation coverage that need to be exercised.

Controlling CDC-FX Checks

A CDC-FX/MFX checker has metastability-modeling injection logic and coverage point accounting logic.
It also has one or more assertions: the cdc_fx checker has cdc_fx, glitch_caught and glitch_swallowed
assertions; the cdc_mfx checker has just a cdc_mfx assertion.

The cdc_fx and cdc_mfx assertions fire (that is, fail) when the Tx signal changes in the metastability
window. At this point, the checker can inject metastability by randomly delaying or advancing bits in
the signal. For many schemes, you want to inject metastability. So by default, these checks are Off for
those schemes. However for the following schemes, the Tx signal typically is expected to be stable

Questa® CDC User Guide  319
CDC-FX Metastability Injection

Controlling CDC-FX Checks                                                                                    

through metastability windows, and these checks are On by default: multi_bits, dmux, simple_dmux,
multi_sync_mux_select, handshake, and no_sync.

The cdc_fx checker has two additional assertions (or checks) that are triggered by Tx signal glitches:

     · glitch_caught

        Ensures metastability injection does not cause a glitch at the rx_reg input to be reflected as a
        pulse at the rx_reg output, unless the glitch is also caught in simulation. The check reports a
        bitmap showing those rx_reg bits that had a glitch caught.

       · glitch_swallowed

          Ensures metastability injection does not cause a glitch at the rx_reg input to be swallowed (that
          is, missed) at the rx_reg output unless the glitch is also swallowed in simulation. The check
          reports a bitmap showing those rx_reg bits that had a glitch swallowed.

By default, the glitch_caught and glitch_swallowed checks are Off.

cdcfx check

The cdcfx check directive turns on specified cdc_fx/cdc_mfx checks.

     cdcfx check

     [-scheme scheme] [-tx_clock clock_signal] [-rx_clock clock_signal] [-fx] [-glitch_swallowed]
     [-glitch_caught]

Use the cdcfx check directive to turn On any of the -fx, -glitch_swallowed and -glitch_caught checks for
matching crossings.

Running Metastability-Injected Simulation

Metastability-injected simulation uses a similar flow as simulation with protocol checkers. The cdc
generate fx command compiles the metastability injection logic and sets up the arguments needed to run
metastability-injected simulation.

                                   Figure 118. Metastability-injected Simulation Flow

Results from metastability-injected simulation can be merged back into the CDC GUI for review and
debugging.

        Metastability-Injected Simulation
        Metastability Injection Control

Metastability-Injected Simulation

The following procedure uses the Questa vsim simulator.

Procedure

     1. Set up the design library and compile the design.
         For example:

            prompt> vlib work
            prompt> vmap work work
            prompt> vlog dut.vhdl

     2. Run CDC analysis.

            cdc run -d dut

     3. Generate the information to compile the metastability injection logic.

Questa® CDC User Guide                                                                             321
CDC-FX Metastability Injection

Metastability Injection Control                                                                      

           cdc generate fx

     4. Compile the CDC-FX metastability injection logic.
        Specify the vlog argument file. For example:
           prompt> vlog -f cdc_fx/simulation/cdc_fx_vlog.arg

     5. Compile the testbench.
           prompt> vlog tb.v

     6. Optimize the design.
           prompt> vopt tb -f cdc_fx/simulation/cdc_fx_vopt.arg -o tb_opt

     7. Run simulation.
        Specify the vsim argument file. For example:
           prompt> vsim -c tb_opt \
           -f cdc_fx/simulation/cdc_fx_vsim_3step.arg \
           -do "add log -r /*; run 1000; quit -f"

     8. Run the CDC GUI.
        Load the cdc_sim.db database generated by vsim. This database contains the merged data from
        static CDC analysis and simulation with protocol assertions and CDC_FX analysis.
           prompt> qverify cdc_sim.db

Metastability Injection Control

CDC-FX injects metastability randomly in designs to identify issues by replicating hardware behavior. To
dynamically control the operation of the metastability injectors, testbenches can include PLI function calls,
arguments, and control the glue logic.
The metastability injection is controlled in the following ways:

       · Control Random Injection

       · Control Specific-path Injection

       · Control Glue Logic

Control Random Injection

The random injection can be controlled using the following PLI calls in the testbench:

322                              Questa® CDC User Guide
                                                        CDC-FX Metastability Injection

                                                        Metastability Injection Control

       · $cdc_fx_always_invert_metastable_signals ();
          Inverts signals when they are metastable.

       · $cdc_fx_never_invert_metastable_signals ();
          Leaves the cdc_fx checkers active, but disables metastability injection.

       · $cdc_fx_randomly_invert_metastable_signals ();
          Randomly injects metastability into CDC signals when they are metastable. This is the default
          behavior.

The random injection can also be controlled using the following argument in simulation:

   vsim +args+CDC_FX_RANDOM+1

Control Specific-path Injection

CDC-FX injects metastability on all promoted paths, by default. Use the following PLI calls in the
testbench to enable or disable injection dynamically on specific paths.

  · $cdc_fx_on ();
     Inject metastability on the specified path.

       · $cdc_fx_off ();
          Do not inject metastability on the specified path.

The random injection can also be controlled using the following argument in simulation:

   vsim +cdc_fx_suppress_name+<path_name>

The path_name must be replaced with the cdcfx checker path. Section 3: CDC FX Details of the
cdc_fx.rpt report, which is generated by simulation with metastability injection, lists these cdc-fx checkers.
Following is a snippet of the section:

  =================================================================
  Section 3 : CDC FX Details
  =================================================================

  Type/Scheme : cdc_fx cdc_fx.two_dff_37036

  ----------------------------------------------------

  Check cdc_fx          : Off <Default Off>

  Check glitch_caught : On <Default Off>

  Check glitch_swallowed : Off <Default Off>

  TX REG                : r2

  TX CLOCK              : clk1

  RX REG                : meta2

  RX CLOCK              : clk2

  TX RESET              : 1'b0

  RX RESET              : 1'b0

  RX ARESET             : 1'b0

Questa® CDC User Guide                                                                                   323
CDC-FX Metastability Injection

Metastability Injection Control                                                                             

     RX LOAD ENABLE              : 1'b1

...
...

For example, to control the random injection on the cdc_fx.two_dff_37036 path, use the following:

vsim +cdc_fx_suppress_name+ cdc_fx.two_dff_37036

Control Glue Logic

Glue logic for Verilog and VHDL is added to the FX simulation setup. The glue logic has the following
structure:

   initial begin
     `ifdef CDC_FX_NO_FORCE
     `else
      if (!($test$plusargs("cdc_fx_disable_force"))) begin
        force top.U1.U12.dout = force_wire_0;
      end
     `endif

   end

Glue logic is controlled with:

       · CDC_FX_NO_FORCE
          This option can only be used during compiling the design. It permanently removes the force
          statement. For example,

            % vlog +define+CDC_FX_NO_FORCE cdc_fx_bind.sv

          or

            % vcs +define+CDC_FX_NO_FORCE cdc_fx_bind.sv

     · +cdc_fx_disable_force
        This option can only be used during simulation. It disables the force statements for that specific
        simulation run. For example,

          % vsim tb
          \ +cdc_fx_disable_force
          \ -f Output_directory/cdc_fx/simulation/cdc_fx_vsim_2step.arg

        or

          % ./simv +cdc_fx_disable_force

     · $cdc_fx_never_invert_metastable_signals

324                                               Questa® CDC User Guide
                        CDC-FX Metastability Injection

                        Metastability Injection Control

  This option does not impact the force statements. It only changes the random number generator
  during simulation to always produce 0. Hence, the forced values are supposed to be identical to
  the original values.

  The glue logic can produce data values different from the original RTL, especially for Xs. Hence,
  this option can result in change in simulation behavior.

  Sometimes a customer uses the $cdc_fx_never_invert_metastable_signals option while
  the chip is loading the configuration registers. During this phase, the users has external
  circuitry to ensure that the different clocks are in sync. Next, the user enables CDC-FX by
  calling the $cdc_fx_randomly_invert_metastable_signals option. Also, the user has the
  $cdc_fx_always_invert_metastable_signals option to get better coverage if the number of
  metastable cycles is limited in the testbench.

Questa® CDC User Guide  325
CDC-FX Metastability Injection

Metastability Injector Simulation Methodology                                                                  

Metastability Injector Simulation Methodology

Metastability injectors in simulation uncover problems that arise from CDC metastability effects. These
problems cannot be detected with basic simulation.

        Detecting Problems With Basic Simulation
        Assertion Violations

Detecting Problems With Basic Simulation

Use the following methodology to detect problems with basic simulation.

Procedure

     1. Start with a "clean" design.

         · End-to-end tests run completely, without errors.

         · If the design is instrumented with assertions, then plain simulation with assertions does not
             violate any assertions.

     2. Run metastability injected simulation.
     3. Use the qverify database viewer to analyze the results.

         · End-to-end test errors indicate receive logic is not tolerant of CDC metastability effects.

         · Assertion failures indicate receive logic is not tolerant of CDC metastability effects.

         · The cdc_fx checker coverage shows how completely each metastability injector covers the
             range of metastability effects during simulation.

     4. If needed, suppress some checkers and rerun metastability injected simulation.
     5. Debug any cdc_fx checker firings. The cdc_fx checker has three transfer protocol checks that by

         default are turned off.

         · The cdc_fx check ensures that the data input to the receive register does not change in a
             cycle for which the transmit/receive clock edges align (that is, metastability is not possible
             for the corresponding register). The generated cdc_fx directives for the CDC data buses are
             automatically included by the tool.

         · The glitch_caught check ensures that metastability injection does not catch a glitch if it is not
             detected by simulation.

         · The glitch_swallowed check ensures that metastability injection does not swallow a glitch if it is
             detected by simulation.

326                                            Questa® CDC User Guide
                        CDC-FX Metastability Injection

                        Assertion Violations

Assertion Violations

If metastability injected simulation produces assertion violations (that is, check firings), then you can
analyze them the same as you do firings from basic simulation with assertions.

Use the qverify viewer to examine details of the check firings and to display their waveforms (see Figure
119 on page 327). These violations are caused by design defects in the fan-outs of the receiving
registers that make the circuit intolerant of random delays in the transmission of their driving CDC signals.

                                  Figure 119. CDC GUI with Merged CDC_FX Results

The cdc_fx checker entries in the .db database provide a variety of information about the metastability
injectors during simulation.

Each cdc_fx checker maintains coverage information about its performance during simulation. The
checker entry in the simulation database (checksim.db) has this information.

The cdc_fx checker's cdc_fx check fires if the active edge of the transmit clock is in the metastability
window of the receive clock and the transmit data change in this window. These cycles are candidates
for metastability injection. The Metastable Cycles evaluation statistic increments each cycle this happens.
Normally, this is not problematic. The logic in the fan-out of the receive register is expected to tolerate this
situation.

By default, the cdc_fx assertions are enabled on unsynchronized paths. If a check is fired on any of those
unsynchronized paths, it implies that there is a probability of metastability and therefore, such firings are
marked in red. However, cdc_fx assertions can also be enabled on synchronized paths by specifying
them using the cdcfx check directive.

Some design styles have transmitting circuitry that presumes data is stable during cycles when both clock
edges occur in the metastability window. No metastability can occur and the receiving logic does not
need to account for CDC metastability effects. In such cases, you can use the cdc_fx check to verify the
transmit data remains stable when metastability can occur.

Notice in the Checker Report that the -rx_q field identifies the register output from the original circuit that
is replaced in the new circuit (remodeled with the metastability injection logic) with the rx_q output from
the checker. When cdc run compiles the design for simulation, each cdc_fx checker is connected so the
output from the transmit register is routed to the cdc_fx checker and the rx_q output from the checker
drives the load from the original receive register.

For most cycles, the transmit data is latched by the checker and passed through to the rx_q output when
the receive clock activates. This mimics the behavior of the original circuit under normal simulation. But,

Questa® CDC User Guide  327
CDC-FX Metastability Injection

Assertion Violations                                                                                         

when the checker determines it should inject metastability, randomly selected bits of the rx_q output are
inverted. The rx_q output reflects a corrupted value unrelated to the original transmission. This condition
emulates data transmission metastability from crossing clock domains. The circuit must be immune to
these effects.

Static CDC analysis identifies logic patterns relevant to clock tree topology and clock domain verification.
Groups of related patterns identify specific classes of logic subcircuits called CDC schemes. Each CDC
scheme represents a specific type of clock domain crossing (CDC) structure or a relevant clock tree
topology. Static CDC analysis reports two classes of schemes: clock domain crossings and clock tree
checks. Dynamic CDC analysis promotes two types of SVA checkers that are packages of assertions and
cover groups: CDC Protocol checkers and CDC-FX metastability injection checkers.

CDC Clock Checks                                                                                        

CDC Clock Checks

Clock tree detection during domain model compilation identifies certain kinds of clock logic patterns.
Groups of related patterns identify specific classes of clock tree architecture called CDC clock checks.
Each CDC clock check represents a specific type of clock tree architecture that could be a potential clock
function issue.

This section consists of the data sheets for the various CDC clock checks (see Table 30). Each data
sheet has the following information:

     · Short description.

     · Schematic representation.

     · Description.

       · Examples -- examples of directives that change the default behavior.
Clock checks are off by default. To turn each check on, use the cdc clockcheck on Tcl directive. Clock
checks are printed as messages and are summarized in the cdc_clock_checks.rpt file.
To change the status of a clock check message, use the msg report item directive.

                                                  Table 30. CDC Clock Checks

Check                             Description

clock_as_constant                 Clock signal to catch all sequential elements (flops/latches)
                                  receiving constant at their clock pin.
clock_as_data                     Clock signal connected to data.
clock_as_mux_select               Clock signal connected to MUX select.
clock_as_reset                    Clock signal used as reset.
clock_cascaded_dividers           Two or more clock dividers are connected in series.
clock_combo_loop                  Clock signal is a combinational feedback loop.
clock_combo_glitch                Clock enable signal is not driven by a latch-based clock gate.
clock_data_loop                   Clock signal is a feedback loop of a flop output through a
                                  combinational logic or a latch.
clock_dual_polarity               Signal used as both a posedge and negedge clock.
clock_enable_async                Asynchronous signal affecting clock path.
clock_mux                         Signal gated by a MUX clocks a storage element.
clock_path_convergence            Clock signal splits, converges at combinational logic and clocks a
                                  storage element.
clock_reset_race                  Clock and reset pins of a flop are driven by same signal.
clock_unexpected_gate             Signal gated by an XOR or XNOR gate clocks a storage element.

clock_as_constant

Clock signal to catch all sequential elements (flops/latches) receiving constant at their clock pin.

                                                Reference
Default: off; Warning: clockcheck-15  clock_as_constant

Problem

This check is to catch if a signal tied to constant or having netlist constant directive is blocking the clock
propagation to a sequential element.

By default, one warning is reported for each clock signal. To see the warning for each register, even if the
same clock signal reaches those registers, use the following command.

   cdc preference clockcheck report_all_const_sequential

The section 9 of cdc.rpt shows all the affected register instances for each corresponding constant signal
under the Unclocked Registers section.

Following is the sample snippet from Section 9 of cdc.rpt:

   Unclocked Registers:
   --------------------

      Clock pin driven by constant (4)
      -----------------------------

        Constant signal = sig (3)
      -----------------------------
      reg0 (1)
      reg1 (1)
      ff (1)

     Constant signal = w2 (1)
     ------------------------------

      reg2 (1)
      reg3 (1)

Solution

Review the flagged violation and fix the design or directive to ensure that the clock propagation is not
blocked. If this is intended, then ignore this warning.

Questa® CDC User Guide                339
Reference

clock_as_constant                                                                                         

Examples

     1. The following is the command to turn on detection of clock_as_constant checks.
            cdc clockcheck on clock_as_constant

     2. The following example shows that a signal is tied to a constant in design and blocking the clock
          propagation.

     1 module test (input in1, in2, clk, rst, output reg q);
     2 reg r1;
     3 always @ (posedge clk or negedge rst)
     4 if (!rst) r1 <= 1'b0;
     5 else r1 <= in1;
     6 assign clk1 = clk & in2;
     7 always @ (posedge clk1 or negedge rst)
     8 if (!rst) q <= 1'b0;
     9 else q <= r1;
     10 endmodule
     qverify -c -do " \

               netlist constant in2 0; \
               cdc clockcheck on clock_as_constant; \
               cdc run -d test"

                                      clock_as_data
clock_as_data

Clock signal connected to data.
Default: off; Warning: clockcheck-11

Problem

Clock signal is connected to data pin. The check does not flag violations for clock dividers and clock
passing through reset MUX before connecting to the data pin of a flop. By default, the check detects
clock signals connected to data pins between the clock paths of user-defined or primary clocks and the
register. To trace beyond the user defined clocks, use the detect_beyond_user_clock option with the cdc
preference clockcheck directive.

Solution

Review the flagged violation and ignore, if intended. Avoid the use of clock signal as data.

Examples

     1. The following is the command to turn on detection of clock_as_data checks.

            cdc clockcheck on clock_as_data

     2. Clock signal clk1 is connected to the data pin of registers q2 and q3.

Questa® CDC User Guide                341
Reference

clock_as_data                                                                 

     module dut(input clk1, clk2, data, output reg q1, q2, q3);
      always @ (posedge clk1) begin
          q1 <= data;
      end
      always @ (posedge clk2) begin
          q2 <= clk1;
          q3 <= clk1;
      end

     endmodule

     Warning (1)

        Clocked Register: q1

clock_as_mux_select

Clock signal connected to MUX select.
Default: off; Warning: clockcheck-12

Problem

Clock signal is connected to the MUX select pin. The check reports clock signals that drives both the
select signal of a MUX and the clock pin of a register. However, the clock check ignores the MUX that is
designed to be used as synchronous reset. By default, the check detects clock signals connected to MUX
select pins between the clock paths of user-defined or primary clocks and the register. To trace beyond
the user defined clocks, use the detect_beyond_user_clock option with the cdc preference clockcheck
directive.

Solution

Review the flagged violation and ignore, if intended. Avoid usage of clock signal as MUX select.

Examples

     1. The following is the command to turn on detection of clock_as_mux_select checks.

            cdc clockcheck on clock_as_mux_select

     2. The clock signal, clk, is driving the select signal of a MUX and the register.

     2. Signal clk1 drives the reset signals of registers r2 and r3:

Questa® CDC User Guide                345
Reference

clock_as_reset                                                                

     module dut(input data, clk1, clk2, output out);
      reg r1, r2, r3;
      wire rst;
      assign rst = clk1;

      always @ (posedge clk1) begin
        r1 <= data;

      end

      always @ (posedge clk2 or posedge rst) begin
        if(rst) begin
          r2 <= 0;
          r3 <= 0;
        end else begin
          r2 <= r1;
          r3 <= r2;
        end

      end
      assign out = r3;
     endmodule

                                                     clock_cascaded_dividers
clock_cascaded_dividers

Two or more clock dividers are connected in series.
Default: off; Warning: clockcheck-5

Problem

Cascaded clock dividers are ripple counters used to create clock signals of a lower frequency than a
master clock. They are used sometimes to reduce peak power consumption. However in many cases,
their implementation should be avoided. The further down the cascaded chain you go, the more flops are
involved in the clock tree. Data crossing from a faster clock domain to a lower frequency domain will have
increasing skew. So, timing adherence can be difficult.

CDC does not consider output ports during clock inference. Therefore, if the output of the last register
in a clock cascaded divider crossing is connected to an output port, the register will not be reported as
part of the clock check. By default, the check detects cascaded clock dividers between the clock paths
of user-defined or primary clocks and the register. To trace beyond the user defined clocks, use the
detect_beyond_user_clock option with the cdc preference clockcheck directive.
Solution

To handle timing analysis, SDC constraints must include clock definitions on each clock signal stage,
even when they are not being used.

Examples

     1. The following is an example to turn on detection of clock_cascaded_dividers checks.

            cdc clockcheck on clock_cascaded_dividers

     2. Two half-frequency clock dividers connected in series:

Questa® CDC User Guide                               347
Reference

clock_cascaded_dividers                                                                        

     module top (input mstrclk, rst, in, output reg out,
                            logic [1:0] clk);

        reg q, halfclk, quarterclk; assign clk = {quarterclk, halfclk};
        always @ (posedge mstrclk) q <= in;
        always @ (posedge quarterclk) out <= q;
        always @ (posedge mstrclk or posedge rst)

            if (rst) halfclk <= 1'b0;
            else halfclk <= ~halfclk;
        always @ (posedge halfclk or posedge rst)
            if (rst) quarterclk <= 1'b0;
            else quarterclk <= ~quarterclk;
     endmodule
     ==================================================================
     Warning (1)
     ==================================================================

     [clockcheck-5] Two or more clock dividers are connected in series.
     ------------------------------------------------------------------
     Warning : Two or more clock dividers are connected in series. Clock
     'mstrclk', File 'top.v', Line '1'. [clockcheck-5]
     (status:Uninspected)

                   Clocked Register : out
                   Clock Divider Chain [2] : halfclk, quarterclk

          Note:
          In the Clock Check Report, if a Clock Divider Chain exceeds a length of 10, it gets
          truncated to 10 automatically. The whole chain can be inspected in the GUI only.

     3. To waive the warning reported in the example:

           msg report item ­id clockcheck-5 ­arg clock=mstrclk ­arg file=top.v
           ­arg line=1 -status waived -owner jdoe
           ­comment "clock as cascaded divider approved for mstrclk" ­reviewer

             tsmith

clock_combo_loop

Clock signal is a combinational feedback loop.
Default: off; Warning: clockcheck-6

Problem

A clock combinational feedback loop can cause potential glitches in the design. By default, the check
detects a combinational loop between the clock paths of user-defined or primary clocks and the register.
To trace beyond the user defined clocks, use the detect_beyond_user_clock option with the cdc

Solution

Resolve the existing combo loop and avoid such constructs.

Examples

     1. The following is the command to turn on detection of clock_combo_loop checks.

            cdc clockcheck on clock_combo_loop

     2. A signal with a combinational loop clocks a register:

module top (input clk, in, en, output reg out);
     reg q;
     wire gclk;
     assign gclk = (gclk & en) | clk;
     always @ (posedge clk) q <= in;
     always @ (posedge gclk) out <= q;

endmodule

                                                                clock_combo_glitch
clock_combo_glitch

Clock enable signal is not driven by a latch-based clock gate.
Default: off; Warning: clockcheck-10

Problem

A clock enable signal when not driven by a latch-based clock gate can cause potential glitches in the
design. By default, the tool reports a violation if the design does not match the specified requirements and
the combining signals (enable signal and clock signal) are in different domains. To report violations when
the combining signals are in the same domain, use the clock_combo_glitch_for_same_domain option with
the cdc preference clockcheck directive.

Solution

The clock enable signal must always be latched. The tool recognizes a clock enable signal as latched
when one of the inputs of the clock gated by AND/OR/NAND/NOR output of the latch.

Examples

     1. The following is an example to turn on detection of clock_combo_glitch checks.

            netlist clock clk
            cdc clockcheck on clock_combo_glitch

          Specify the clock using the netlist clock directive.

     2. Signal driving the clock enable is not latched:

module dut(input en1, en2, in, clk, data, output reg out);
   wire w1, w2, w3;
   assign w1 = clk | en1;
   assign w2 = w1 & in;
   assign w3 = w2 & en2;
   assign clk1 = w3;
   always @(posedge clk1) out <= data;

Questa® CDC User Guide                                          351
Reference

     endmodule

     File 'top.v', Line '1'. [clockcheck-10](status:Uninspected)

        Combining signal(s) : en1;
        Clocked Register: out

Signal used as both a posedge and negedge clock.
Default: off; Warning: clockcheck-3

Problem

half to meet the timing during STA.

clock_enable_async                                                                                            

clock_enable_async

Asynchronous signal affecting clock path.
Default: off; Error: clockcheck-14

Problem

When an asynchronous enable signal merges with a clock signal before the clock signal reaches the
register, then the tool reports a clock_enable_async clock check error. Such design logic might be a
potential reason for a glitch in the clock path.

The tool reports asynchronous signal affecting the clock path driving the En pin of a latch as well.
By default, the check detects asynchronous signals affecting clock paths between the clock paths
of user-defined or primary clocks and the register. To trace beyond the user defined clocks, use the
detect_beyond_user_clock option with the cdc preference clockcheck directive.
You must specify the cdc preference clock directive with either -priority_direct_indirect or
priority_direct_indirect_combo to enable the clock check.

Solution

To fix, you should try one of the following:

       · Review the specified asynchronous enable signals and if required, fix the domain to make it
          synchronous with the clock.

       · If missed, specify a constant or a stable signal as asynchronous enable signal.

       · If the asynchronous enable signal is intended to be a clock signal, use netlist clock to define the
          signal as a clock.

360                                        Questa® CDC User Guide
                                                                                         Reference

                                             clock_enable_async

Examples

     1. The following is the commands to turn on detection of clock_enable_async check.

            cdc preference clock -priority_direct_indirect
            cdc clockcheck on clock_enable_async

  2. Clock clk1, before reaching to register q2, merges with clk2, temp1 register output, and temp2
       register output:

        Directive
        netlist clock clk1
        netlist clock clk2
        cdc clockcheck on clock_enable_async
        cdc preference clock -priority_direct_indirect

        Design
        module dut(input data, clk1, clk2, output reg q);
        wire gc1;
        reg temp1, temp2;

  always @(posedge clk1)
     temp1<= data;

  always @(posedge clk2)
     temp2 <= data;

  assign gc1 = clk1 & temp1 & temp2;

  always @(posedge gc1)
     q <= data;

  assign gc2 = clk1 & clk2 & temp1 & temp2;

  reg q2;
  always @(posedge gc2)

         q2 <= data;
  endmodule

clock_mux

Signal gated by a MUX clocks a storage element.
Default: off; Warning: clockcheck-1

Problem

This is a methodological check. Gated muxed clock is connected to a storage element. The check does
not flag the scenarios where the output of the MUX is constant.
Solution

waive the corresponding warning.

            cdc clockcheck on clock_mux

     assign gclka = sel ? clk[0] : clk[1];
     assign gclkb = sel ? clk[1] : clk[0];

     always @ (posedge gclkb) out <= q;

Clock and reset pins of a flop are driven by same signal.

                                                        Reset Checks

Reset Checks

A reset check item is a subcircuit that fits a specific type of reset logic pattern, called a reset check. A
reset check represents a class of netlist topologies and associated specifications that have similar issues
with functional properties, usage and reset behavior.

This section consists of the data sheets for the various CDC reset checks (see Table 31). Each data sheet
has the following information:

  · Short description

  · Schematic representation

  · Description

       · Examples -- examples of directives that change the default behavior.

Reset checks are off by default. To turn each check on, use the cdc resetcheck on Tcl directive. Reset
checks are printed as messages and are summarized in the cdc_clock_checks.rpt file.

Table 31 shows the reset checks detected by CDC analysis.

reset_convergence

Convergence in reset path: Reset signal splits into two paths that converge at a signal used as an
asynchronous reset. Defaults: Off; Warning.

Description

If a single source drives two combinational paths that converge to drive a signal used as an asynchronous
reset, then the converged reset has a potential for a glitch when it is asserted or released. The register
output is therefore prone to glitches. Signal can be used as a synchronous reset without issue.

         Restriction:
         Currently, reset convergence inside an expression or function might not be reported.

Examples

     1. The following is the command to turn on detection of reset_convergence checks.
            cdc resetcheck on reset_convergence

     2. Turn status to bug:
            msg report item -status bug -id resetcheck-8

     3. Asynchronous reset signal rst drives two gated resets rst0 and rst1. These signals converge at an
          AND gate to produce asynchronous reset conv_rst, which is used as async reset for register d.

Reference

             assign rst1 = rst & en1;

reset_data_loop

reset_pragma_mismatch

Reset usage different from pragma specification: Register's reset implementation mismatches its
set_reset synthesis specification. Defaults: Off; Error.

Description

To efficiently connect synthesized registers to their reset logic, HDL synthesis recognizes reset/set
signal pragma specifications for registers. The compiler can generate a sanity check report showing any
registers with mismatches between their implementation and specification.

Questa CDC reset tree analysis performs the same checks for the design's resettable registers
and reports reset_pragma_mismatch violations for registers with implementation/specification

Questa® CDC User Guide                                                                           391
Reference

reset_pragma_mismatch                                                                                

mismatches. The application recognizes all set_reset pragmas: sync_set_reset, sync_set_reset_local,
sync_set_reset_all, async_set_reset, async_set_reset_local and async_set_reset_all.

Examples

     1. The following is the command to turn on detection of reset_pragma_mismatch checks.
           cdc resetcheck on reset_pragma_mismatch

     2. Turn status to bug:
           msg report item -status bug -id resetcheck-10

     3. Following example shows two registers--one resets synchronously and the other resets
          asynchronously--that do not match their pragma specifications.

     module dut(dina, dinc, clk, rst0, rst1);
      input dina, dinc, clk, rst0, rst1;
      // synopsys async_set_reset rst0
      // synopsys sync_set_reset rst1
      reg a, c;
      always @(posedge clk)
        if (!rst0) a <= 1'b0;
        else a <= dina;
      always @(posedge clk or negedge rst1)
        if (!rst1) c <= 1'b0;
        else c <= dinc;endmodule

reset_unexpected_gate

Unexpected gate in reset tree: Signal gated by XOR, XNOR, NAND or NOR is used as a reset.
Defaults: Off; Warning.

Description

Combinational reset logic gates typically are restricted to AND and OR gates. Other gate types, such as
XOR, XNOR, reduced XOR/XNOR/NAND/NOR, and arithmetic operators, are not used in many reset
logic design architectures. The reset_unexpected_gate check detects these instances of reset logic and
reports the unexpected gate type and the top-level reset signal. In addition, the check reports the gate's
fanout signal and one of the gate's inputs.

         Note:
         The reset_unexpected_gate check currently works for asynchronous resets only.

Questa® CDC User Guide                                                                     393
Reference

reset_unexpected_gate

            cdc resetcheck on reset_unexpected_gate

     2. Turn the status to bug.
           msg report item -status bug -id resetcheck-14

     3. The following example demonstrates two asynchronous reset trees originating from the set port
          and the gated signal t_rst. The set tree has an XOR gate driving rst_xor_set, while the t_rst tree
          originates from the XOR gate with inputs rst and set.

     Directive

      cdc resetcheck on reset_unexpected_gate;

     Sample Design:

      module top (q, d, clk, rst, set, flag);
        input d, clk, rst, set, flag;
        output reg q;
        reg la;
        wire t_rst = rst ^ set;
        wire rst_xor_set = la ^ flag;
        always @(posedge clk or negedge t_rst)
         if (!t_rst) la <= 1'b0;
         else la <= set;
        always @(posedge clk or negedge rst_xor_set)
         if (!rst_xor_set) q <= 1'b0;
         else q <= d;

reset_unexpected_latch

Unexpected latch in reset tree: Reset tree has a latch. Defaults: Off; Warning.

Description

architectures assume no reset signals go through latches or use latches in a restricted way. The
reset_unexpected_latch check detects latches in reset trees and reports the first 10 latches in each such

reset_unexpected_tri

Unexpected tristate logic in reset tree: Signal driven by a tristate logic component is used as a reset.
Defaults: Off; Warning.

Decription

Tristate logic elements (bufif0, bufif1, notif0, notif1 and tristate registers/latches) in reset trees might
produce high impedance signals (Z), which can introduce unexpected or undesired reset behavior. The
reset_unexpected_tri check detects tristate elements in reset trees and reports them for all reset domains.

         Note:
         The reset_unexpected_tri check currently works for asynchronous resets only.

reset_unused

Reset tree not used: Signal is not used as a reset but has a netlist reset specification. Defaults: Off;
Warning.

Description

The netlist reset directive adds reset trees to a reset domain and specifies reset domain attributes. Each
matching signal or port in a given netlist reset directive is assumed to be the originator signal of a reset
tree in the designated reset domain. If reset tree detection finds that a domain's user-specified reset tree
(identified by a netlist reset directive) does not actually reset any logic, it reports the reset tree as an
instance of a reset_unused scheme.

         Tip
         In addition to adding reset trees to reset domains, the netlist reset directive also can be used to
         remove trees from reset domains (with -remove) and to direct reset analysis to ignore the trees
         (with -ignore).

                                                                                       Reference

                                CDC Schemes

CDC Schemes

CDC analysis identifies logic patterns relevant to CDC verification. Groups of related patterns identify
specific classes of situations called CDC schemes. Each CDC scheme represents a specific type of CDC
synchronizer architecture or a potential CDC issue.

         Note:
         Line number reporting displays the line where the register is initialized.

Table 32 lists various CDC schemes. The data sheet for each scheme has the following information:
       · General Information -- qverify message, schematic representation, description, and the following
          information:
             Crossing Type -- signal, data bus, both, or reset applicable.
             Default Severity -- evaluation, caution, or violation.
             Promoted Checkers -- CDC checkers promoted to check the associated transfer protocol.
             FX Support -- Whether or not FX/MFX checkers can be promoted.
             Examples -- examples of directives that change the default behavior.

In addition, some data sheets show the following:
       · Potential Problems -- information about consequences you should consider.
       · Notes -- additional information relevant to the scheme.

Scheme                          Table 32. CDC Schemes
and_gate_dmux
async_reset                         Description

and_gate_dmux                                                                                               

and_gate_dmux

AND-gate DMUX synchronization. Default Severity: caution.
Crossing: synchronized control signal and muxed data bus; Promotion: cdc_dsel (default on); FX: yes
(default on).

The AND-gate DMUX scheme is a restricted version of the general DMUX scheme. For the general
scheme, the fanin logic of the Rx signal can contain any logic and the synchronized control signal can
use any logic to turn off the Tx signal (not just a MUX). The control signal can be synchronized by any of
the following signal synchronizers: two_dff_phase, dff_sync_gated_clk, four_latch, two_dff, pulse_sync,
dff_sync_with_enable, and custom.
The AND-gate DMUX scheme has the following restrictions:

       · Logic between the Tx and Rx signals has an AND gate.

       · Tx signal drives one input of the AND gate.

       · Tx and Rx drivers are registers.

       · Except for the AND gate, no combo logic is between the Tx register and the Rx register.

       · No combo logic is between select output from the synchronizer and the AND gate.

         Note:
         The physical design of the select logic (that controls the path from the Tx register to the Rx
         registers) must not allow glitches at the input to an Rx register when the Tx register changes
         value.

Use the cdc preference dmux directive to recognize CDC crossings as DMUX schemes where Tx or Rx
signals are memories (but not black box memories).

408            Questa® CDC User Guide
                                                                            Reference
                                                                     and_gate_dmux

     cdc_protocol.rpt):

async_reset                                                                                             

async_reset

Asynchronous resets in the Rx clock domain are driven by a synchronizer. Default Severity: evaluation.
Crossing: 1-bit signal; Promotion: cdc_sync (default off); FX: yes (default off).

Reset trees that span clock domains must be synchronized to the Rx clock domain if they are used as
asynchronous resets. A crossing where the reset signal used as an asynchronous reset in the Rx domain
is reported as async_reset when the crossing has a recognized synchronizer (two_dff, four_latch, and
custom_sync) and the signal that deasserts the Rx register is either a constant value or a non-constant
signal.
By default, internal asynchronous reset signals are considered as resets for CDC analysis. To turn off the
detection of such signals as resets, use the -internal_async_resets_off option with the cdc preference
directive.

         Note:
         Consider the following:
          · Instances of redundant synchronizers can be identified by the cdc-101 warning. For further

            details, refer to the cdc section in the Messages Reference document.
          · To enable promotion for this scheme, use cdc preference protocol -promote_async_reset.

Examples

     1. Turn severity to violation.

            cdc report scheme async_reset -severity violation

     2. An async_reset crossing that uses an asynchronous reset input to drive the reset pins of the
          synchronizer. Synchronizer input is tied high.

async_reset_clockoff

A particular clock can be specified as off when specific reset(s) deasserts. Default Severity: evaluation.

Promotion: cdc_clockoff (default off); FX: yes (default off).

To avoid reset deassertion synchronization issue, the clock and reset architecture is designed such that
the clock is guaranteed off while the async reset is active. This avoids any chance of metastability while
the reset is deasserted.

Directives

Turn on the clock off specification:

   cdc specification on ­clockoff
   cdc specification clockoff -reset <reset-list> ­rx_clock <clock-list>

     [-module <module-list>]
