                        async_reset_no_sync

async_reset_no_sync

Signal that drives the asynchronous reset of the receiving register has no synchronizer. Default Severity:
violation.
Crossing: 1-bit signal; Promotion: cdc_sample (defaul off); FX: yes (default off).

Synchronization using an asynchronous reset is a standard method of synchronizing a 1-bit signal, but
the Tx register output must drive a control signal synchronizer before driving receive domain logic. A
crossing is reported as async_reset_no_sync when the signal driving the asynchronous reset of the Rx
register is:

       · not driven by a control synchronizer

       · driven by a synchronizer, but, the input value to the synchronizer does not deassert the Rx
          register

By default, an async_reset_no_sync scheme is reported for each crossing, individually. However, you
can use the -single_async_reset_no_sync option with the cdc preference directive if you want the tool to
report one asyn_reset_no_sync scheme for all the crossings in which multiple registers are driven by the
same clock and reset signals.

         Note:
         To enable promotion for this scheme, use cdc preference protocol -promote_async_reset and cdc
         protocol on -type cdc_sample.

Examples

     1. The following example changes the default severity for the async_reset_no_sync scheme to
          evaluation:

            cdc report scheme async_reset_no_sync ­severity evaluation

async_reset_combo_logic                                                                               

async_reset_combo_logic

Combinational logic before a recognized reset synchronizer that drives asynchronous resets in the Rx
clock domain. Default: On; Violation.

Crossing: reset synchronizer; Promotion: cdc_glitch (default off); FX: yes (default on).

Reset tree crosses a clock domain boundary to a recognized reset synchronizer through combinational
logic and is used as an asynchronous reset in the Rx clock domain.

Reset trees that span clock domains must be synchronized to the Rx clock domain if they are used as
asynchronous resets. A reset CDC used as an asynchronous reset in the Rx domain is reported as a
async_reset_combo_logic crossing if it has a recognized reset CDC synchronizer (two_dff, four_latch,
shift_reg, and custom_sync), but the reset driving the synchronizer comes from combinational logic.
Such a subcircuit can have reset glitches, which might prevent reset activation from propagating to the
resettable Rx clock domain registers.

If you cannot remove the combinational logic, try one of the following:

       · Add a Tx register just after the combo logic.

       · If the contributing signals are stable, identify them with cdc signal -stable directives.

       · If the combinational logic output is constant during normal operation, glitches cannot be
          generated. Specify the signal that feeds the combinational logic as a constant value using the
          netlist constant directive.

       · If the violation is not an issue--a transfer protocol might ensure only one contributing signal
          changes value at a time--waive the violation.

       · To enable combo logic for reconvergence, use the cdc preference reconvergence
          combo_as_recon_start Tcl directive.

In case of custom synchronizers, if the no_combo assumption specified on reset port fails, the crossing is
reported as a combinational logic before reset synchronizer with base type CUSTOM.

         Note:
         To enable promotion for this scheme, use cdc preference protocol -promote_async_reset.

418                      Questa® CDC User Guide
                                                                         Reference

                        async_reset_combo_logic

                        async_reset_incorrect_polarity

async_reset_incorrect_polarity

A reset synchronizer drives asynchronous resets in the Rx clock domain with incorrect polarity. Defaults:
On; Caution.
Crossing: reset synchronizer; Promotion: cdc_sync (default off); FX: yes (default off).

Description

A reset synchronizer drives reset signals in Rx clock domain with incorrect polarity. Whenever an
asynchronous reset is asserted, the register driven by the output of the reset synchronizer gets
deasserted asynchronously and can lead to metastability.
If the reset signal is used as reset in the synchronizer, then output of synchronizer must be used
as active-low and if reset signal is used as set in the synchronizer, then output of synchronizer
must be used as active-high. If the specified conditions are not met, the crossing is reported as an
async_reset_incorrect_polarity crossing.

         Note:
         Consider the following:
          · To enable promotion for this scheme, use cdc preference protocol -promote_async_reset.
          · The 'cdc specification clockoff' will not be applied on async_reset_sync_incorrect_polarity

            cases. For these cases, you need to fix the usage of the synchronizer rather than implementing
            clock-off mechanisms.

Examples

     1. Turn severity to evaluation:

            cdc report scheme async_reset_incorrect_polarity ­severity evaluation

     2. Assertion of asynchronous reset results in asynchronous deassertion of register d1.

Questa® CDC User Guide  421
Reference

async_reset_inferred_stable                                                                                

            module test (input in1, in2, clk1, clk2, output reg q);
            reg r1, r2, rst1;
            always @ (posedge clk1)

              rst1 <= in1;
            always @ (posedge clk2 or negedge rst1)

              if (!rst1) begin
               r1 <= 1'b0;
               r2 <=1'b0;

              end else begin
               r1 <= in1;
               r2 <=r1;

              end
            always @ (posedge clk2 or posedge r2)

              if (r2) begin
               q <=1'b0;

              end else begin
               q <=in2;

              end
            endmodule

          The async_reset_incorrect_polarity scheme reports the following caution in this case:

            Cautions
            =================================================================
            Asynchronous reset synchronizer has incorrect polarity
            (async_reset_incorrect_polarity)
            -----------------------------------------------------------------
            clk1 : start : rst1 (test.v : 4)

              clk2 : end : r1 (test.v : 10)
                 (ID:async_reset_incorrect_polarity_89011)
                 (Status : uninspected)

              Synchronizer output used as incorrect polarity : q

async_reset_inferred_stable

Reports clock domain crossings on reset paths where either transmitter (Tx) or receiver (Rx) register has
an inferred stable enable pin tied to constant logic 0. Defaults: Off; Evaluation.

422                          Questa® CDC User Guide
                                                        Reference

                        async_reset_inferred_stable

Description

A signal crosses a clock domain boundary on reset paths between registers. A register is marked inferred
stable when:

       · En pin is tied to constant 0.
Key characteristics:

       · Specifically analyzes reset path crossings

       · Reports both Tx and Rx inferred stable cases.

       · Only considers enable pin tied to 1'b0

       · Explicit stability directives (cdc signal -stable/tx_stable/rx_stable) always take precedence over
          automatically inferred stability.

Examples

     1. To turn on the scheme:

            cdc scheme on async_reset_inferred_stable

          Turning on the scheme reports reset path crossings where either Tx or Rx has inferred stable
          status. If a signal is explicitly marked as stable using cdc signal -stable/tx_stable/rx_stable, that
          specification takes precedence over inferred stable detection.

     2. Example of reset path crossing with inferred stability:
          In this example, the reset synchronization in the RX module ensures stable crossings on the reset
          path. The design uses a reset signal (rst) to control the state of the transmitter (tx) and receiver
          (rx) registers, and ensures that the reset path remains stable across different clock domains.

  Sample DUT

   module top(input d, rst, clk1, clk2, en, output q);
      reg tx, rx;
      always@(posedge clk1 or posedge rst)
          if(rst)
              tx<=0;

async_reset_series_redundant

Detects redundant reset synchronizers that are connected in series to another reset synchronizer. Default
Severity: Caution.

Crossing: synchronized 1-bit signal; Promotion: none; FX: no.

Identifies reset synchronizers that are connected in series to another reset synchronizer, both
synchronizing the same reset deassertion in the same clock domain. These series-connected reset
synchronizers are considered redundant. This scheme helps detect and eliminate unnecessary reset
synchronizers in your design.

The scheme is reported when the base synchronizer follows one of the following schemes:

424                                          Questa® CDC User Guide
                                                                                          Reference

                        async_reset_series_redundant

       · async_reset

       · async_reset_incorrect_polarity

       · async_reset_sync_module

       · async_reset_combo_logic
If the directive cdc synchronizer reset -strict_constant_check is used, then only a constant d input is
supported.
Directive
Use the directive to enable the detection of redundant reset synchronizers connected in series.

   cdc scheme on async_reset_series_redundant

            cdc report scheme async_reset_series_redundant -severity violation

  2. The following is an example of asynchronous reset series redundant synchronization.

async_reset_sync_incorrect_domain

Differentiates between scenarios with potential reset synchronizer and no synchronizer at all. Default
Severity: On; Violation.

Promotion: cdc_sample (default off); FX: yes (default off).

In a potential reset synchronizer, the output is not used as reset in its own domain. For example, in the
figure below, flops r3 and q1 make a potential reset synchronizer as their output is not used in the green
domain. Output of reset synchronizer (green domain) is going to reset of flop in other domain (violet
domain). So here async_reset_sync_incorrect_domain is reported.

426                                          Questa® CDC User Guide
                        Reference

                        async_reset_sync_incorrect_domain

The async_reset_sync_incorrect_domain scenarios are supported by the HDM. This support extends to
all async_reset supported situations that already exists within the HDM framework, ensuring accurate
design handling. However, this scheme is not supported for user specified HDM.

         Note:
         Consider the following:
          · The 'cdc specification clockoff' will not be applied on async_reset_sync_incorrect_domain

            cases. For these cases, you need to fix the usage of the synchronizer rather than implementing
            clock-off mechanisms.
          · To enable promotion for this scheme, use cdc preference protocol -promote_async_reset and
            cdc protocol on -type cdc_sample.

blackbox

Crossing to an instance of an inferred black box. Default Severity: caution.
Crossing: control signal or data bus; Promotion: none; FX: no.

A black box is a module/entity that:
       · is explicitly declared as a black box (with the netlist blackbox directive) ,
       · contains unsupported constructs,
       · is an unresolved module and the -auto_blackbox option is specified to cdc run, or
       · is an empty module and cdc preference-black_box_empty_module is specified.

Table 33 shows how CDC analysis handles black boxes.
                                                Table 33. Handling Black Boxes

User-Specified Black Box  Port Domain Specified              Port Domain Not Specified
Inferred Black Box                                           no crossing
                          no_sync (port domain not async)
                          blackbox_sync (port domain async)  blackbox warning
                          blackbox warning

User Specified Black Box  Port Domain Specified              Port Domain Not Specified
                          sync check (e.g., no_sync)         no crossing

436                                                                 Questa® CDC User Guide
                                                                    Reference
 Inferred Black Box                                                   blackbox

                        Table 33. Handling Black Boxes (continued)

                        sync check (e.g., no_sync)                  sync check (e.g., no_sync)

Examples

     1. The following is an example to turn severity to violation:
            cdc report scheme blackbox ­severity violation

     By default, the datain inputs are assumed to be in different clock domains. Similarly, dout and

      #Input port domains
      netlist port domain datain0 -async -module black_box

blackbox_sync

Crossing to an async port of an instance of a user-specified black box. Default Severity: evaluation.
Crossing: control signal or data bus; Promotion: none; FX: no.

A black box might contain synchronization logic for an input port. In this case, a crossing to the port is
properly synchronized. To specify this case:

       · Declare the module as a black box with a netlist blackbox directive.
       · Declare the port as asynchronous with a netlist port domain -async directive.
See "blackbox" on page 436 for details of how CDC analysis handles black boxes in general.

Examples

     1. The following is an example to turn severity to caution:
            cdc report scheme blackbox_sync ­severity caution

     2. The following example shows an instance (BB) of a module (black_box) declared as a black box.

  The following directives set up this implementation for CDC analysis:

   netlist clock tx_clk
   netlist clock rx_clk
   netlist port domain dout -clock tx_clk
   netlist blackbox black_box
   netlist port domain datain0 -async -module black_box
   netlist port domain datain1 -async

Questa® CDC User Guide                                                                                 439
Reference

blackbox_sync                                                                                              

     -clock clock -module black_box
     netlist port domain dataout -clock clock -module black_box
     netlist port domain status -clock clock -module black_box
     netlist reset reset -module black_box

     Without the netlist port domain directive for datain0, the crossing from din0 to datain0 is reported
     as a no_sync or multi_bits violation. The same is true for datain1. But, because the port domains
     are marked -async, the black box is assumed to synchronize the crossings. Therefore, the
     crossings are reported as blackbox_sync evaluations:

     Evaluations
     =================================================================
     Black box synchronization. (blackbox_sync)
     -----------------------------------------------------------------
     tx_clk : start : tx_sig0 (/cdc/blackbox_sync.v : 24)

                   Unspecified : end : BB.datain0 (/cdc/blackbox_sync.v : 40)
                                     (ID:blackbox_sync_96097)

     tx_clk : start : tx_sig1 (/cdc/blackbox_sync.v : 25)
                       rx_clk : end : BB.datain1 (/cdc/blackbox_sync.v : 40)
                                     (ID:blackbox_sync_97105)

     Specifying just -async or specifying both -async and -clock <clock> makes no difference to
     CDC analysis. However, specifying the port domain clock changes the reporting of the crossing
     paths. Without -clock <clock>, the clock for the end point on the black box is Unspecified (clock
     information not available). With the -async -clock <clock> specification, the clock for the end point
     is identified (in this example: rx_clk).

                                           bus_custom_sync

bus_custom_sync

Multiple-bit signal synchronized by custom CDC synchronizer that satisfies its connection assumptions.
Default Severity: evaluation.

Crossing: data bus; Promotion: none; FX: no.

Custom synchronizers are instances of modules declared as custom synchronizers using the cdc custom
sync and cdc custom sync data directives (see "Custom Synchronizers" on page 67). A cdc custom sync
data directive identifies the two end ports of each synchronization path through the synchronizer.

By default, the clock domain crossing for a data synchronization path is assumed to be external:
the crossing is just before the data synchronization path. However, if the crossing is internal to the
synchronizer (that is, the synchronizer has both Tx clock and Rx clock ports), the cdc custom sync
directive for the module (containing the crossing) must specify the -internal_crossing argument. The
internal_* schemes are reported for custom synchronizers with internal crossings.

The hier assume directive specifies hierarchical CDC port connection assumptions. When the two end
ports of an external crossing custom synchronizer's data path are connected to signals in different
clock domains, the custom synchronizer is identified as either a (single-bit) custom_sync crossing or
a (multiple-bit) bus_custom_sync crossing--but only if the custom synchronizer instance satisfies the
custom synchronizer's port connection assumptions. If any connection assumption is unsatisfied, the
crossing is reported as a custom_sync_mismatch or bus_custom_sync_mismatch violation.

Hierarchical information about the logic inside a custom synchronizer is specified with hier port domain,
hier clock, hier reset, hier stable, and hier constant directives. This information is used to detect crossings
and violations external to the custom synchronizer and to detect unsatisfied port connection assumptions.

Examples

     1. Define the custom synchronizer module dff_sync as the type dff custom synchronizer. The
          synchronization path is from the din input port to the dout output port. The two hier port domain
          directives guarantee the din and dout ports are connected internally to signals in the same clock
          domain as the signal driving the clk port. The first hier port domain directive also guarantees the
          din input internally drives only a synchronizer to the clk domain. The second hier port domain
          directive guarantees the dout output is driven by a synchronizer to the clk domain.

  cdc custom sync dff_sync -type dff
  cdc custom sync data -module dff_sync \

     -from din -to dout
  hier clock clk -module dff_sync

Questa® CDC User Guide                     441
Reference

bus_custom_sync                                                                                            

     hier port domain din -module dff_sync \
        -clock clk

     hier port domain dout -module dff_sync \
        -clock clk

     hier assume port din -no_combo
        -module dff_sync

     Evaluations
     =============================================================
     Multiple-bit signal synchronized by Custom CDC Scheme:

          dff(dff_sync)(bus_custom_sync)

     tx_clk : start : tx_data (bus_custom_sync.v : 21)

        rx_clk : end : S.din (bus_custom_sync.v : 29)
          (ID:bus_custom_sync_5359)

     2. Define the custom synchronizer module dmux_sync as the type dmux1 custom synchronizer.
          The synchronization path is from the TXDATA input port to the RXDATA output port. The three
          hier port domain directives guarantee the TXSEL, TXDATA and RXDATA ports are connected
          internally to signals in the same clock domain as the signal driving RXCLK. The first hier port
          domain directive also guarantees the TXSEL input internally drives only a synchronizer to the
          RXCLK domain. The second hier port domain directive guarantees the TXDATA input drives
          combinational logic internally.

            cdc custom sync dmux1_sync -type dmux1
            cdc custom sync data -module dmux1_sync -from TXDATA -to RXDATA
            hier port domain TXSEL -module dmux1_sync -clock RXCLK -sync
            hier port domain TXDATA -module dmux1_sync -clock RXCLK -combo_logic
            hier port domain RXDATA -module dmux1_sync -clock RXCLK

Potential Problems

     1. CDC analysis does not promote a checker for this scheme. You should implement a transfer
          protocol checking scheme using one or more checkers.

442              Questa® CDC User Guide
                        Reference

                        bus_custom_sync_mismatch

bus_custom_sync_mismatch

Multiple-bit signal synchronized by custom CDC synchronizer that does not satisfy all of its connection
assumptions. Default Severity: violation.

Crossing: data bus; Promotion: cdc_hamming_one (default off); FX: no.

Custom synchronizers are instances of modules declared as custom synchronizers using the cdc custom
sync and cdc custom sync data directives (see "Custom Synchronizers" on page 67). A cdc custom
sync data directive identifies the two end ports of each synchronization path through the synchronizer.
Typically, hierport domain directives (and other hier directives) indicate logic connectivity properties
guaranteed to be satisfied by the custom synchronizer internal logic.

The hier assume port directives specify external port connection properties that must be satisfied by
the synchronizer placement. If a custom synchronizer instance for a bus is connected so that all of its
connection assumptions are satisfied, the clock domain crossing is reported as a bus_custom_sync
crossing. But, if any connection assumption for the synchronizer is not satisfied, the crossing is reported
as a bus_custom_sync_mismatch violation.

For example, if a custom synchronizer has a hier assume port -no_combo directive for a port driven by
combinational logic, then CDC analysis reports a bus_custom_sync_mismatch violation instead of a
combo_logic violation.

Examples

     1. Defines the custom synchronizer module dff_sync as the type dff custom synchronizer and
          specifies that input din must be driven by a register (-no_combo). Since din is actually connected
          to combinational logic, the connection assumption is not satisfied. The tx_clk/rx_clock crossing is
          reported as a bus_custom_sync_mismatch violation.

Questa® CDC User Guide                                                                                   443
Reference

bus_custom_sync_mismatch                                                                      

     cdc custom sync dff_sync -type dff
     cdc custom sync data -module dff_sync \

        -from din -to dout
     hier assume port din -module dff_sync \

        -no_combo
     Violations

     Multiple-bit signal synchronized by Custom CDC Scheme does

                        bus_custom_sync_with_crossing

bus_custom_sync_with_crossing

Multiple-bit signal synchronized by an internal crossing custom CDC synchronizer that satisfies its
connection assumptions. Default Severity: evaluation.

Crossing: control signal or data bus; Promotion: none; FX: no.

Custom synchronizers are instances of modules declared as custom synchronizers using the cdc custom
sync and cdc custom sync data directives (see "Custom Synchronizers" on page 67). A cdc custom sync
data directive identifies the two end ports of each synchronization path through the synchronizer. If the
crossing is internal to the synchronizer (that is, the synchronizer has both Tx clock and Rx clock ports),
the cdc custom sync directive for the module (containing the crossing) must specify the -internal_crossing
argument.

When the two end ports of an internal crossing custom synchronizer's data path are connected
to signals in different clock domains, the custom synchronizer is identified as either a (single-bit)
custom_sync_with_crossing crossing or a (multiple-bit) bus_custom_sync_with_crossing crossing
--but only if the instantiation of the custom synchronizer satisfies the custom synchronizer's port
connection assumptions. If any connection assumption is unsatisfied, the crossing is reported as a
custom_sync_with_crossing_mismatch or bus_custom_sync_with_crossing_mismatch violation.

Examples

     1. Defines the custom synchronizer module idff_sync as the type idff custom synchronizer with
          an internal crossing. The synchronization path is from the din input port to the dout output port.
          The two hier port domain directives guarantee the din and dout ports are connected internally to
          signals in the same clock domain as the signal driving their respective clock ports. The second
          hier port domain directive guarantees the dout output is driven by a synchronizer to the rclk
          domain.

  cdc custom sync idff_sync -type idff
  cdc custom sync data -module idff_sync -from din -to dout

                -internal_crossing
  hier clock tclk rclk -module idff_sync
  hier port domain din -module idff_sync -clock tclk
  hier port domain dout -module idff_sync -clock rclk
  Evaluations

     Custom synchronization with internal multiple-bit crossing:

               rx_clk : end : S.din (int_bus_custom_sync.v : 29)
                                         (ID:bus_custom_sync_with_crossing_5359)

     2. Defines the custom synchronizer module dmux_sync as the type dmux2 custom synchronizer
          with an internal crossing. The synchronization path is from the TXDATA input port to the RXDATA
          output port. The first hier port domain directive guarantees the TXSEL and TXDATA ports are
          connected internally to signals in the same clock domain as the signal driving TXCLK. The
          second hier port domain directive guarantees the RXDATA output is driven internally only by a

bus_data_latch

bus_dff_sync_combo_clk

Multiple-bit signal synchronized by DFF synchronizer clocked by signal with a combinational loop. Default
Severity: caution.
Crossing: multiple-bit data bus; Promotion: cdc_hamming_one (default on) and data_stability (default
off); FX: yes (default on).

Synchronization using two flip-flops is a standard method of synchronizing a gray-coded data bus. If the
synchronizer is clocked by a regular clock signal, the crossing is reported as a bus_two_dff style crossing.
However, if the synchronizer is clocked by a signal with a combinational feedback loop, an asynchronous
condition might be possible. Multiple-bit DFF synchronization clocked by signals with combinational loops
are reported as bus_dff_sync_combo_clk crossings.

Examples

     module dut (input clk1, clk2, rst, logic [3:0] data, output reg q);
        reg [3:0] r, s1;
            wire gclk2;
            assign gclk2 = !gclk2 ^ clk2;
            always @(posedge clk1) r <= data;
            always @(posedge gclk2 or posedge rst)
               if (rst) begin
                   q <= 0;
                   s1 <= 0;
               end

                s1 <= r;

bus_dff_sync_with_enable                                                                               

bus_dff_sync_with_enable

Multiple-bit signal synchronized by DFF synchronizer with enable port or ports.
Default Severity: evaluation; Crossing: Multiple-bit data signal; Promotion: cdc_hamming_one (default
on); FX: yes (default on).

Multiple bit data bus is synchronized by two cascaded flop-flops that have enable port. The data bus must
be gray encoded to ensure that only one bit changes its value in any cycle. The data bus is assumed to
be gray encoded. It assures that only one bit of data changes in any cycle. Specifying cdc scheme on
dff_sync_with_enable enables the bus_dff_sync_with_enable scheme. If the preference is not specified,
the CDC crossings are reported as multi-bits.

         Note:
         DFF synchronizer can be any DFF-style synchronizer as well as the standard 2DFF synchronizer.
         Crossing is reported for DFF-style synchronizers with at least one enable signal For example for
         a 2DFF synchronizer: DFF1 can have an enable signal, DFF2 can have an enable signal or both
         DFFs can have (possibly different) enable signals. All of these crossings prevent metastability
         propagation.

Examples

     1. The 2DFF synchronization of a data bus assumes the bus is gray-coded. Any data buses that
          cross clock domains that are not gray-coded should be identified as requiring complete data
          synchronization. Any of these crossings synchronized by 2DFF synchronizers should be flagged
          as violations. To set these schemes to violations, use the cdc report directives. Following is an
          example to turn severity to violation:

            cdc report scheme bus_dff_sync_with_enable -severity violation

     2. Following is an example to turn off promotion:

            cdc promote scheme bus_dff_sync_with_enable -promotion off

     3. Example of promoted transfer protocol checker for the bus_dff_sync_with_enable synchronization
          scheme (in cdc_protocol.rpt):

bus_four_latch                                                                                        

bus_four_latch

Multiple-bit signal synchronized by latch synchronizer. Default Severity: evaluation.
Crossing: multiple-bit data bus; Promotion: cdc_hamming_one (default on) and data_stability (default
off); FX: no.

     Tip
     : To promote cdc_hamming_one checkers with this check turned on, specify cdc preference
     -sample_data_stability.

Synchronization using four latches is a standard method of synchronizing a gray-coded data bus. Here,
the latch enables are of alternating polarity.
Gray coding (that is, hamming distance 1) assures that only one bit of data changes in any cycle, so a
four-latch synchronizer (typically used for 1-bit signal crossings) is appropriate if the data changes only at
the frequency of the receiving domain.

bus_port_sync                                                                                                      

bus_port_sync

Multi-bit signal synchronized outside primary output port. Default Severity: evaluation.
Crossing: multiple-bit data bus; Promotion: cdc_hamming_one (default on); FX: no.

If a primary output port of the current design drives external logic in a different clock domain, the design
environment must synchronize the signal from the output port to the driven logic. Typically this is done
by adding a synchronizer outside the design. However, CDC analysis cannot detect this external
synchronizer from information for the current design. To notify CDC analysis that a primary output port is
"externally synchronized" specify the external_sync option of the cdc port attribute command.
For example, the following command specifies that primary port a_to_clk2_sync drives a synchronizer
outside the current design:

   cdc port attribute a_to_clk2_sync -external_sync

If a primary port has the -external_sync attribute, CDC analysis checks to ensure the port is registered--
that is, whether or not the driver of the port (inside the current design) is a register (or latch). A registered
multiple-bit port is reported as a bus_port_sync crossing.

Examples

     1. The following is an example to turn severity to caution:

            cdc report scheme bus_port_sync ­severity caution

     2. The following example shows a multiple-bit primary output port with the external sync attribute.
          Here, the port is registered, so the logic is reported as a bus_port_sync crossing.

          Design:

460            Questa® CDC User Guide
                        Reference

                        bus_port_sync

   module dut (
      input [3:0] in, clk,
      output logic [3:0] out);
      logic [3:0] r;
      always @(posedge clk) r <= in;
      assign out = r;

   endmodule

  Directives:

   netlist clock clk
   cdc port attribute out -external_sync
   Evaluations
   =================================================================
   Multiple-bit port synchronization. (bus_port_sync)
   -----------------------------------------------------------------
   clk : start : r (port_sync.v : 5)

              <na>: end : out (port_sync.v : 6) (ID:bus_port_sync_25032)

bus_sync_gray                                                                                    

bus_sync_gray

Multiple-bit signal synchronized by a DFF synchronizer with Tx specified as gray coded. Default
Severity: evaluation.
Crossing: multiple-bit data signal; Promotion: cdc_hamming (default on); FX: yes (default on).

Specify the Tx signal as gray coded using the directive cdc signal <Tx> -gray_coded. Synchronization
using two flip-flops is a standard method of synchronizing a gray-coded data bus. Gray coding
(hamming_distance_1) assures that only one-bit data changes in a cycle. This scheme allows flip-flops to
have an enable signal. Note that CDC analysis does not detect gray encoders and decoders.

Examples

     1. To turn severity to violation:

            cdc report scheme bus_sync_gray ­severity violation

     2. To turn off promotion:

            cdc promote scheme bus_sync_gray ­promotion off

Crossing: multi-bit signal; Promotion: cdc_hamming_one (default off); FX: yes (default off).
Reports the Valid DFF structures, for multi-bit crossings which satisfy the cdc syncmodule specification
constraint in case the syncmodule flow is on.

                                                                    bus_two_dff

bus_two_dff

Multiple-bit signal synchronized by DFF synchronizer. Default Severity: evaluation.
Crossing: multiple-bit data bus; Promotion: cdc_hamming_one (default on); FX: yes (default off).

Synchronization using two flip-flops is a standard method of synchronizing a gray-coded data bus. Gray
coding (that is, hamming distance 1) assures that only one bit of data changes in any cycle, so a 2DFF
synchronizer (typically used for 1-bit signal crossings) is appropriate if the data changes only at the
frequency of the receiving domain. Note that CDC analysis does not detect gray encoders and decoders.

         Tip
         : To promote cdc_hamming_one checkers with the data_stability check turned on, specify cdc
         preference -sample_data_stability.

Examples

     1. The following is an example to turn severity to violation:
            cdc report scheme bus_two_dff ­severity violation

  2. The following is an example to turn off promotion:
        cdc promote scheme bus_two_dff ­promotion off

  3. Example of a promoted transfer protocol checker for a bus_two_dff synchronization scheme (in
       cdc_protocol.rpt):

  Type/Scheme : cdc_hamming1 top.bus_two_dff_74733

  Check hamming                 : On <Default On>

  Check data stable             : Off <Default Off>

  TX SIGNAL                     : inst0.data_reg_d

  TX CLOCK                      : tx_clk

  TX_MIN                        :2

  4. A bus 2-DFF synchronizer:

Questa® CDC User Guide                                                                            465
Reference

bus_two_dff                                                                                    

           reg [width-1:0] tx_reg, rx_reg;
           reg [width-1:0] sync1, sync2;
           always @(posedge rx_clk) begin

               sync1 <= tx_reg; // 1st FF
               sync2 <= sync1; // 2nd FF
           end
           Evaluations
           =============================================================
           Multiple-bit signal synchronized by DFF synchronizer. (bus_two_dff)
           -----------------------------------------------------------------
           tx_clk : start : tx_reg (bus_two_dff.v : 11)

                        rx_clk : end : sync1 (bus_two_dff.v : 11)
                                          (ID:bus_two_dff_8942)

     5. A bus 2-DFF synchronizer with enable. CDC analysis only recognizes this instance as a
          bus_two_dff scheme if cdc preference -allow_enable_in_sync is specified.

     reg [width-1:0] tx_reg, rx_reg;
     reg [width-1:0] sync1, sync2;
     always @(posedge rx_clk)

        if (enable) begin
            sync1 <= tx_reg; // 1st FF
            sync2 <= sync1; // 2nd FF

        end
     Evaluations
     =============================================================
     Multiple-bit signal synchronized by DFF synchronizer. (bus_two_dff)

              rx_clk : end : sync1 (bus_two_dff_en.v : 11)
                              (ID:bus_two_dff_8942)

Potential Problem

The 2DFF synchronization of a data bus assumes the bus is gray-coded. Any data buses that cross clock
domains that are not gray-coded should be identified as requiring complete data synchronization. Any

466          Questa® CDC User Guide
                                                             Reference

                                                             bus_two_dff

of these crossings synchronized by 2DFF synchronizers should be flagged as violations. To set these
schemes to violations, use the cdc report directives.

  cdc report item -severity violation -scheme bus_two_dff \
       -tx_clock clk_a

Notes

If you use a DFF synchronization scheme that has more than two flip-flops, then you can get CDC
analysis to recognize the scheme by specifying a cdc synchronizer directive.
For example, the following global CDC directive identifies 4 DFF synchronizers as valid "two_dff"
schemes for CDC paths from the tx_clk domain to the rx_clk domain:

   cdc synchronizer dff -level 4 -tx_clock tx_clk -rx_clock rx_clk

If you specify cdc synchronizer dff -level 4, the first three back-to-back flip-flops are not recognized as
bus_two_dff scheme. It recognizes four or more back-to-back flip-flops as bus_two_dff scheme.

bus_two_dff_phase

Multiple-bit signal synchronized by DFF synchronizer and multiple-bit signal synchronized by DFF of
opposite clock polarity. Default Severity: caution.

Crossing: multiple-bit data bus; Promotion: cdc_hamming_one (default on); FX: yes (default off).

Synchronization using two opposite polarity flip-flops reduces the time the signal takes to settle. When
using this synchronization scheme, be sure the MTBF is acceptable.
When used to synchronize a data bus, the bus should be gray-coded (that is, have hamming distance
1), which assures that only one bit of data changes in any cycle, and the data should change only at the
frequency of the receiving domain.

         Tip
         : To promote cdc_hamming_one checkers with the data_stability check turned on, specify cdc
         preference -sample_data_stability.

Examples

     1. The following is an example to turn severity to evaluation:

            cdc report scheme bus_two_dff_phase ­severity evaluation

          Rx clock:

     reg [width-1:0] tx_reg, rx_reg;
     reg [width-1:0] sync1, sync2;
     always @(negedge rx_clk)

        sync1 <= tx_reg; // 1st FF
     always @(posedge rx_clk)

        sync2 <= sync1; // 2nd FF

cdc_inferred_stable

Reports clock domain crossings where either transmitter (Tx) and/or receiver (Rx) are inferred stable
registers. Defaults: Off; Evaluation.

Description

A signal crosses clock domain boundaries between Tx and Rx registers in a CDC path. The crossing is
identified as cdc_inferred_stable when:

       · En pin is tied to constant 0.
Key characteristics:

Questa® CDC User Guide                                               469
Reference

       · Reports both Tx and Rx inferred stable cases.

       · Only considers enable pin tied to 1'b0.

       · Applies to data path crossings only.

          propagate through Rx in either cases.

clock_gate_sync

Synchronized Tx domain signal driving combinational logic controls receiving clock. Default Severity:
caution.
Crossing: synchronized control signal and data bus at clock pin; Promotion: cdc_clockgate_sync
(default on); FX: none.

The clock_gate_sync scheme ensures the following constraints:

       · A clock_gate_sync crossing has a clock gating signal transmitted from the Tx clock domain and
          synchronized to the Rx domain.

       · CDC analysis also performs a functional check of such structures to verify that the clock_gate
          signal controls the clock to reach the receiving logic.

     a. Latch gating with negative edge triggered latch.

                        clock_gate_sync

Sample DUT:

   module dut(input tx_clk, rx_clk, selin, din, rx_sig, rsta, rstb, output reg
     dout);

   reg tx_sel, sel, rx_sel, tx_data;
   always@(posedge tx_clk or negedge rsta) begin

      if(!rsta) tx_sel <= 1'b0;
      else tx_sel <= selin;
   end
   always@(posedge rx_clk or negedge rstb) begin
      if(!rstb) sel <= 1'b0;
      else sel <= tx_sel;
   end
   always@(posedge rx_clk or negedge rstb) begin
      if(!rstb) rx_sel <= 1'b0 ;
      else rx_sel <= sel;
   end
   // DATA
   always@(posedge tx_clk or negedge rsta) begin
      if(!rsta) tx_data <= 4'b0000;
      else tx_data <= din;
   end
   assign gated_clk = rx_sel & rx_clk;
   // OUT
   always@(posedge gated_clk or negedge rstb) begin
      if(!rstb) dout <= 4'b0000;
      else dout <= tx_data;
   end
   endmodule

clock_sync_enable

A crossing with clock_sync_enable scheme must satisfy functional checks that ensure that the enable

                                                                                     combo_logic

combo_logic

Combinational logic before synchronizer. Default Severity: violation.
Crossing: control signal or data bus; Promotion: cdc_glitch (default on); FX: yes (default on).

Static CDC analysis checks for combo logic in every CDC path that has a detected synchronizer.
Combinational logic in a synchronization path is a significant problem for synchronized signals, because
the data used to determine an acceptable failure rate on synchronization paths assumes a single
transition on a CDC signal during each clock period. But if combinational logic is placed on the path, then
this assumption is false because of glitch propagation. As a result, the error rate rises significantly. To
address this problem, you typically remove all combinational logic from the logic path.
If you cannot remove the combinational logic, try one of the following:

       · Add a Tx register just after the combo logic.

       · If the contributing signals are stable, identify them with cdc signal -stable directives.

       · If the combinational logic output is constant during normal operation, glitches cannot be
          generated. Specify the signal that feeds the combinational logic as a constant value using the
          netlist constant directive.

       · If the violation is not an issue--a transfer protocol might ensure only one contributing signal
          changes value at a time--waive the violation.

       · To enable combo logic for reconvergence, use the cdc preference reconvergence
          combo_as_recon_start Tcl directive.

In case of custom synchronizers, if the no_combo assumption specified on data port fails, the crossing is
reported as a combinational logic before synchronizer with base type CUSTOM.

Examples

     1. The following is an example to specify that the MUX select in the combinational logic feeding a
          CDC signal is constant 1'b1 (so the crossing can be checked for proper synchronization):

            netlist constant din 1'b1

  2. The following is an example to turn severity for the CDC signal en to caution:

        cdc report item -severity caution -scheme combo_logic \
              -from dut.U0.en

Questa® CDC User Guide                                                                           477
Reference

custom_sync                                                                                           

custom_sync

Single-bit signal synchronized by custom CDC synchronizer that satisfies its connection assumptions.
Default Severity: evaluation.

Crossing: control signal; Promotion: none (or cdc_sync/cdc_hamming_one if specified with cdc
protocol); FX: no.

Custom synchronizers are instances of modules declared as custom synchronizers using the cdc custom
sync and cdc custom sync data directives (see "Custom Synchronizers" on page 67). A cdc custom sync
data directive identifies the two end ports of each synchronization path through the synchronizer.

By default, the clock domain crossing for a data synchronization path is assumed to be external:
the crossing is just before the data synchronization path. However, if the crossing is internal to the
synchronizer (that is, the synchronizer has both Tx clock and Rx clock ports), the cdc custom sync
directive for the module (containing the crossing) must specify the -internal_crossing argument. The
internal_* schemes are reported for custom synchronizers with internal crossings.

The hier assume directives specify hierarchical CDC port connection assumptions. When the two end
ports of an external crossing custom synchronizer's data path are connected to signals in different
clock domains, the custom synchronizer is identified as either a (single-bit) custom_sync crossing or
a (multiple-bit) bus_custom_sync crossing--but only if the instantiation of the custom synchronizer
satisfies the custom synchronizer's port connection assumptions. If any connection assumption is
unsatisfied, the crossing is reported as a custom_sync_mismatch or bus_custom_sync_mismatch
violation. In case of no_combo assumption failure on data ports, the crossing is reported as a
combinational logic before synchronizer with base type CUSTOM and not as custom_sync_mismatch or
bus_custom_sync_mismatch.

Hierarchical information about the logic inside a custom synchronizer is specified with hier port domain,
hier clock, hier reset, hier stable, and hier constant directives. This information is used to detect crossings
and violations external to the custom synchronizer and to detect unsatisfied port connection assumptions.

Examples

     1. The following example defines the custom synchronizer module dff_sync as the type dff custom
          synchronizer. The synchronization path is from the in input port to the out output port. The two
          hier port domain directives guarantee the in and out ports are connected internally to signals in
          the same clock domain as the signal driving the clk port. The first hier port domain directive also
          guarantees the in input internally drives only a synchronizer to the clk domain. The second hier
          port domain directive guarantees the out output is driven by a synchronizer to the clk domain.

482          Questa® CDC User Guide
                        Reference

                        custom_sync

  cdc custom sync dff_sync -type dff
  cdc custom sync data -module dff_sync \

                -from in -to out;
  hier clock clk -module dff_sync
  hier port domain in -module dff_sync \

                -clock clk
  hier port domain out -module dff_sync \

                -clock clk
  hier assume port in -no_combo

                -module dff_sync
  Evaluations
  =============================================================
  Single-bit signal synchronized by Custom CDC Scheme:

                       dff(dff_sync)(custom_sync)
  -------------------------------------------------------------
  tx_clk : start : tx_sig (custom_sync.v : 21)

            rx_clk : end : S.in (custom_sync.v : 29) (ID:custom_sync_5359)

Potential Problems

     1. CDC analysis does not automatically promote a checker for this scheme. You can provide a
          transfer protocol checking scheme using the cdc protocol directive.

custom_sync_mismatch                                                                                          

custom_sync_mismatch

Single-bit signal synchronized by a custom CDC synchronizer that does not satisfy all of its connection
assumptions. Default Severity: violation.

Crossing: control signal; Promotion: none; FX: no.

Custom synchronizers are instances of modules declared as custom synchronizers using the cdc custom
sync and cdc custom sync data directives (see "Custom Synchronizers" on page 67). A cdc custom
sync data directive identifies the two end ports of each synchronization path through the synchronizer.
Typically, hierport domain directives (and other hier directives) indicate logic connectivity properties
guaranteed to be satisfied by the custom synchronizer internal logic.

The hier assume port directives can specify external port connection properties that must be satisfied
by the synchronizer placement. If a custom synchronizer instance for a 1-bit signal is connected so that
all of its connection assumptions are satisfied, the clock domain crossing is reported as a custom_sync
crossing. But, if any connection assumption for the synchronizer is not satisfied, the crossing is reported
as a custom_sync_mismatch violation.

If a custom synchronizer has a hier assume port -no_combo directive for a port driven by combinational
logic, then CDC analysis reports a combo_logic violation instead of a custom_sync_mismatch violation.

Examples

     1. The following example defines the custom synchronizer module dff_sync as the type dff custom
          synchronizer and specifies that input din must be driven by a register (-no_combo). Since din is
          actually connected to combinational logic, the connection assumption is not satisfied. The tx_clk/
          rx_clock crossing is reported as a custom_sync_mismatch violation.

custom_sync_with_crossing                                                                          

custom_sync_with_crossing

Single-bit signal synchronized by an internal crossing custom CDC synchronizer that satisfies its
connection assumptions. Default Severity: evaluation.

Crossing: control signal; Promotion: none; FX: no.

Custom synchronizers are instances of modules declared as custom synchronizers using the cdc custom
sync and cdc custom sync data directives (see "Custom Synchronizers" on page 67). A cdc custom
sync data directive identifies the two end ports of each synchronization path through the synchronizer.
Typically, hierport domain directives (and other hier directives) indicate logic connectivity properties
guaranteed to be satisfied by the custom synchronizer internal logic.

If the crossing is internal to the synchronizer (that is, the synchronizer has both Tx clock and Rx
clock ports), the cdc custom sync directive for the module (containing the crossing) must specify the
-internal_crossing argument.

When the two end ports of an internal crossing custom synchronizer's data path are connected
to signals in different clock domains, the custom synchronizer is identified as either a (single-bit)
custom_sync_with_crossing crossing or a (multiple-bit) bus_custom_sync_with_crossing crossing
--but only if the instantiation of the custom synchronizer satisfies the custom synchronizer's port
connection assumptions. If any connection assumption is unsatisfied, the crossing is reported as a
custom_sync_with_crossing_mismatch or bus_custom_sync_with_crossing_mismatch violation.

Examples

     1. The following example defines the custom synchronizer module idff_sync as the type idff custom
          synchronizer with an internal crossing. The synchronization path is from the din input port to
          the dout output port. The two hier port domain directives guarantee the din and dout ports are
          connected internally to signals in the same clock domain as the signal driving their respective
          clock ports. The second hier port domain directive guarantees the dout output is driven by a
          synchronizer to the rclk domain.

     cdc custom sync idff_sync -type idff
     cdc custom sync data -module idff_sync -from din -to dout \

              -internal_crossing
     hier clock tclk rclk -module idff_sync
     hier port domain din -module idff_sync -clock tclk
     hier port domain dout -module idff_sync -clock rclk

            rx_clk : end : S.din (int_custom_sync.v : 29)
                                      (ID:custom_sync_with_crossing_5359)

  2. The following example defines the custom synchronizer module dmux_sync as the type dmux2
       custom synchronizer with an internal crossing. The synchronization path is from the TXDATA
       input port to the RXDATA output port. The first hier port domain directive guarantees the TXSEL
       and TXDATA ports are connected internally to signals in the same clock domain as the signal
       driving TXCLK. The second hier port domain directive guarantees the RXDATA output is driven

        hier port domain RXDATA -module dmux2_sync -clock RXCLK

Potential Problems

     1. CDC analysis does not promote a checker for this scheme. You should implement a transfer
          protocol checking scheme using one or more checkers.

data_latch

Single-bit data latch signal across clock domain boundary. Default Severity: violation.
Crossing: 1-bit signal; Promotion: none; FX: no.

The data_latch violation is issued when a crossing from or to a latch is enabled by control logic (not by a
clock). See "Unclocked Latch Crossings" on page 95 for more information about this violation.

         Note:

dff_sync_combo_clk

Single-bit signal synchronized by DFF synchronizer clocked by signal with a combinational loop. Default
Severity: caution.
Crossing: 1-bit signal; Promotion: cdc_sync (default on); FX: yes (default on).

Synchronization using two flip-flops is a standard method of synchronizing a 1-bit signal. If the
synchronizer is clocked by a regular clock signal, the crossing is reported as a two_dff style crossing.
However, if the synchronizer is clocked by a signal with a combinational feedback loop, an asynchronous
condition might be possible. Single-bit DFF synchronization clocked by signals with combinational loops
are reported as dff_sync_combo_clk crossings.

         Note:
         DFF synchronizer can be any DFF-style synchronizer as well as the standard 2DFF synchronizer.

Examples

     1. The following is an example to turn severity to evaluation:
            cdc report item dff_sync_combo_clk ­severity evaluation

            cdc promote scheme dff_sync_combo_clk ­promotion off

     3. A single-bit signal with a 2DFF synchronizer clocked by a signal with a combinational loop:

  module dut (input clk1, clk2, rst, d, output reg q);
   reg r, s1;
   wire gclk2;
   assign gclk2 = !gclk2 ^ clk2;
   always @(posedge clk1) r <= d;
   always @(posedge gclk2 or posedge rst)
     if (rst) begin

dff_sync_with_enable

Single-bit signal synchronized by DFF synchronizer with enable port or ports. Default Severity:
evaluation.
Crossing: Single-bit control signal; Promotion: cdc_sync (default on); FX: yes (default off).

In this scheme, a 1-bit control signal is synchronized by two cascaded flip-flops that have enable ports.
Synchronization using two flip-flops is a standard method of synchronizing a 1-bit signal. When compared
to the two_dff scheme, this scheme has enable ports. Specifying cdc scheme on dff_sync_with_enable
enables the dff_sync_with_enable scheme. If the directive is not specified, the CDC crossings are
reported as no_sync.

         Note:
         DFF synchronizer can be any DFF-style synchronizer as well as the standard 2DFF synchronizer.
         Crossing is reported for DFF-style synchronizers with at least one enable signal For example for
         a 2DFF synchronizer: DFF1 can have an enable signal, DFF2 can have an enable signal or both
         DFFs can have (possibly different) enable signals. All of these crossings prevent metastability
         propagation.

Examples

     1. The following is an example to turn severity to violation:
            cdc report scheme dff_sync_with_enable -severity violation

  2. The following is an example to turn off promotion:
        cdc promote scheme dff_sync_with_enable -promotion off

  3. Example of promoted transfer protocol checker for the dff_sync_with_enable synchronization
       scheme (in cdc_protocol.rpt):

                        dmux

dmux

DMUX synchronization. Default Severity: caution.
Crossing: synchronized control signal and data bus; Promotion: cdc_dsel (default on); FX: yes (default
on).

Synchronization using a DMUX scheme is a standard method of synchronizing a data bus. The MUX
select signal can be synchronized by any of the following signal synchronizers: bus_dff_sync_gated_clk,
bus_four_latch, bus_two_dff, bus_two_dff_phase, or two_dff_phase, dff_sync_gated_clk, four_latch,
two_dff, pulse_sync, custom_sync, dff_sync_with_enable, and custom_sync_with_crossing. The physical
design of the MUX logic (that controls the path from the Tx register to the Rx registers) must not allow
glitches at the input to an Rx register when the Tx register changes value.

DMUX synchronization uses a synchronized enable-load signal to control the transfer of multibit values
from the Tx clock domain to the Rx clock domain. The receiving clock domain logic must not sample the
multibit signal until the synchronized enable passes through synchronization and arrives at the load input
of the receiving register. Data at the multi-bit Tx register is not expected to change for two receiving clock
cycles while the control signal is synchronized.

DMUX synchronization has several advantages over other multibit synchronization schemes:

       · CDC multibit signal does not require gray-coding.

       · CDC multibit signal does not require one synchronizer for each bit (i.e., n synchronizers for an n-
          bit bus).

       · Only one synchronizer is needed (i.e., for the enable signal).

Structurally, a DMUX crossing has an enable signal transmitted from the Tx clock doman and
synchronized to the Rx domain, that drives logic that causes the CDC multibit signal to be loaded in the
Rx clock domain. CDC analysis performs a functional check of such structures to verify that the enable
signal controls all possible data loads at the receiving logic. Those structures that pass the check are
reported as DMUX crossings. Those that do not pass are reported as partial_dmux crossings.

         Tip
         Use the cdc preference dmux directive to recognize CDC crossings as DMUX schemes where Tx
         or Rx signals are memories (but not black box memories).

Questa® CDC User Guide  499
Reference

dmux

     1. Turn severity to evaluation:
            cdc report scheme dmux -severity evaluation

     2. Turn off promotion:
           cdc promote crossing scheme dmux -promotion off

          cdc_protocol.rpt):

           RX CLOCK   : mac_clk_in

     4. 4-bit bus synchronized by a DMUX synchronizer:

      always @(posedge rx_clk)
         begin: DMUX
             reg s1, rx_sel;
             s1 <= tx_sel; // 1st DFF
             rx_sel <= s1; // 2nd DFF
             if (rx_sel)
                rx_data <= tx_data;
             else
                rx_data <= rx_data ^ 4'b1111;
         end

dmux_no_hold

DMUX no hold synchronization. Default Severity: caution.
Crossing: single-bit or multi-bit data signal; Promotion: cdc_dsel (default off); FX: yes (default off).

Synchronization using a DMUX No Hold scheme synchronizes a data bus. When compared with
the dmux scheme, in the dmux_no_hold scheme the Rx register does not contain the data holding
logic. The MUX select signal can be synchronized by any of the following signal synchronizers:

Specifying the cdc scheme on dmux_no_hold directive enables the dmux_no_hold scheme. If the
directive is not specified, the CDC crossings are reported as DMUX.

Use the cdc preference dmux directive to recognize CDC crossings as DMUX schemes where Tx or Rx
signals are memories (but not black box memories).

fanin_different_clks                                                                                       

fanin_different_clks

Fanin logic from multiple clock domains. Default Severity: violation.
Crossing: control signal or data bus; Promotion: cdc_glitch (default on); FX: yes (default on).

Fanin logic for the input to a synchronizer must be synchronized to a single transmit clock domain for
CDC analysis to properly identify the synchronization scheme. CDC analysis reports multiple fanin logic
from different clock schemes (one crossing for each path) if it finds two unsynchronized signals from two
or more different clock domains in the fanin logic of the input to a synchronizer.

In some cases, the signals from one domain are constant during normal operation. For example, the fanin
logic from one of the domains might consist of test MUXes or configuration logic. In some other cases,
signals from one domain are marked as stable. How these cases are handled depends on how many
signals are in the fanin of the crossing:

     · Two signals in the fanin of the crossing

      If one signal is stable, it is not an instance of a fanin_different_clks or combo_logic scheme.

     · More than two signals in the fanin of the crossing
        If one signal is stable:

      If the remaining signals start from the same domain, the crossing is reported as an instance
        of a combo_logic scheme.

      If the remaining signals start from more than one domain, the crossing is reported as an
        instance of a fanin_different_clks scheme.

             The filtered crossing is an instance of a filtered combo_logic scheme.
To remove the fanin_different_clks violations for crossings to a single Rx node, do one of the following:

     · Keep one signal and use netlist constant to identify the remaining signals coming from that logic
        as constants. The removed signals do not appear in the CDC report.

     · Keep one signal and use cdc signal to identify the remaining signals coming from that logic as
        stable. If you specify cdc preference -filtered_report, the removed signals appear in the CDC
        report. The fanin_different_clks scheme is reported as the scheme detected for the remaining
        signal. When setting signals as stable:

504                                                        Questa® CDC User Guide
                                                                                              Reference

                        fanin_different_clks

             CDC analysis assumes fanin logic from a different clock domain is combo logic if the
                remaining signals are from the same domain.

             CDC analysis assumes a CDC signal has a valid synchronizer scheme if it is the only
                remaining signal after filtering the stable signals. The filtered signals are also reported using
                the scheme.

             Filtered stable signals are reported as instances of the combo_logic scheme whenever fanin
                is still detected after filtering them.

             Stable signals are reported in the CDC report if you specify cdc preference filtered_report.

       · Separately synchronize signals from each Tx clock domain into the Rx domain.

       · If the violation is not an issue--a transfer protocol might ensure only one contributing signal
          changes value at a time--waive the violation.

                                                                         fifo
fifo

FIFO synchronization. Default Severity: evaluation.
Crossing: data bus; Promotion: cdc_fifo (default: on). FX: no.

By default, memories with read and write clocks are reported as FIFO memories and FIFO-style
memories (see "FIFO Memory and FIFO Crossings" on page 61). Those FIFO-style crossings that pass
the criteria for FIFO memories are identified as belonging to the fifo_memory scheme. Specifying cdc
scheme on fifo directive turns on FIFO detection. Here, static CDC analysis determines whether or
not what was previously a fifo_memory scheme passes the criteria for being a crossing with true FIFO
synchronization.
FIFO synchronization passes data between clock domains without synchronizing the data. However, to
prevent FIFO overflow, transmit logic must know when the FIFO is full and to prevent FIFO underflow, the
receive logic must know when the FIFO is empty. In the FIFO synchronization scheme, the values of the
address pointers are synchronized to the clock domains of the opposite logic: the read address pointer is
synchronized to the transmit domain and the write address pointer is synchronized to the receive domain.
The templates CDC static analysis uses to detect FIFO schemes can be adjusted using the cdc
preference fifo directive.

         Tip
         : To promote cdc_hamming_one checkers with the data_stability check turned on, specify cdc
         preference -sample_data_stability.

Examples

     1. The following is an example to turn severity to caution:

            cdc scheme on fifo
            cdc report scheme fifo ­severity caution

     2. The following is a typical FIFO crossing.

fifo_empty_read                                                      

fifo_empty_read

Empty FIFO is read at the Rx register. Default Severity: violation.
Crossing: data bus; Promotion: cdc_fifo (default: on); FX: no.

Synchronizing CDC crossings using FIFO is a standard method. However, a structurally well-placed FIFO
is not enough to avoid metastability; it is also important to ensure that FIFO output is not sampled at the
receiving register when FIFO is empty.
If the output of a FIFO is directly read by the receiving register without the empty signal controlling the
output, the crossing is reported as an instance of the fifo_empty_read scheme. The scheme is detected
only for the FIFO-synchronized crossings.
To turn on detection of the fifo_empty_read scheme, use the -check_empty_read option with the cdc
preference fifo directive. To then specify the FIFO empty signal, use the cdc fifo directive with the -empty
option. Crossings that pass the functional check with the specified empty signal are reported as fifo.
Use the -ignore_empty option to bypass the check for empty FIFO for the crossings in which the FIFO
is already determined as empty. Crossings with the FIFOs specified with this option are also marked as
fifo. By default, if the fifo_empty_read preference is specified and neither of the options for cdc fifo is
specified, the analysis reports -fifo_empty_read violations for all crossings with empty FIFOs.

         Note:
         Enable signal must be in the Rx domain and must be scalar or single-bit vector.

Examples

     1. To turn on the scheme detection:

            cdc preference fifo -check_empty_read

     2. A FIFO-style synchronizer is reported as a fifo_empty_read crossing because the rd_data_1 is
          read by the receiving register without a control logic. Whereas, rd_data_2 is read with a logic
          controlled by the fifo_empty signal.

                                                               fifo_empty_read

  Directives
  netlist port domain wr_addr -clock wr_clk
  netlist port domain rd_addr -clock rd_clk
  cdc scheme on fifo
  cdc preference fifo -check_empty_read
  cdc fifo Mem -empty fifo_empty
  module fifo (

   input wr_clk , rd_clk ,
   input [7:0] wr_data ,
   input [2:0] wr_addr , rd_addr ,
   output fifo_empty, reg [7:0] rd_data1, rd_data2);

  reg [7:0] Mem [7:0];
  always @(posedge wr_clk) begin

   Mem [wr_addr]<= wr_data ;
  end

  reg [2:0] wr_addr_ff, wr_addr_ff2, rd_addr_ff, rd_addr_ff2;
  always @(posedge rd_clk) begin

   wr_addr_ff <= wr_addr;
   wr_addr_ff2 <= wr_addr_ff;
  end

  always @(posedge wr_clk) begin
  rd_addr_ff <= rd_addr;
  rd_addr_ff2 <= rd_addr_ff;
  end

  assign fifo_empty = (wr_addr_ff2 == rd_addr) ? 1'b1 : 1'b0;

  wire [7:0] fifo_output, fifo_output_gated;

  assign fifo_output    = Mem [rd_addr];

  assign fifo_output_gated = Mem[rd_addr] & {8{~fifo_empty}};

  always @(posedge rd_clk) begin

  rd_data1 <= fifo_output;

  rd_data2 <= fifo_output_gated;

  end

  endmodule

                                                         fifo_memory
fifo_memory

FIFO memory synchronization. Default Severity: caution.
Crossing: data bus; Promotion: none; FX: no.

By default, memories with read and write clocks are reported as FIFO memories and FIFO-style
memories (see "FIFO Memory and FIFO Crossings" on page 61). Those FIFO-style crossings that pass
the criteria for FIFO memories are identified as belonging to the fifo_memory scheme:

     1. The crossing involves a memory or a register file.

     2. Memory is in the same clock domain as the write data signal to the memory.

     3. The write address pointer must be in the same clock domain as the memory write address
          input. Similarly, the read address pointer must be in the same clock domain as the memory read
          address input.

Examples

     1. Turn severity to evaluation:

            cdc report scheme fifo_memory ­severity evaluation

     2. FIFO-style synchronizer reported as a fifo_memory crossing, because the clock domains of the
          address pointers are identified explicitly:

            netlist port domain wr_addr -clock wr_clk
            netlist port domain rd_addr -clock rd_clk

          No further FIFO detection is performed because cdc scheme on fifo is not specified.

Questa® CDC User Guide                                   515
Reference

fifo_memory                                                                       

     module dut(
        input wr_clk, rd_clk ,
        input [7:0] wr_data,
        input [2:0] wr_addr, rd_addr,
        output reg [7:0] rd_data,
        output reg full, empty);
        // Memory array is a FIFO
        reg [2:0] Mem [7:0];
        always @(posedge wr_clk) begin
            Mem[wr_addr] <= wr_data;
            full <=((wr_addr+1) == rd_addr) ? 1 : 0;
        end
        always @(posedge rd_clk) begin
            rd_data <= Mem[rd_addr];
            empty <= (rd_addr == wr_addr) ? 1 : 0;
        end

     endmodule

     =================================================================
     Single-bit signal does not have proper synchronizer. (no_sync)

     wr_clk : start : wr_addr (.../fifo_memory.v : 5)

                        fifo_memory_ptr_mismatch

fifo_memory_ptr_mismatch

FIFO-style memory with mismatching data/pointer clock domains. Default Severity: violation.
Crossing: data bus; Promotion: none; FX: no.

By default, memories with read and write clocks are reported as FIFO memories and FIFO-style
memories (see "FIFO Memory and FIFO Crossings" on page 61). A fifo_memory_ptr_mismatch scheme
is a FIFO-style memory crossing that fails the following criterion, so it cannot be a true FIFO memory
crossing (fifo_memory):

Write address pointer must be in the same clock domain as the memory write data input. Similarly, the
read address pointer must be in the same clock domain as the memory read data output.

The clock domains of the pointers and data mismatch (or cannot be detected). Check the clock domains
of the write and read address registers. The mismatching address driver is reported if it is a single source.
But if the mismatching address driver is made up of single-bit registers, they are not reported.

If needed, set the port domains (hier port domain) of the read and write data registers or black boxes.
Also, try increasing the fifo effort level with cdc preference fifo -effort.

Examples

     1. The following is an example to turn severity to caution:

            cdc report scheme fifo_memory_ptr_mismatch ­severity caution

     2. A FIFO-style synchronizer is reported as a fifo_memory_ptr_mismatch crossing because the port
          domains of wr_addr and rd_addr are not specified.

                                                                                  fifo_ptr_no_sync
fifo_ptr_no_sync

Synchronization of memory pointer input is missing. Default Severity: violation.
Crossing: data bus; Promotion: none; FX: no.

By default, memories with read and write clocks are reported as FIFO memories and FIFO-style
memories (see "FIFO Memory and FIFO Crossings" on page 61). Those FIFO-style crossings that pass
the criteria for FIFO memories are identified as belonging to the fifo_memory scheme.

Specifying cdc scheme on fifo turns on FIFO detection. Here, static CDC analysis determines whether
or not what was previously a fifo_memory scheme passes the criteria for being a crossing with true
FIFO synchronization. The fifo_ptr_no_sync scheme is a FIFO memory crossing that fails the following
criterion, so it cannot be a true FIFO crossing (fifo):

Write address pointer must synchronize in the Rx domain and the read address pointer must synchronize
in the Tx domain.

By default, FIFO detection looks up to two sequential levels from an address source to find its
synchronizer and reports a fifo_ptr_no_sync crossing if not found. If the synchronizers are further away
from their address sources, you can increase the address distance checked by specifying cdc preference
fifo -sync_effort with level medium or high.

You also can relax these requirements with the -no_write_sync and no_read_sync options to the cdc
preference fifo directive.

Examples

     1. Turn severity to caution:

            cdc scheme on fifo
            cdc report scheme fifo_ptr_no_sync ­severity caution

     2. FIFO detection is performed because the -fifo scheme is specified:

            cdc scheme on fifo

Questa® CDC User Guide                                                            519
Reference

                        forward_simple_dmux

forward_simple_dmux

Forward simple DMUX synchronization. Default Severity: caution.
Crossing: synchronized control signal and muxed data bus; Promotion: cdc_dsel (default off); FX: yes
(default on).

The forward simple DMUX scheme is a restricted version of the general DMUX scheme. For the general
scheme, the fanin logic of the Rx signal can contain any logic and the synchronized control signal can
use any logic to turn off the Tx signal (not just a MUX). The control signal can be synchronized by any of
the following signal synchronizers: two_dff_phase, dff_sync_gated_clk, four_latch, two_dff, pulse_sync,
dff_sync_with_enable, and custom.
The forward simple DMUX scheme has the following restrictions:

       · Logic between the first and second Rx signals has a MUX.

       · Second Rx output feeds back to the MUX input.

       · Tx signal drives the D-input of the Rx register.

       · Tx and Rx drivers are registers.

       · No combo logic is between the Tx register and the first Rx register.

       · No combo logic is between select output from the synchronizer and the MUX.

         Note:
         The physical design of the MUX logic (that controls the path from the Tx register to the Rx
         registers) must not allow glitches at the input to an Rx register when the Tx register changes
         value.

Use the cdc preference dmux directive to recognize CDC crossings as DMUX schemes where Tx or Rx
signals are memories (but not black box memories).

Questa® CDC User Guide  521
Reference

                                                                                     four_latch
four_latch

Single-bit signal synchronized by latch synchronizer. Default Severity: evaluation.
Crossing: control signal; Promotion: cdc_sync (default on); FX: no.

Synchronization using four latches is a standard method of synchronizing a 1-bit signal. Here, the
latch enables are of alternating polarity. The end Rx signal for the synchronizer is the first latch in the
synchronizer.

Examples

     1. The following is an example to turn severity to caution:

            cdc report scheme four_latch -severity caution

2. The following is an example to turn off promotion:
      cdc promote scheme four_latch -promotion off

3. Example of a promoted transfer protocol checker for the four_latch synchronization scheme (in
     cdc_protocol.rpt):

Type/Scheme : cdc_sync t16.four_latch_87631

Check data stable              : On <Default On>

TX SIGNAL                      : s3

TX CLOCK                       : clk1

TX_MIN                         :2

4. A four-latch synchronizer:

always @ (*)
   if (rx_clk) begin
       sync1 <= tx_sig;// 1st latch

                        functional_false_path

functional_false_path

False paths that are structurally connected but functionally unconnected. Default Severity: evaluation.
Crossing: single-bit or multi-bit data signal; Promotion: none; FX: no.

By default, Questa CDC filters out paths that are structurally connected but functionally unconnected,
and does not report the associated CDC crossings. To view all the filtered paths, enable the
functional_false_path scheme using the cdc scheme on functional_false_path directive. The tool reports
false CDC paths as the functional false path scheme.

Examples

     1. To turn the severity to violation:

            cdc report scheme functional_false_path -severity violation

     2. In the following example, no path connects u1.q to u4.q. If select is 1, the MUX in u4 passes D1
          instead of D0. If select is 0, MUX in Expr passes D0 instead of u1.q. So u1.q cannot drive u4.q
          functionally.

            module dut (input clk1, input clk2, input select, input in1, input
              in2, input in3, output out);
               dff u1 (clk1, in1, w1);
               dff u2 (clk2, in2, w2);
               assign w4 = select?w1:w2;
               dff u3 (clk2, in3, w3);
               dffs u4 (clk2, select, w3, w4, out);

            endmodule

            module dffs (input clk, input sel, input a, input d, output reg q);
               always @(posedge clk)
                   if (sel)
                       q <= a;
                   else
                       q <= d;

            endmodule

            module dff (input clk, input d, output reg q);
               always @(posedge clk)
                       q <= d;

            endmodule
